title: Cognitive tests of pattern separation as sleep-sensitive measures in middle-aged and older adults: An exploratory study
abstract: Sleep disturbances are considered both a dementia risk factor and symptom. The present research aimed to identify cognitive tests sensitive to objective sleep quantity or quality, focusing on tests designed to evaluate the earliest cognitive changes in dementia. We recruited adults who were 50 years or older and remotely monitored their sleep patterns for 7 consecutive days using wrist actigraphy and sleep diaries. On day 7, participants completed different cognitive tests; the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), the Prodromal Alzheimers and Mild Cognitive Impairment battery from the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), the Mnemonic Similarity Task (MST), taxing pattern separation, and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The final sample included 34 participants (mean age: 65.56, SD: 9.57). There were significant correlations between objective sleep quantity and PVT and MST performance. MoCA scores were correlated with performance on CANTAB and MST. Objective sleep quantity predicted MST performance when controlling for age, sex, and education. Tests of pattern separation are sensitive to objective sleep quantity and early cognitive changes associated with dementia. The sensitivity of pattern separation tests to sleep should be evaluated in a larger study, aiming to identify suitable clinical trial outcome measures for sleep-promoting treatments in older adults.

title: Neuroelectrophysiological correlates of extended cessation of consciousness in advanced meditators: A multimodal EEG and MEG study
abstract: In some contemplative traditions, 'extended cessation' (EC) refers to a state of advanced meditation in which the meditator self-reports intentionally suppressing their own consciousness and re-emerging with a profound sense of clarity and equanimity. Here, we present the first electrophysiological study of EC, in which five meditators underwent concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) recording. EC significantly increased high-frequency global coherence in all five of the participants, yet it did not consistently affect Lempel-Ziv complexity or power across participants. Our results provide preliminary evidence that the neural signatures of EC may be distinct from other states that are characterized by a loss of consciousness, including deep sleep and anesthesia. EC may not be simply 'switching off' consciousness but rather reorganizing the neural dynamics that underlie consciousness.

title: Source-Decomposed Multimodal Graph Connectivity: A Temporal Mixture-Manifold Pipeline for Tracking Ischemic Injury and Treatment
abstract: To capture the complex, dynamic network reorganization following acute focal brain injuries that standard static or unimodal neuroimaging frameworks routinely miss, we present an open, reproducible computational multimodal pipeline that integrates resting state functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) into dynamic, source-decomposed graph networks. This framework preserves sub-voxel, multi-peak distributional dynamics over time by modeling regional blood-oxygen-level-dependent signals within sliding windows using a Gaussian mixture model, with model complexity dynamically optimized. The resulting pairwise similarities define time-varying edge weights across local, nonlocal, and DTI-supported structural sources, unifying them into a multimodal connectivity manifold that precisely quantifies node strength, topological turnover, and boundary modifications. Applied to a non-human primate model of photothrombotic ischemia, the methodology revealed severe post-injury disruptions, with 66 of 144 nodes (45.8%) fundamentally altering their connectivity across localized sources. Furthermore, coupling this architecture with an Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) allowed for the continuous tracking of a tissue reversibility coordinate, yielding earlier detection of metabolic state collapse than uni-modal baselines and generating a forecast-divergence index as a rigorous early-warning signal. Extended across post-injury treatment boundaries to evaluate network recovery toward baseline, this interpretable, modality-aware framework establishes a standardized, shareable methodological foundation for tracking complex pathophysiological dynamics in neuroinformatics research.

title: NeuroMark dFNC: Transferable Dynamic-State Templates for Subject-Specific and Frequency-Resolved Chronnectomics
abstract: Dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) commonly identifies recurring connectivity states from resting-state fMRI, but states derived independently in each dataset lack guaranteed correspondence across studies and cannot be directly estimated in new participants. We introduce NeuroMark dFNC, which extends the NeuroMark principle of prior-guided network estimation to dynamic connectivity by using reproducible reference states as priors for estimating corresponding subject-specific states. Reference-state templates were derived from UK Biobank using windowed functional network connectivity and time-frequency moments (TFMs), with split-sample reproducibility evaluated for k-means, independent component analysis (ICA), and principal component analysis (PCA) template-generation approaches. Constrained ICA then used the templates to estimate subject-specific state patterns and continuous loadings in independent FBIRN schizophrenia and ADNI Alzheimer's disease cohorts. ICA loadings were calibrated by their contribution to reconstruction of the original feature matrix. Fractional occupancy and conditional mean dwell time were calculated from the state with the largest absolute calibrated loading at each observation. The predefined templates avoided the need for dataset-specific state discovery and post-hoc state matching. In both clinical cohorts, the analysis identified state-dependent, distributed edgewise differences and differences in selected temporal summaries. Nominal frequency-resolved findings varied across states and moment-frequency bins and were treated as exploratory. NeuroMark dFNC provides a common state space for cross-cohort comparison while retaining subject-specific connectivity patterns and continuous state expression.

title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading
abstract: Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388-800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group x task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229-334 ms and 377-538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618-723 ms interval, and a group x task interaction in the 562-636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508-629 ms and 660-800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

title: Brain-thought states during movie-watching reflect shared sensory anchors and film- and person- specific processes in association cortex
abstract: Naturalistic paradigms such as movie-watching have transformed functional neuroimaging by capturing cognitive dynamics during rich, real-world experiences. A fundamental challenge, however, is determining whether the neural signatures identified during these experiences reflect general principles of cognition or the specific contexts in which they are measured. To address this question, we combined fMRI data from participants watching eight diverse films with continuous reports of ongoing thought. We found that the generalizability of brain-thought relationships depends on the cognitive process being recruited. Neural signatures linked to sensory processing remained robust across films, whereas those involving memory-related association networks depended on how we modelled between-film variability, indicating that cognition becomes increasingly context-dependent along the cortical hierarchy from sensory to association cortex. Within default and limbic networks, we identified two contrasting memory-related states with opposite consequences for comprehension. One, reflecting the integration of prior knowledge with ongoing experience, predicted better narrative comprehension and was revealed only after accounting for between-film variability. The other, associated with stimulus-independent thought, predicted poorer comprehension and emerged only when between-film variability was not modelled. Together, these findings establish when brain-experience relationships measured during naturalistic paradigms can generalize across contexts and when they instead reflect interactions between cognition and the specific environments in which cognition unfolds. More broadly, the consistency of a given brain-experiential association may depend less on where it occurs in the brain and more on the viewer's contextual experience: perceiving the film, drawing on memory to understand it, or drifting away.

title: Neural categorisation of rhythm in human newborns
abstract: Music is ubiquitous across cultures, and humans engage in social interactions through music from early in life. A cornerstone of these interactions is rhythm categorisation, allowing the sheer diversity of rhythmic inputs to be mapped onto internal rhythm categories. The pervasiveness of certain rhythm categories across cultures suggests that rhythm categorisation may be partially rooted in neurobiological predispositions constraining the internal representations of rhythm. However, this view appears to conflict with the diversity of music practices across cultures, which points to a role of experience in rhythm categorisation. To assess the relative contributions of neurobiological predispositions and experience, we tested 0- to 3-day-old newborns, capitalising on their minimal postnatal experience with music. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we recorded, in newborns and adults, brain responses to drum sounds whose pattern of relative interval duration ranged from isochronous to long-short rhythms (1:1 - 2:1 interval ratio). Results indicate significant categorisation in newborns's neural responses, with a representational structure that correlate with those of adults, yet with a greater degree of differentiation across rhythms. These findings reveal neurobiological predispositions enabling rhythm categorisation to be present at birth and further shaped across the lifespan, highlighting the evolutionary roots and plasticity supporting this human cultural practice.

title: Brainstem cholinergic cell loss causes slowly-developing motor impairments
abstract: Pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) cholinergic degeneration is a feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is difficult to isolate the symptoms and circuit alterations caused by cholinergic cell loss in PD, where multiple nuclei are simultaneously degenerating. Here we develop a novel mouse model of brainstem cholinergic cell loss to define the timeline of symptom development and map physiological adaptations within the brainstem. Mild motor symptoms, including balance and motor learning deficits reminiscent of early-stage PD, developed after cholinergic lesion with an unexpected long delay. Ex vivo whole-cell recordings showed that cholinergic cell loss increased excitatory synaptic drive onto glutamatergic PPN neurons and increased their intrinsic ability to generate sustained action potential output. In parallel, fiber photometry experiments revealed a slight increase in glutamatergic sensory responsiveness that closely tracked the delayed onset of behavioral symptoms. Together, these results reveal that brainstem cholinergic cell loss triggers the reorganization of motor-related brainstem circuits, providing critical insight into the consequences of non-dopaminergic degeneration in PD.

abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) plasma biomarkers are cost-effective tools to detect early stage amyloid pathology. We investigated how interactions between AD genetic risk (apolipoprotein E ( APOE ) ε4, AD polygenic risk score (excluding APOE; PRS AD )), age, and sex affected AD plasma biomarkers concentrations in a population-based cohort. We included 5913 participants from the Netherlands Twin Register age 30 – 80 (64.1% females, 29.8% ε4 carriers) and measured plasma phosphorylated-tau-217 (p-tau217), amyloid-β−42/40 (Aβ−42/40), neurofilament light (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). We showed that the PRS AD did not associate with biomarker concentrations over age. In ε4 carriers, decreases in Aβ−42/40 became steeper after age 50, and increases in p-tau217 and GFAP became steeper after age 55 and 60 compared to non-carriers, respectively. Analyses in a separate longitudinal cohort (EMIF-AD) confirmed that p-tau217 concentration changes in ε4 carriers reflect AD pathology. These results highlight the potential of plasma biomarkers, especially p-tau217, for early detection of preclinical AD pathology.

abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics with data-independent acquisition benefits from advanced instrumentation and computational analysis. Despite continued improvements, the quality of quantification may be poor for some measurements. As the scale of proteomic experiments increases, these poor-quality measurements are challenging to characterize by hand, yet they undermine the detection of differentially abundant proteins and the downstream biological conclusions. We introduce MSstats + , a computational workflow that takes as input not only peak intensities reported by tools such as Spectronaut or DIA-NN, but also quality metrics such as peak shape and retention time, and longitudinal run order profiles of these metrics. MSstats+ translates these metrics into a single measure of quality, and downweights poor quality measurements when detecting differentially abundant proteins. The method offers a natural treatment of missing values, weighting the imputed values according to the quality metrics in the run. We demonstrate the accuracy of the resulting differential analysis in five experiments: two custom benchmarking studies with intentionally induced anomalies, a controlled mixture of proteomes, and two large-scale clinical investigations. MSstats+ is implemented in the family of open-source R/Bioconductor packages MSstats.

abstract: Deciphering the highly coupled regulatory circuits that drive cellular dynamics remains a fundamental goal in biology. However, capturing the multi-scale time-lagged dynamics and combinatorial regulatory logic of gene regulation remains challenging. Here we present scMagnify, a deep-learning-based framework that leverages chromatin accessibility and gene expression via Granger causality to reconstruct and decompose multi-scale gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Diverse benchmarks demonstrate scMagnify’s favorable performance. scMagnify employs tensor decomposition to identify combinatorial TF modules and their activation profiles across multiple time-lags. We applied scMagnify to human hematopoiesis and mouse pancreas development, where it recovered known lineage-driving regulators and provided further insights into the combinatorial logic underlying cell fate decisions. Furthermore, in the context of kidney injury, scMagnify’s intercellular communication module mapped key signaling-to-transcription cascades linking microenvironment cues to pathological epithelial cell changes. In summary, scMagnify provides a robust computational framework for dissecting the multi-scale regulatory logic that governs complex biological processes in development and disease.

abstract: The reward positivity (RewP) is an event-related brain potential (ERP) component associated with feedback and goal completion. Although the component is said to be generated in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), this inference is disputed because of the inverse problem. Recent intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) current source density analyses provided direct evidence that the RewP is generated in caudal ACC, specifically Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’. To further test this hypothesis, we examined the effects of damage to frontal cortex damage on RewP amplitude. Scalp EEG was recorded from 68 stroke patients with frontal lesions while they performed a trial-and-error guessing task used to elicit a canonical RewP. Non-parametric voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping revealed that damage to Brodmann areas 24c’ and 32’ significantly attenuated RewP amplitude. These results align with evidence suggesting a single generator of the RewP in the caudal ACC, supporting the role of caudal ACC in motivation of extended behaviors.

abstract: Flow diverter (FD) implantation is standard for unruptured intracranial aneurysms (UIAs), but cerebrovascular complications persist. This nested study within a prospective multicenter cohort evaluates whether short-term, low-dose glucocorticoid use is associated with cerebrovascular outcomes after FD implantation. Propensity-score matching with exact matching on UIA location yielded 1327 patients (360 glucocorticoid-treated; 967 controls). Intravenous glucocorticoids, initiated within 2 hours of the FD procedure and administered for ≥2 days, were associated with fewer in-hospital cerebrovascular events (6.9% vs. 13.1%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.53) and major cerebrovascular events (4.7% vs. 12.4%; aOR, 0.37). Over a median 2-year follow-up, glucocorticoid use was also associated with fewer new-onset major cerebrovascular events (3.6% vs. 8.7%; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.41) and less in-stent stenosis (7.9% vs. 13.2%; aOR, 0.55). Findings remained robust in unmatched patients on sensitivity analyses. We demonstrate that perioperative glucocorticoid regimens may reduce cerebrovascular events and in-stent stenosis in FD-treated patients, warranting randomized trials.

title: Category-preferring patches in human orbitofrontal cortex
abstract: The human ventral occipitotemporal cortex (VOTC) contains multiple category-preferring areas, organized along posterior-to-anterior and medial-to-lateral axes. Whether this organization extends beyond the VOTC remains unclear. Using two millimeter-scale 7T fMRI datasets, we identified face- and color-preferring patches in the lateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) in most participants, and word-preferring patches in half, replicating across runs. As in the VOTC, OFC face and word patches lay lateral to color patches, and OFC patches were as selective as the most anterior VOTC patches. Perception and mental imagery evoked opposite activation gradients across patches, and distinct connectivity patterns, with OFC-anterior temporal coupling persisting during imagery. In congenital aphantasia, OFC selectivity and representational content were comparable to those of typical imagers, but OFC coupling with anterior temporal cortex was weaker. These results suggest OFC and VOTC category-preferring patches belong to shared, functionally connected networks engaged by both visual input and memory.

title: Retuning ventral hippocampal output improves social memory and reduces anxiety-related behavior in temporal lobe epilepsy
abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is associated with cognitive, social, and emotional comorbidities that persist between seizures and remain poorly addressed by seizure-focused treatment. We examined whether these interictal deficits reflect altered ventral CA1/subiculum (vCA1/Sub) output and whether shifting principal-cell excitability can improve behavior despite persistent pathology. In pilocarpine-treated mice, vCA1/Sub principal neurons were depolarized and showed altered recruitment, alveus/oriens stimulation produced diminished hyperpolarizing responses, and parvalbumin- and somatostatin-immunopositive cell densities were reduced in stratum oriens. Epileptic mice did not demonstrate social discrimination above chance despite retained social approach and social-odor preference and showed increased open-field center avoidance. Multiplexed chemogenetic inhibition of vCA1/Sub principal cells improved social discrimination and center exploration, whereas stronger inhibition did not reproduce the social-memory benefit. Within individual mice, discrimination was higher in predicted retuned than off-optimal states, and performance across inferred excitability states followed an inverted-U-like relationship. Anxiety-related and social improvements covaried across epileptic mice, consistent with shared dependence on vCA1/Sub circuit state. In a separate EEG cohort, moderate inhibition suppressed local hippocampal activity during the behavior-aligned interval without detectably reducing spontaneous seizures or early interictal spikes. These findings identify excessive vCA1/Sub output as a modifiable contributor to socio-affective dysfunction in TLE and show that retuning a disease-altered circuit can improve interictal behavior without acute seizure suppression.

title: A compressed code for memory discrimination
abstract: The ability to discriminate similar visual stimuli has been used as an important index of memory function. This ability is widely thought to be supported by expanding the dimensionality of relevant neural codes, such that neural representations for the similar stimuli are maximally distinct, or "separated." An alternative hypothesis is that discrimination is supported by lossy compression of visual inputs, efficiently coding sensory information by discarding seemingly irrelevant details. A benefit of compression, relative to expansion, is that it allows the individual to efficiently retain fewer essential dimensions underlying stimulus variation---a process linked to higher-order visual processing---without hindering discrimination. Under the compression hypothesis, memory discrimination is facilitated when more redundant information from similar stimuli can be discarded to emphasize distinct information. We test the compression versus expansion hypotheses by predicting performance on a memory discrimination task (combined n = 723). First, we train neural networks to compress perceptual and semantic factors of stimuli, and measure the lossiness of those representations using the mathematical framework underlying compression. Consistent with the compression hypothesis, we find that greater lossiness predicts the ease and performance of lure discrimination. We empirically confirm these predictions across image sets, four behavioral datasets, and alternative metrics of lossiness. Using representational similarity analysis and two task fMRI datasets (combined n = 91), we identify compressed representations in the higher-order visual stream inferotemporal cortex (IT) as well as hippocampal subregion dentate gyrus/CA3. Finally, we observe retrieval-related compression in biologically realistic neural network models of cortico-hippocampal pattern separation. These results suggest lossy compression may support memory discrimination.

title: Astrocytic Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay regulates calcium signaling to support synapse function and influence anxiety-like behavior
abstract: How astrocytes achieve their diverse roles in the brain at the molecular level is poorly understood. In this study, we leverage mouse models, electrophysiology, calcium imaging, behavioral assays, and bioinformatic approaches to demonstrate that astrocyte activity and astrocyte-mediated mouse behavior depends on the highly conserved and selective RNA turnover pathway-nonsense-mediated RNA decay (NMD). Conditional deletion of the core NMD gene, Upf2, in mature astrocytes leads to enhanced basal Ca2+ signaling coupled with synapse dysfunction and elevated anxiety-like behavior. Restoring basal Ca2+ signaling in NMD-deficient astrocytes shifted synaptic transmission and minimized anxiety-associated behavior. Molecular bioinformatic analysis identified specific NMD target transcripts in astrocytes as candidates influencing calcium signaling pathways and neuro-glia interactions that support brain function. Our study is the first to demonstrate specific roles for NMD in astrocytes.

title: Inter- and intra-individual trajectories of brain sex in different neuroendocrine profiles
abstract: Sex hormone fluctuations modulate structural and functional brain dynamics, yet little is known on how sex steroid levels map onto the expression of sex differences in the brain. Here, we trained machine learning models for brain sex classification based on magnetic resonance imaging regional volumes in cross-sectional data of N = 1090 individuals (50% females, age matched). Applied to densely sampled data of one male and two females in different hormonal states (naturally cycling, oral contraceptive user, pregnancy), we associated inter- and intra-individual fluctuations in brain sex with neuroendocrine profiles. We found lower variation in brain sex across scan sessions in the male compared to the female subjects. Oral contraceptive use was associated with a more female-like brain, while opposite brain sex trajectories emerged across menstrual cycle phases and pregnancy trimesters. Overall, our findings suggest that changes in brain sex capture hormone-related plasticity over time in densely sampled individuals.

title: Systematic comparison of color representations between humans and deep neural networks: towards predicting human color perception in a vast color space
abstract: The representational structure of human color perception across a vast color space remains incompletely understood. While classical studies measured numerous color pairs, these measurements compared only similar colors, and exploring the global relationships among thousands of colors has been infeasible due to the time costs of psychophysical experiments. Given these constraints, deep neural networks (DNNs) have attracted attention as a promising tool for providing proxies or predictions of human perception beyond psychophysical experiments. However, it remains unclear which DNNs possess embeddings that geometrically align with human color perception. Furthermore, it is unclear which learning paradigm enables DNNs to acquire a color representation that aligns with that of humans. Here, we systematically investigate which learning paradigm enables DNNs to produce a color representation that is structurally congruent with that of humans, with a focus on three types: self-supervised learning (SSL) that trains on images alone by image reconstruction, supervised learning (SL) that trains on images with category labels, and contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP) that trains on image-text pairs. We compared the embeddings of DNNs with the human similarity judgments of 93 colors using a rigorous unsupervised method, Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport (GWOT). Our results show that, while each learning paradigm acquires color representations that strongly align with human data at the fine-item level in early layers, only CLIP sustains such a representation at the output. Furthermore, when we leveraged a key advantage of DNNs and investigated the representational structure of 4096 colors, the early layers of each learning paradigm and the output of CLIP consistently converged on their own characteristic structures. These structures present plausible predictions for the large-scale human color representation. Our work demonstrates an approach for exploring unknown territories of human perception using computational models validated in a limited empirical space, and provides predictions for future large-scale psychophysical experiments.

title: The modular nature of long-association pathways in the human brain
abstract: Human brain functions are facilitated by large-scale networks, yet the organization of the long-range association pathways that form the wiring of these networks remains poorly understood. The advent of diffusion MRI (dMRI) tractography enabled, for the first time, the non-invasive mapping of these pathways, albeit at low resolutions. This contributed to a simplistic view of these pathways in the neuroimaging field, where they are conceptualized as monolithic entities, each linking a pair of distant cortical regions. This contrasts with classical anatomic tracer studies showing that each of these pathways is a network in itself, serving as a conduit for multiple fiber systems including short- and long-range projections. While higher-resolution dMRI and optical microscopy techniques for imaging the wiring of the human brain have emerged in recent years, our simplistic view of long association pathways from low-resolution tractography has not yet evolved. Here we present the first proof-of-principle study showing that, with these techniques, we can now replicate the modular nature of human brain pathways, as it has been known from tracer studies in animals. We demonstrate this on the most dorsal branch of the superior longitudinal fasciculus, the proposed backbone of the dorsal attention network. We show that the long-range, frontoparietal connections that we see with dMRI tractography at lower resolution (1.5 mm) are in fact composed of multiple, layered fiber systems of varying lengths that can be reconstructed with dMRI tractography at higher resolution (<750 m). We validate this result across species, modalities, and scales by combining in vivo and ex vivo diffusion MRI with anatomic tracing in macaque and polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography in human. These findings underline that advancing from macroscopic to mesoscopic imaging has the potential to transform our understanding of the wiring of the human brain, and allow the study of human brain networks in health and disease at a level of detail heretofore only possible in animal models.

title: A reinforcement learning framework for goal-directed stimulation of engineered neuronal networks
abstract: Systematically perturbing neuronal circuits under controlled conditions offers a promising route to understanding how they encode and process information, yet remains methodologically demanding. In vitro neuronal networks can be cultured on microelectrode arrays (MEAs) that allow stimulation and recording, and microfluidic patterning can constrain network topology to yield stable stimulation-evoked responses. Yet, the space of possible spatiotemporal stimulation patterns remains too large for exhaustive exploration. Additionally, the evoked responses depend on prior stimulation history. Here, we present an open-source framework that sustains closed-loop reinforcement-learning (RL) control of engineered neuronal networks, sending electrical stimuli to the MEA and evaluating the evoked responses to identify stimulation patterns that drive specific target activity motifs. We extend inkube, a low-cost, open-source electrophysiology system from off-the-shelf components, with closed-loop electrophysiology. This enables reliable delivery of stimulation at single-sample precision with millisecond-range round-trip times. It also allows independent RL agents to control multiple networks simultaneously. As a proof-of-principle application, we benchmarked different agents on the task of identifying stimulation patterns that maximise the length of clockwise-circular firing sequences. We first demonstrated that stimulation-evoked responses in engineered recurrent networks were stable and separable across the action space over hours of continuous operation. We characterised the dependency of responses on prior stimulation history, finding state dependence in a subset of stimulus pairs. The agents learned to improve reward during training with respect to random stimulation. Agents converged on non-trivial stimulation patterns that span the full action space rather than mirroring the target motif. All hardware designs and software are publicly available, providing an accessible platform for goal-directed functional characterisation of engineered neuronal networks at single-spike resolution.

title: Relating layer fMRI signals to acoustics and intracranial neuronal activity in the human auditory cortex in a naturalistic design
abstract: Naturalistic auditory perception engages feedforward and feedback dynamics across cortical depths, yet how these are organized in the human auditory cortex has been difficult to verify noninvasively. Here, we examine depth-dependent coupling between neuronal activity and fMRI during passive music listening. Depth-specific fMRI responses were modeled using neuronal oscillation envelopes elicited by the same naturalistic stimuli from a separate group of patients under intracranial EEG monitoring. From deep toward superficial depths, the relationship between oscillatory power and fMRI responses systematically changed: alpha/beta activity (8-30 Hz) was increasingly associated with negative fMRI responses, mapping top-down feedback, while gamma band (>30 Hz) oscillations showed increasingly positive associations. Relative to a purely acoustical fMRI baseline, broadband high-frequency activity (>70 Hz), a proxy for neuronal firing, showed the strongest coupling to BOLD signals at intermediate cortical depths receiving feedforward inputs from earlier auditory pathways. Our findings reveal a spectrolaminar organization of neurovascular coupling in the human auditory cortex.

title: Vigilance profiles at sleep onset in patients with difficulty initiating sleep, with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms
abstract: Study Objectives: Difficulty initiating sleep (DIS) is a core insomnia complaint, frequently associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms, yet its objective correlates remain elusive. Insomnia subtypes were merged into a single diagnosis in DSM-5 and ICSD-3 because their criteria lacked reliability, leaving open whether objective markers could help characterize insomnia heterogeneity. Conventional polysomnography (PSG) reduces the wake-sleep transition to a single 30-s epoch. We combined conventional and continuous EEG-based vigilance markers to characterize sleep onset in patients with and without a DIS complaint, and in patients with DIS with and without depressive or anxiety symptoms. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed PSG recordings from 2,952 sleep-clinic patients, grouped by the self-reported complaint of difficulty falling asleep (Insomnia Severity Index item 1 [≥] 2: DIS, n = 1,328; no DIS, n = 1,624). In unmedicated patients with DIS (n = 556), depressive (BDI-II [≥] 14) and anxiety (STAI-T [≥] 45) symptoms were assessed. Vigilance was quantified on 3-s epochs with an intrinsic Vigilance Score (iVS), a probability-of-wakefulness index calibrated on each participant's own scored night, alongside the theta/alpha ratio and micro-sleep detection, and on 30-s epochs with automated hypnodensities. Results: Patients with DIS showed a longer sleep latency and slightly higher vigilance markers during both wakefulness and sleep, whereas the duration of the SOP itself was only marginally different (median 11.5 min in both groups). Deep sleep also accumulated later across the night (hypnodensity). In wakefulness preceding sleep onset, higher vigilance coexisted with more frequent brief vigilance drops. Among patients with DIS, depressive symptoms were associated with a less wake-like sleep-onset period despite more severe insomnia complaints, a finding not explained by differences in wake amount and convergent with hypnodensity. Anxiety symptoms showed a similar but weaker, non-significant pattern. Conclusions: In patients complaining of difficulty initiating sleep, the delay lies mainly before the first sleep epoch: once it is reached, progression to consolidated sleep is only marginally delayed, although its vigilance content may differ. Continuous EEG markers detect such differences, which are not captured by sleep staging. The association of depressive symptoms with a less vigilant sleep onset, despite worse complaints, suggests that similar insomnia complaints may rest on partly different physiological substrates, and that continuous vigilance markers could help revisit insomnia heterogeneity.

title: Neural signatures of glioma progression using implanted neural interfaces
abstract: High-grade glioma is an incurable brain cancer with a median survival of approximately 14 months. Over the last 50 years, small improvements in patient outcomes have been overshadowed by significant progress in most other cancers. Yet, emerging research has revealed that neural circuits play an active and central role in driving glioma growth and proliferation, highlighting the nervous system as a promising avenue for both disease monitoring and therapeutic intervention. Here, we present a platform for chronically monitoring tumor progression using neural recordings in freely behaving mice with gliomas. Using this platform across multiple mouse strains and glioma models, we show that neural recordings can accurately track tumor progression in vivo. Cancer progression was consistently associated with elevated gamma-band neural activity in the tumor microenvironment across both adult glioblastoma (GBM) and pediatric diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) cancer models. Interestingly, lower frequency neural activity exhibited distinct, cell-line specific changes over time: GBM models exhibited decreases in low frequency neural activity whereas DIPG models exhibited increases over time. Finally, using machine learning models applied to chronic neural recordings from tumor-bearing mice treated with or without standard-of-care chemotherapy (temozolomide for GBM), we accurately predicted tumor burden as inferred through in vivo bioluminescence imaging. By fitting low-dimensional mathematical models to gamma-band neural trajectories, we could further predict individual tumor growth rates over a 5-week period with high accuracy. These results establish that pathological neural-tumor interactions can be harnessed to monitor glioma progression in vivo. Coupling this monitoring capability with therapeutic electrical stimulation in the same device could open up a new class of implantable, closed-loop neurotechnologies with the potential to transform glioma treatment.

title: Basal forebrain projections to the lateral habenula regulate ethanol and sucrose consumption
abstract: Background: The lateral habenula (LHb) receives afferent input from various basal forebrain (BF) regions known for their role in aversion-related behaviors, depression, and addiction. However, little is known about the role of this circuitry in ethanol consumption, including in the presence of aversive stimuli. Here, we assessed the role of BF input to the LHb in alcohol and sucrose consumption using a chemogenetic approach. Methods: Following long-term intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) or control conditions, male and female Long-Evans rats underwent surgery for the expression of designer receptors in BF-to-LHb projections. We then excited this pathway in rats with IAA history, or inhibited this pathway in rats with limited ethanol history, before testing consumption of ethanol and natural reward both in the presence and absence of quinine adulteration. Results: Long-term IAA elevated ethanol drinking in all rats, and enhanced ethanol preference with and without quinine adulteration in males. Chemogenetic activation of BF-to-LHb neurons in rats with IAA history produced different effects in males and females: excitation enhanced ethanol intake in females, but reduced ethanol preference in males, regardless of quinine adulteration. Activation also led to a relative insensitivity to quinine adulteration of sucrose when compared to controls, particularly in females. Chemogenetic inhibition in rats with limited ethanol history did not alter consumption of ethanol or sucrose, with or without quinine adulteration. Conclusions: Our results suggest a role for BF-to-LHb circuitry in ethanol drinking that may vary based on sex, and a potential role for this circuitry in the sensitivity to quinine when combined with natural reward.

title: Limitations of pupil diameter as a proxy for modes of locus coeruleus activity
abstract: The locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system plays multiple roles in higher brain function that are thought to depend on its mode of activation, which reflects relationships between baseline and evoked activation levels. These relationships are evident in both single-unit LC activity and proposed physiological proxies of LC-NE activity, such as pupil size. Here we used measurements in awake monkeys to show that the baseline-evoked relationships evident within these two different measures are unreliably coupled between them: baseline-evoked relationships of the pupil are not predictive of those in the LC, and vice versa. These results imply that pupil modulations, which can reflect LC-NE activity, should be used with caution to make inferences about "phasic" (moderate baseline, high evoked) and "tonic" (high baseline, low evoked) LC-NE activity modes that are thought to support different forms of information processing in the brain.

title: Nasal inhalations and exhalations evoke distinct prefrontal-cortex responses with constant latency
abstract: Neuronal activity synchronous to breathing is salient across the mammalian brain. These modulations are typically characterized as oscillating signals phase-locked to the ongoing breathing rhythm and treated as evidence for respiratory 'entrainment' of cortical and subcortical oscillations. Since activation of the olfactory circuitry has been identified as their preponderant source, we wondered whether respiratory brain signals could be better understood as sequences of evoked sensory potentials. To help distinguish between these scenarios, we set out to quantify the detailed alignment of prefrontal cortex local field potentials (LFPs) to the nasal airflow cycle across the natural repertoire of rat breathing. We found that, while LFP and breathing show salient synchrony for all breathing modes, the phase of their locking is a strict linear function of respiratory rate. We explain this by showing that LFPs align to nasal airflow with a constant time lag of 100 ms, irrespective of breathing rate. Segmenting by breathing cycles revealed that LFP peaks and fast-gamma bursts are time-locked to inhalations, while LFP troughs and slow-gamma activity time-lock to exhalations. Our results support the view that respiratory signals across the frontal brain of rodents are sensory potentials evoked by cyclic ortho- and retronasal airflow.

title: Dendritic turnover zones support switching between rules without expanding the cortical engram
abstract: Flexible behavior depends on frontal circuits that use experience to adjust subsequent decisions. Yet how synaptic connections in these circuits are structurally reorganized when new associations compete with established ones remains unclear. Here, we used a novel rule-switching behavioral paradigm, longitudinal spine imaging, and circuit modeling to investigate how dendrites accommodate changing associations. Inactivation of secondary motor cortex (M2) impaired rule switching but not learning or maintenance in control conditions. Switching increased spine turnover on apical tuft dendrites in M2, concentrating spine formation, elimination, and new-spine clustering within persistent dendritic turnover zones, with pre-existing spines lost early during adaptation. The model reproduced these dynamics and predicted preferential elimination of synapses encoding the prior rule. Preventing dendritic compartment reuse increased the neuronal population representing the rules. These findings suggest that persistent turnover zones support synaptic reorganization during behavioral updating, with reuse offering a potential economy in neuronal recruitment.

title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

title: Context Shapes Alpha-Band Electrophysiological Signatures Under Psilocybin
abstract: Background: Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic that provides a pharmacological tool for examining neural activity associated with altered states of consciousness. Existing studies report reduced power (4-30 Hz) in posterior regions and altered functional connectivity (FC) at rest, but have typically involved small samples and coarse anatomical parcellations. Additionally, perceptual engagement has been shown to attenuate psilocybin-related whole-brain FC changes. However, how naturalistic context modifies psilocybin's frequency-specific electrophysiological effects remains incompletely characterised. Methods: We analysed the largest psilocybin electroencephalography (EEG) dataset to date (n = 56), with matched baseline recordings acquired before psilocybin administration. EEG was recorded during movie viewing, eyes-closed rest, guided meditation, and music listening. Cortical source activity was estimated using minimum-norm estimation and analysed across six canonical frequency bands (1-80 Hz). Spectral power, alpha peak frequency (APF), and magnitude-squared coherence within and between seven functional networks were quantified. Psilocybin effects were assessed using permutation testing with FDR correction, and linear mixed-effects models separated the contributions of drug, context, and their interaction to alpha-band connectivity. Results: At rest, psilocybin decreased alpha (8-13 Hz) power, increased gamma-range power, and elevated APF. Alpha-band FC decreased within and between higher-order networks implicated in top-down control. Relative to eyes-closed rest, psilocybin-context interactions showed that structured sensory environments attenuated or reversed psilocybin-related alpha-band connectivity changes. Conclusions: These findings identify alpha-band activity as a key electrophysiological correlate of psilocybin-related changes in cortical communication. Structured sensory input reshapes psilocybin-related cortical dynamics, particularly alpha-band connectivity across large-scale cortical networks, with the strength and direction of this modulation differing by context.

title: Validation of a Commercially Available Non-Woven Fabric Electrode for Mouse Electroretinography
abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the performance and usability of a commercially available nonwoven fabric electrode as a cost-effective and user-friendly alternative to standard corneal contact lens electrodes for recording murine electroretinography (ERG). Methods: Full-field ERGs were recorded in the same individual mice using both the commercially available non-woven fabric electrode and a conventional contact lens electrode in a paired design. Key parameters evaluated included (1) baseline noise stability, (2) dark-adapted intensity-response curves (0.01-100 cd{middle dot}s{middle dot}m-2), (3) light-adapted intensity-response curves (3-100 cd{middle dot}s{middle dot}m-2), (4) 20 and 30 Hz flicker responses, (5) extended recordings targeting slow c-wave kinetics under dark-adapted conditions, and (6) inter-eye consistency via bilateral simultaneous recordings. Results: Eliminating the need for viscous lubricants, the non-woven fabric electrode simplified corneal placement, alignment, and re-application. It yielded a- and b-wave amplitudes and peak times comparable to those obtained with standard contact lens electrodes. Notably, during prolonged recordings, the non-woven fabric electrode yielded significantly larger c-wave amplitudes while maintaining equivalent baseline noise stability. Bilateral simultaneous recordings demonstrated high inter-eye correlation and low measurement variability between contralateral eyes. Conclusions: The non-woven fabric electrode provides high-quality, reproducible ERG recordings comparable to, and for c-waves superior to, standard corneal contact lens electrodes. This accessible method facilitates standardized data acquisition and enhances inter-laboratory reproducibility in murine ERG. Translational Relevance: By reducing financial and technical barriers, this non-woven fabric electrode offers an alternative to specialized recording setups, improving experimental throughput and efficiency in ophthalmic research.

title: Acute stress reorganizes pregenual cingulate and subthalamic coupling to approach-avoidance decisions in remitted depression
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is highly recurrent, and psychosocial stress is a central precipitant of relapses. Daily choices require weighing potential rewards against costs, a process disrupted in MDD that may contribute to relapse. Here, we tested whether a psychosocial stressor affects neural and computational mechanisms underlying approach-avoidance decision making in individuals with remitted MDD (rMDD, N=50) and healthy controls (N=74), prioritizing pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC) and subthalamic nucleus (STN) due to their roles in value integration and decision caution, respectively. Participants performed a dynamic approach-avoidance conflict task with fMRI before and after psychosocial stress. Hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion modeling evaluated whether stress modulated computational and neural mechanisms, with trial-wise pgACC and STN activity entered as neural regressors on evidence accumulation and decision threshold, respectively. Before stress, groups did not differ in any decision parameter, but pgACC activity contributed to evidence accumulation toward avoidance in controls only. After stress, rMDD showed larger increases than controls in the impact of both reward and aversiveness on accumulation toward approach and avoidance, respectively, predominantly for net-aversive offers. Furthermore, in rMDD, stress rendered both approach and avoidance decisions more sensitive to pgACC activity, and STN activity was more strongly coupled to the decision threshold than in controls. Finally, stress-induced increases in reward sensitivity in rMDD predicted one-year course of depressive symptoms. Thus, MDD remission is not characterized by a generalized blunting of decision-making, but by a latent circuit difference that acute stress reorganizes and predicts future symptoms.

title: Sequential Sampling as a Computational Principle of Episodic Memory
abstract: Visual perception unfolds through sequential eye movements, yet computational models of episodic memory typically assume that event representations already exist. Here, we propose that sequential gaze sampling does not simply supply memory with visual information, but contributes to the construction and organisation of episodic representations. We introduce a computational model in which successive fixations are integrated into an evolving internal representation, subsequently stored in associative memory and later retrieved through partial reinstatement of the original sampling trajectory. Within to-be-remembered elements, successive samples support progressive individuation; between elements, more frequent transitions strengthen relational binding. As sampling proceeds, internal representations become progressively lower-dimensional while retaining information about where samples were taken and when they occurred in the sequence. Sampling history also remains embedded in the resulting representation: changing the order of otherwise identical samples alters both the representation itself and element-specific retrieval. At retrieval, reinstating more of the original sampling trajectory improves access to specific elements, while competition is strongest when memories share both semantic category and sampling history. Finally, an exploratory generative readout shows that regions sampled during encoding are reconstructed more faithfully than unsampled regions. Together, these findings suggest that sequential sampling provides a candidate computational process through which episodic representations are constructed, shaping their subsequent storage and retrieval.

title: Hypothesis-Driven Identification of Neural Algorithms With Dynamical Structure-Preserving Manifolds.
abstract: Neuroscience aims to uncover the algorithms by which the brain builds and manipulates rich internal representations of objects, agents, and places. Existing reverse-engineering frameworks remain ineffective for identifying these algorithms. Here, we present Dynamical Structure-Preserving Manifolds (dSPMs)---a novel multilevel reverse-engineering framework that programs, without training, recurrent neural networks to enable hypothesis-driven identification of the brain's algorithms that generate symbolic, structure-preserving representations of the world around. We apply dSPM to identify an algorithm for physical scene prediction in the dorsomedial frontal cortex (DMFC) of macaques intercepting a ball on a Pong-like virtual gameboard. dSPM better explained DMFC than alternatives, made predictions confirmed in neural data, and revealed an algorithm of DMFC that we term 'manifold-based simulation': perceived initial conditions rapidly collapse neural activity onto a low-dimensional manifold whose geometry encodes a physics-based representation of the scene, supporting far-out predictions without traditional next-step simulation. dSPM supports effective exploration of the computational foundations of biological intelligence.

title: CortexDecoder: fMRI-to-image Reconstruction from Cortical Flatmaps
abstract: Recent advances in brain decoding work has shown the potential of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to learn mappings from neural representation to visual features. Here we present CortexDecoder, a brain decoding framework mapping fMRI flatmaps to images viewed by subjects. Flatmaps are neural responses projected onto cortical surfaces and then unfolded into 2D images. We demonstrate that (1) flatmaps preserve sufficient signal to achieve high performance in brain decoding; raw fMRI data has noisy signals and high-dimensionality which makes decoding a difficult task. (2) Reshaping raw fMRI data into flatmaps allows for clean patch-based tokenization. This allows us to harness state-of-the-art Vision Transformers to learn meaningful neural representations and preserve spatial encoding. To do this, we pass flatmap patches into a pretrained CortexMAE encoder to obtain brain tokens. A lightweight cross-attention bridge then learns to map these brain tokens to image features. Our cross-attention bridge is split into two modules; the semantic module for predicting CLIP embeddings and the lower-level module to generate low-level image reconstruction. Finally, a fine-tuned SDXL (Stable Diffusion XL) takes this low-level reconstruction image as the initial image. Conditioned by the CLIP semantic embedding, the SDXL produces the final reconstruction image. In single-subject evaluations, CortexDecoder achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art brain decoding methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of flatmap based neural representations for visual reconstruction.

title: Dissection of neuropsychiatric-relevant behavioral and structural phenotypes utilizing neuron type-specific ablation of the Bassoon gene in mice
abstract: Rare pathogenic mutations in the human BSN gene, which encodes the presynaptic cytomatrix protein Bassoon-a key organizer of the neurotransmitter release apparatus have been linked to neuropsychiatric conditions including schizophrenia. Here we began to dissect the potential contribution of Bsn deficiency in distinct populations of mouse (fore)brain neurons on behavioral and anatomical alterations resembling schizophrenia-like phenotypes. To this end, conditional knockout mice lacking Bassoon in subsets of inhibitory synapses (BsnDlx5/6cKO), in forebrain excitatory synapses (BsnEmx1cKO), or at dopaminergic release sites (BsnDATcKO) were generated. The mice were assessed using prepulse inhibition, a paradigm that models sensorimotor gating, which is often impaired in schizophrenia, and a fear/safety learning paradigm. Further, anxiety-related behaviors were evaluated and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed to assess anatomical brain alterations. Our data reveal synapse-specific effects of the Bassoon deficiency. Sensory gating deficits were observed in both BsnDlx5/6cKO and BsnEmx1cKO mice. BsnDlx5/6cKO mice further demonstrated impaired discrimination between conditioned fear and safety-a condition frequently observed in individuals with schizophrenia. By contrast, BsnDATcKO mice displayed enhanced discrimination between conditioned fear and safety. All mouse strains showed elevated anxiety-like behavior in the light/dark box. Structural MRI revealed increased brain volumes in BsnDlx5/6cKO and BsnEmx1cKO mice, with the most pronounced changes in the hippocampus and cortex. Previous studies have shown that BsnDlx5/6cKO mice display autistic-like behaviors, altered hippocampal network activity and epilepsy. Our findings support the notion that deficits in Bsn-mediated functions, particularly in interneurons, may contribute to the etiology of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions.

title: Depth-Dependent Alterations in Cerebral Blood and Tissue Oxygenation Associated with Tau in Alzheimer's Disease Models
abstract: Vascular dysfunction is an increasingly recognized feature of Alzheimer's disease, and inadequate oxygen delivery may contribute to neuronal death. However, how cerebral oxygenation relates to neuronal pathology remains unclear. Here, we used two-photon phosphorescence lifetime microscopy with Oxyphor2P to measure intravascular and tissue partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) at 0, 100 and 200 um cortical depth in awake rTg4510 and THY-Tau22 mice. Relative to WT, capillary and venular pO2 in rTg4510 mice were elevated at 6 months but reduced at 9 months, mainly in deeper layers, with increased oxygen extraction fraction. Suppressing the tau transgene with doxycycline for three months did not restore vascular pO2. THY-Tau22 mice, despite limited tangle pathology, showed even greater reductions in capillary pO2 at every depth. In 6-month-old rTg4510 mice, tissue pO2 trended lower than in WT, and the fraction of low pO2 values (< 18 mmHg) increased with depth, reaching 33% at 200 um versus 4% in WT. Labeling neurofibrillary tangles with the tau-binding dye HS84 revealed significantly lower tissue pO2 in tangle-positive areas at 100 and 200 um. Longitudinal imaging of 2,282 neurons showed that disappearing neurons were not located in relatively hypoxic tissue within an animal. Finally, ex vivo immunostaining revealed neuronal loss and increased astrogliosis in rTg4510 mice, with unchanged vascular architecture. These results indicate that tau disrupts cerebrovascular and tissue oxygenation in a depth- and age-dependent manner, and that neuronal loss is not explained by a neuron's local oxygen microenvironment but may reflect a global reduction in cortical oxygenation.

title: Oral Bacterial Translocation Promotes Lung Dysbiosis and Infection Risk after Spinal Cord Injury
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes systemic pathophysiology that extends beyond the injured spinal cord. Respiratory infections remain a leading cause of death after SCI and can impair neurological recovery, yet the microbial source of these infections remains poorly defined. This study defined the onset and origin of pulmonary dysbiosis after SCI by testing whether commensal bacteria move to the lung from the gut or oral cavity. In a murine model, bacterial culture, 16S rRNA sequencing and source-tracking analyses showed that SCI rapidly increased lung bacterial burden and shifted the pulmonary microbiome toward an oral-like community. Gut-associated bacteria did not measurably reach the lung through lymphatic or vascular routes. Systemic antibiotics commonly used to treat infection failed to reliably reduce post-SCI lung bacterial burden. In contrast, oral and lung-directed antibiotic delivery reduced bacteria linked to post-injury dysbiosis more effectively. These findings identify the oral cavity as a proximal source of lung dysbiosis after SCI, and support route-specific strategies to prevent respiratory infection after SCI.

title: Serotonergic psychedelics delay resting state neurovascular coupling dynamics
abstract: Psychedelics are increasingly explored as tools to investigate consciousness and cognition, and as potential treatments for mood disorders. While neuroimaging has been central to characterizing their mechanisms of action, the interpretation of these studies may be confounded by the neurovascular effects elicited by these drugs. Here, we investigated the modulation of resting state neurovascular coupling by the serotonergic psychedelics LSD and DMT. Applying a blind deconvolution algorithm to blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals, we found that both drugs increased the estimated hemodynamic delays in regions overlapping with the distribution of serotonin receptors implicated in psychedelic action and vascular regulation. Deconvolution enhanced the detection of psychedelic-induced changes in whole-brain functional connectivity, suggesting that vascular effects obscure connectivity changes instead of generating spurious results. Finally, a biophysical whole-brain model linked these effects to increased flow-dependent feedback and slower dissipation of the vasoactive drive. These findings underscore the need to account for vascular effects in future psychedelic neuroimaging studies.

title: A human model of the neurodevelopmental metabolic shift
abstract: The neurodevelopmental metabolic shift transitions the metabolic pathways used by neurons to generate energy in order to critically support survival, growth, and functional maturation. To better understand metabolic regulation during human neuronal development and to facilitate the study of early neurodevelopmental disorders impacting this time window, establishing a combination of effective human model systems will be required. We report that a streamlined strategy using the genetic induction of neuronal differentiation by NGN2 expression recapitulates hallmarks of metabolic reprogramming associated with neurodevelopment. The approach is refined to increase the uniformity of differentiation, allowing reproducible high-throughput assessments. We validate appropriate readouts of metabolic function, including gene expression, cellular respiration, and mitochondrial morphology, which can be combined to present a cohesive assessment of metabolic status and reliance on oxidative phosphorylation relative to glycolysis. Collectively, the strategy presented will enhance the ability of investigators to gather foundational and disease-related insights into regulatory mechanisms of the metabolic shift critical to successful neuronal differentiation.

title: Central platelet-rich plasma administration promotes weight loss in diet-induced obese mice
abstract: Aims: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) contains diverse bioactive factors, but its potential role in central regulation of energy balance remains unexplored. This study investigated whether central PRP administration alters metabolic homeostasis in diet-induced obese (DIO) mice and examined associated hypothalamic responses under obese and inflammatory conditions. Materials and Methods: PRP was administered intracerebroventricularly in mouse models of DIO and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced systemic inflammation. Body weight, food intake, energy metabolism, and adiposity were assessed alongside hypothalamic microglial morphology and transcriptomic profiling. Results: A single intracerebroventricular PRP injection reduced body weight in DIO mice, with the effect persisting throughout the 7-day observation period. PRP also decreased cumulative food intake, relative gonadal white adipose tissue weight, and fasting glucose, accompanied by increased energy expenditure, oxygen consumption, fat utilization, and physical activity. In both DIO and LPS-treated mice, PRP reduced IBA1-positive area per microglial cell in the arcuate nucleus without altering microglial number. Hypothalamic RNA sequencing revealed changes in immune and metabolic signaling, extracellular matrix organization, and growth-related pathways, suggesting a complex transcriptional response rather than uniform suppression of inflammation. Conclusions: A single central PRP administration induces sustained weight loss and favorable metabolic changes in DIO mice, accompanied by region-specific hypothalamic microglial and transcriptional responses. These findings identify central PRP as a potential modulator of energy balance and provide a basis for investigating its active components and underlying mechanisms.

title: Nonlinear sensory integration drives configural olfactory representations
abstract: Natural environments are composed of complex stimulus mixtures that can be perceived either as combinations of known components (elemental coding) or acquire entirely new qualities (configural coding). While configural representation is traditionally viewed as a high-order emergent property of cortical processing, the underlying circuit mechanisms remain elusive. Employing C. elegans, we demonstrate that the neural foundations of configural representation can be established already at the sensory periphery. For most mixtures, single neuron responses arise through linear integration of the individual components. However, for a subset of mixtures, a small number of sensory neurons exhibit strong nonlinear integration, including NAND/XOR-like logic-gates computations. These nonlinear integrations collectively generate configural population codes. We present a novel quantitative predictor of configural representation and demonstrate that mixtures classified as configural induce emergent synergistic attraction and may lead to violations of rational choice behavior. Together, our findings identify single-neuron nonlinearities as a mechanistic link between sensory circuit dynamics and complex perceptual and decision-making outcomes.

title: Fiber-Coupled Rotating Two-Photon Light-Sheet Microscopy for Physiological Vestibular Imaging in Larval Zebrafish
abstract: Physiological vestibular stimulation requires macroscopic rotation of the animal, making simultaneous high-resolution neural imaging technically demanding. Here we present a fiber-coupled rotating two-photon light-sheet microscope for physiological pitch-axis vestibular imaging in larval zebrafish. Two-photon excitation is attractive in this context because near-infrared excitation avoids visible-light contamination of the visual environment. Femtosecond pulses were delivered to the rotating microscope through a broadband hollow-core negative-curvature fiber previously characterized in static light-sheet configurations. The rotating instrument maintained the axial mechanical stability required for cellular-resolution imaging, with submicron mean axial displacement over the characterized angular range. Fiber performance under rotation was also stable: bend-induced transmission changes were small in the relevant curvature regime, and circular input polarization suppressed rotation-dependent polarization artefacts to below 1\% in the sample plane. The dominant rotation-sensitive optical limitation was not the fiber but perturbation of the thermal lens in the sample chamber. Reducing fluid motion along the excitation path suppressed this artefact and restored stable imaging during dynamic rotation. With this system, we recorded brain-wide vestibular responses during sinusoidal pitch stimulation and resolved anatomically organized cellular response patterns across the brain. These results establish rotating two-photon light-sheet microscopy as a practical solution for vestibular imaging in experiments that require physiological stimulation together with darkness or controlled visual conditions.

title: Perceived social value is more strongly linked to gossip decisions with age in adolescence
abstract: Gossip is central to social exchange, yet how adolescents select what to share and with whom remains unclear. Across two independent samples aged 10-18 years (behavioural, n = 98; fMRI, n = 101 scanned), adolescents read information about absent third parties, chose whether and with whom to share it, and reported their appraisals. Sharing frequency showed no detectable age association. Valuation-to-decision coupling strengthened with age for interest in both samples, with a smaller age interaction for usefulness. Adolescents selected close friends more often with age when sharing. During scenario reading, before participants reported their choices, BOLD responses in a left inferior frontal cluster tracked subsequent interest ratings more strongly with age (n = 92), also within regions engaged by a separate mental-state judgment task. Together, these findings link age in adolescence to stronger valuation-to-decision coupling for interest and a greater proportion of sharing directed to close friends.

title: Starting strong: A descending analgesic dosing scheme enhances pain relief compared to a conventional ascending dosing scheme
abstract: Managing pain while minimizing opioid-related harm remains a central clinical challenge. Enhancing drug-related placebo effects has been proposed as one strategy for reducing opioid consumption, yet current dosing guidelines which recommend starting analgesic treatment at a low dose and titrating upward may inadvertently generate negative treatment expectations, since initial drug encounters are often associated with minimal pain relief. This study tested whether the inverse approach of a descending dosing scheme that starts with a strong analgesic dose more effectively enhances placebo-related analgesia than the conventional ascending scheme. Eighty-two healthy participants underwent a heat pain paradigm involving a sham analgesic treatment delivered at three different efficacy levels (low, medium, high). Participants were randomly assigned to a descending (high-to-low) or ascending (low-to-high) treatment-history sequence before receiving an identical, medium-intensity treatment during a subsequent test phase. The descending group showed significantly greater pain relief during the test phase than the ascending group, despite receiving identical treatment. These findings suggest that initiating analgesic treatment with a high, effective dose can amplify placebo-related analgesia relative to conventional dosing schemes, offering a potential strategy for reducing cumulative opioid use without compromising pain relief.

title: Adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy enables correlative single-molecule imaging of endogenous proteins in native environments
abstract: Resolving molecular organization and dynamics in native environments remains challenging, as single-molecule imaging requires high sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution while preserving 3D cellular context. Here, we present ALPINE (Adaptive-optics Lattice light-sheet microscopy for endogenous Protein Imaging in Native Environments), a modular framework for quantitative single-molecule imaging into complex biological samples. ALPINE combines adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy, programmable PSF shaping and acquisition stabilization, an engineered cell-specific labelling toolkit for endogenous cell-surface proteins and analysis pipelines assigning molecular localizations and trajectories to 3D cellular compartments. Labelling endogenous AMPA receptors in intact brain tissue, we demonstrate aberration-corrected 3D single-molecule localization and nanoscale organization within neuronal compartments. Importantly, fast optical sectioning of lattice light-sheet illumination further enables 3D single-molecule tracking in live tissue and quantification of molecular dynamics within native cellular environment. Together, ALPINE provides a modular approach to investigate how endogenous molecules are organized and dynamically regulated in complex biological systems, with components adaptable to diverse biological questions and imaging modalities.

title: History of opioid use disorder correlates with altered neuroimmune signatures in the human dorsal root ganglia
abstract: Understanding mechanisms for the negative reinforcing effects of opioids are fundamental to improving patient care. Using human dorsal root ganglia (DRG) from donors with and without opioid use disorder (OUD), we set out to examine functional and molecular correlates of chronic opioid use. At a molecular level, we detected disrupted immune signatures throughout cells in the peripheral nervous system (PNS), spanning glial-neuroimmune interactions to changes in non-neuronal senescence. At the physiological level these changes are paired with sensitization of DRG sensory neurons. Our findings reveal a neuro-inflammatory state in the PNS of individuals with OUD. Targeting therapeutics towards these PNS-based mechanisms could be an approach to alleviating the negative reinforcing effects of opioids.

title: Neuronal avalanches in awake macaque V1 and V4
abstract: Neuronal avalanches are cascades of synchronised activity whose sizes follow power law. Analyses of avalanches shed light on cortical dynamics operating near a critical point. In awake monkeys, avalanches were found in motor and premotor cortex, where they are invariant to temporal binning, detection threshold and the number of electrodes employed. Whether awake primate early visual cortex, which receives strong structured afferent drive, shares these properties has not been tested. We analyzed a public 1,024-channel resting-state dataset from V1 and V4 of two macaques. In both animals avalanche sizes followed power laws over more than 10-fold range, the exponent scaled with bin width as alpha proportional to delta-t to the power beta (beta = -0.045 and -0.031), and the distributions ended at a cutoff proportional to the number of electrodes analysed. Raising the detection threshold from 1.5 to 4.5 standard deviations (SDs) removed over 99% of events but changed alpha by only 0.02-0.05 per SD, whereas randomly removing the same events destroyed the power law. Per-electrode shuffling abolished all heavy tails. Eye closure shifted alpha, beta and the branching ratio by less than predefined equivalence bounds, far below the reproducible differences between recording sites. Avalanche organisation therefore extends to awake early visual cortex.

title: Progressive neurodegeneration of the locus coeruleus drives rapid eye movement sleep fragmentation
abstract: Sleep disturbances are common early features of neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). AD progression is also characterized by early and substantial degeneration of the noradrenergic locus coeruleus (LC), beginning with tau pathology and progressing to major neuronal loss. Although LC degeneration and sleep disruption progress in parallel, whether LC degeneration causally contributes to sleep abnormalities, and which sleep changes are associated with this process, remain unresolved. Human studies are largely correlative, while existing rodent models poorly reproduce progressive LC degeneration. Here, we employed progressive Caspase-3 (Casp3)-mediated LC ablation, with longitudinal sleep and calcium fiber photometry to monitor LC activity across defined stages of degeneration in adult female DBH-Cre mice. Histological analysis demonstrated graded, time-dependent LC degeneration, yielding mild degeneration (~25% neuronal loss) by day 8 post Casp3 injection and moderate degeneration (~50% loss) by day 18. Relative to baseline and to control mice, LC degeneration led to REM sleep fragmentation, emerging already at the mild degeneration stage. By the moderate stage, total REM sleep during light hours had significantly increased, while EEG theta power during REM sleep progressively declined across all stages of degeneration. Degeneration also blunted state-dependent LC calcium activity, significantly reducing the contrast between wakefulness and REM signal. Together, these results establish Casp3-mediated ablation as a model of progressive LC neurodegeneration and identify REM fragmentation and blunted state-dependent LC activity as its early functional signatures, providing a platform for studying how degeneration of neuromodulatory systems shapes sleep in a neurodegenerative disease-like state.
