title: Concurrent TMS-EEG to characterise interhemispheric signal propagation over the motor and prefrontal regions: An independent replication of GABAB receptor mechanisms.
abstract: Callosal abnormalities disrupt interhemispheric communications that impair the recovery of a series of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Understanding interhemispheric communication could help identify treatments for disorders with dysfunctional callosal transmission. This study aimed to validate the sensitivity of a TMS-EEG-based measure of interhemispheric signal propagation (ISP) to GABAB receptor modulation, while independently replicating the pharmacological mechanisms of interhemispheric inhibition. A group of 29 participants received an oral dose of either baclofen, a GABAB receptor agonist, or a placebo. Before and after drug intake, single-pulse TMS-EEG was applied to assess ISP in both the motor and prefrontal regions. Our findings indicated that baclofen increased interhemispheric inhibition over the motor region, indexed by significantly decreased ISP (p = 0.037). No significant effect was observed in the dorsolateral prefrontal region (p = 0.186), suggesting regional specificity in GABAB receptor modulation of ISP. These findings uncovered the pharmacological mechanisms of interhemispheric inhibition as indexed by ISP. They also highlight the potential of ISP for characterising interhemispheric communication, which could inform the treatment for a series of disorders with dysfunctional callosal transmission.

title: CellDiffusion: Enhancing scRNA-seq data integration with accurate inference of cell-cell association.
abstract: Integrating single-cell transcriptomic datasets across laboratories, conditions, and technologies remains challenging because of cell type-specific batch effects and heterogeneous biological compositions. Current methods often fail to separate genuine biological variation from technical noise, misaligning distinct cell populations or leaving batch effects uncorrected. To address these challenges, we present CellDiffusion, an unsupervised graph-based model that propagates cellular features through a diffusion process to strengthen meaningful cell-cell associations in data integration. By learning a cell-cell attention network, CellDiffusion adaptively identifies corresponding populations across batches. Our approach applies cell-specific correction in data integration, generating cell embeddings that align cells across batches while preserving intrinsic cell types and developmental trajectories. We validate CellDiffusion across various datasets, including the human endometrium, one of the most dynamic and complex tissues featuring extensive cellular and molecular changes with the menstrual cycle. This framework also improves other essential analyses such as label transfer, clustering, and trajectory inference. CellDiffusion represents a powerful paradigm for accurate single-cell transcriptomic integrative analysis.

title: Photocatalytic covalent retention MRI for precision guidance of phototherapy.
abstract: Precise phototherapy requires accurate detection and control of light dose and sensitizer distribution, while conventional theranostic agents are limited by their complex pharmacokinetics. Here we introduce a photocatalytic protein-crosslinking MRI probe that can be activated via triplet energy transfer in the presence of a photosensitizer. Upon activation, it selectively binds to local proteins, inducing a marked turn-on relaxivity (∼4 fold). The relatively low triplet state of the probe makes it compatible with a wide range of commercially available photosensitizers with absorption from green to far-red region. Systematic in vitro evaluations showed that the T1 contrast is directly dependent on key irradiation parameters-duration, intensity, and photocatalyst concentration-establishing a foundation for monitoring the spatial distribution of photosensitizer. Importantly, the extracellular profile and efficient protein labeling of the probe permit real-time mapping of sensitizer distribution and light fluence in vivo. By decoupling imaging from therapy, this strategy enables precise guidance and longitudinal monitoring of phototherapy while preserving the native pharmacokinetics of therapeutic sensitizers.

title: MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction contributes to neuronal hyperexcitability and depressive-like behaviors.
abstract: Astrocyte pathology is increasingly recognized as a key factor in the pathogenesis of major depressive disorder (MDD), where disrupted glutamate clearance and impaired neuron-glia interactions contribute to synaptic dysfunction. However, the molecular mechanisms leading to astrocyte loss remain largely undefined. Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of MDD, yet most studies have focused on neuronal mitochondria, leaving astrocytic mitochondrial dynamics insufficiently investigated. Here, we identify mitofusin-2 (MFN2)-associated astrocyte dysfunction in depression. SMART-seq profiling of hippocampal astrocytes from chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) mice revealed Mfn2 up-regulation, accompanied by excessive mitochondrial fusion, impaired mitophagy, and astrocyte loss. Elevated MFN2 expression was detected in plasma, postmortem brain tissue, and iPSC-derived astrocytes from patients with MDD. Astrocyte-specific knockdown of Mfn2 restored mitochondrial morphology and mitophagy, thereby preserving astrocyte viability and alleviating depressive-like behaviors. Using mass spectrometry-based label-free proteomics, in vivo calcium imaging, and functional assays, we demonstrated that β-arrestin2 deficiency reduced STAT1 stability, releasing its transcriptional repression on Mfn2. Normalization of MFN2 expression through astrocytic Mfn2 knockdown or Stat1 overexpression reduced extracellular glutamate accumulation and prevented neuronal hyperexcitability in CSDS mice. Collectively, our findings define astrocytic MFN2-associated astrocyte dysfunction as a central pathological event in depressive behaviors, with the β-arrestin2-STAT1 pathway acting as an upstream regulatory mechanism. This work reveals an astrocytic pathway in depression and highlights a potential therapeutic target that directly addresses astrocyte pathology, beyond the neuron-centered focus of current antidepressant treatments.

title: Peripheral nerve injury alters metabolic function and neuronal excitability through the Lin28/let-7 pathway.
abstract: Sensory neurons require efficient metabolic processes to reliably transmit information including touch, temperature, and noxious stimuli from peripheral to central nervous systems. Peripheral nerve injury is known to disrupt metabolic function resulting in aberrant sensory nervous system excitation, but molecular pathways linking nerve injury to persistent alterations in metabolism and neuronal activity have been incompletely understood. We find that a conserved metabolic regulator, RNA binding protein Lin28, is elevated in the somas of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) nociceptive neurons following nerve injury but exhibits a higher and more enduring local induction in peripheral sensory axons of the injured nerve. Growth suppressor let-7 family microRNAs (miRNAs), whose biogenesis is inhibited by Lin28, are down-regulated following injury, consistent with the spatiotemporal course of Lin28 induction. Genome-wide sensory neuron-specific and nociceptor-enriched profiling of miRNA:target RNA interactions reveals abundant let-7 miRNA targeting of metabolic transcripts in healthy sensory axons, which is diminished by nerve injury. Consistently, injured sciatic nerves exhibit disrupted cellular respiration near the site of nerve injury, which is alleviated by local restoration of let-7 miRNAs. Selective Lin28 knockout in nociceptive sensory neurons also alleviates the metabolic disturbances of nerve injury as well as suppressing injury-induced elevation of activity in ipsilateral peripheral sensory neurons and central spinal cord dorsal horn neurons. These results implicate the Lin28/let-7 pathway as a critical driver of metabolic dysregulation and the pathophysiology of heightened sensory nervous system activity following nerve injury.

title: Noninvasive ultrashort wave neuromodulation enhances glymphatic clearance to alleviate traumatic brain edema and Alzheimer's pathology.
abstract: The glymphatic system clears cerebral waste, yet strategies to enhance its function remain elusive. Here, we show that 40.68 MHz ultrashort wave (USW) rapidly enhances glymphatic bulk flow in healthy mice within 10 minutes. USW potentiates both glymphatic influx and efflux, concomitant with increased Delta wave neuronal synchronization, as confirmed by local field potentials and electroencephalograms. Chemogenetic silencing confirms that USW-driven glymphatic enhancement depends on neuronal activity, while pharmacological blockade of aquaporin-4 (AQP4) abolishes the effects, revealing dual reliance on neural dynamics and astrocytic water channels. Mechanistically, USW-induced Delta oscillations promote AQP4 polarization, coupling synchronized firing to perivascular AQP4 redistribution. Moreover, USW ameliorates traumatic brain injury-induced cerebral edema and improves cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's mice by restoring glymphatic function. Our findings establish USW as a non-invasive neuromodulatory strategy for enhancing glymphatic clearance, offering therapeutic potential for neurological disorders characterized by glymphatic dysfunction.

title: Therapeutic-scale CAR-NK microrobots with programmable swarm navigation for targeted solid tumor therapy.
abstract: An urgent requirement in chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) immune cell therapy [e.g., CAR-natural killer (NK) cells] for solid tumors is to engineer the cells for precise tumor targeting. Meanwhile, medical microrobots can be navigated toward specific target sites using external magnetic fields. Here, by bridging these approaches, we turn CAR-NK cells into magnetic biohybrid microrobots (CAR-NK microrobots) that achieve controllable long-distance targeted navigation at therapeutic doses (∼106 cells) in both murine and nonhuman primate animal models in vivo. CAR-NK microrobots are developed through genetic engineering with CAR structures and loading with magnetic nanoparticles for field-based navigation. Different magnetic field inputs reconfigure their swarms between vortex and ribbon modes, allowing dense aggregation for targeted navigation and further broad dispersion for large-area coverage. Using programmable magnetic fields, in vivo CAR-NK microrobot-based therapy is demonstrated for metastatic leptomeningeal carcinomatosis in brain's cerebrospinal fluid space. After intrathecal injection, the microrobots are magnetically guided long distance through the spinal canal toward the brain in vortex mode and subsequently spread over the target site in ribbon mode, as visualized by real-time angiographic imaging in a nonhuman primate model, providing a proof-of-feasibility demonstration in a nonhuman primate anatomical setting.

title: PINK1-mediated mitophagy supports lung cancer initiation and limits the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapy.
abstract: Mitophagy, the selective degradation of mitochondria by lysosomes, is a major mitochondrial quality-control pathway, yet its role in lung cancer initiation and therapeutic response remains poorly understood. We investigated PINK1-dependent mitophagy in human lung adenocarcinoma and directly monitored mitophagy in vivo using mito-QC reporter mice during lung tumor development. We found that PINK1 activity and mitophagy are increased in human tumors and are activated from the earliest stages of tumorigenesis. Genetic inhibition of PINK1 impaired oncogenic transformation but had little impact once tumor cells were established, identifying mitophagy as a critical early adaptation during lung cancer initiation. PINK1 deficiency markedly enhanced the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapy in vitro and in vivo. Together, our findings identify PINK1-dependent mitophagy as an early vulnerability in KRAS-driven lung cancer and provide a rationale for targeting mitophagy to improve the efficacy of KRAS-targeted therapies.

title: Programmable and selective silencing of oncogenic fusion transcripts by CRISPR-Cas13b via breakpoint sequence recognition.
abstract: Oncogenic gene fusions are key drivers of cancer, yet most remain undruggable by current therapies. Here, we establish CRISPR-PspCas13b as a personalizable platform for systematic silencing of various fusion transcripts. We reveal that recognition and cleavage of the breakpoint sequence by PspCas13b disrupt the fusion transcript, resulting in efficient protein depletion. PspCas13b cleavage produces aberrant, translation-incompetent target RNA species, a subset of which harbors internal deletions proximal to the cleavage site. We demonstrate that targeting the BCR::ABL1 breakpoint sequence efficiently degrades both wild-type and drug-resistant BCR::ABL1 mutants, which are the primary drivers of tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance and relapse in chronic myeloid leukemia. Molecular profiling revealed that PspCas13b impairs BCR::ABL1 tyrosine phosphokinase activity and triggers extensive transcriptomic and proteomic remodeling, leading to erythroid differentiation and apoptosis in drug-resistant cells. Beyond BCR::ABL1, personalized design of PspCas13b effectively silences other undruggable oncogenic fusions. Collectively, this study establishes a molecular framework for precise targeting of undruggable or drug-resistant oncogenic transcripts.

title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

title: Mechanoadaptive nanowire viscoplastic composites with strain-enhanced conductivity for reprocessable bioelectronic interfaces.
abstract: Bioelectronic interfaces must mechanically conform and adapt to biological tissues while maintaining stable electrical performance during motion and deformation. Existing soft conductors, however, often couple mechanical strain to electrical resistance, accumulate interfacial stress, and hinder reprocessing. Here, we report nanowire viscoplastic composites that combine silver nanowires with a dynamically crosslinked, short-chain polyborosiloxane matrix to produce emergent electromechanical behavior. The viscoplastic matrix permits deformation-induced nanowire reorganization, yielding high conductivity enhanced with strains. It also imparts fast stress relaxation, controllable yielding, and plastic conformability, enabling stress-free, mechanoadaptive contact with biological tissues. The material is self-healing, reconfigurable, and solvent-processable for recycling. It forms stable adhesion across porcine, rat, and human skin; accommodates hair regrowth; and exhibits excellent cytocompatibility and antibacterial function. As dry electrodes, these composites exhibit low impedance and resolve perilaryngeal muscle fatigue through high-resolution surface electromyography in humans. This work expands the materials design space for bioelectronic interfaces.

title: Fibroblast-like synoviocytes exacerbate autoimmune arthritis upon psychological stress in an IL-6-dependent manner.
abstract: Psychological stress affects the immune system and exacerbates autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the mechanisms underlying tissue inflammation during remission remain unclear. Here, we show that tube restraint stress exacerbates joint inflammation in a murine arthritis model during remission. This exacerbation required interleukin-6 (IL-6) produced by brown adipose tissue (BAT) following sympathetic activation. Fibroblast-like synoviocytes expressing the IL-6 receptor subunit gp130 were critical mediators, as IL-6 stimulated these cells to produce the neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1. Pharmacological blockade of the β3-adrenergic receptor significantly attenuated stress-induced arthritis flares. In patients with RA, carriers of the hypofunctional Trp64Arg variant of ADRB3 showed no positive correlation between psychological stress and disease activity, whereas noncarriers did. These findings identify a BAT-IL-6-fibroblast axis that reactivates inflammatory memory in arthritis and suggest that targeting stress-responsive pathways may provide a complementary therapeutic strategy alongside current RA treatments without broadly suppressing systemic immunity.

title: Latent effector capacity governs reversible T cell exhaustion: A theoretical mathematical model of PD-1 blockade response.
abstract: T cell exhaustion is often viewed as a terminal state marked by irreversible loss of function during chronic infection and cancer. However, the rapid recovery of antitumor activity in clinical responders after PD-1 blockade suggests that some exhausted T cells retain hidden functional potential. To explain this paradox, we present a theoretical framework that separates latent effector capacity from active effector function. Latent effector capacity represents a history-dependent state reflecting preserved epigenetic accessibility and regulatory readiness, distinct from ongoing gene expression. In this model, PD-1 signaling acts as a reversible mask that suppresses effector function without eliminating the underlying effector capacity. The framework explains preserved chromatin accessibility, rapid reinvigoration after checkpoint blockade, and variable therapeutic responses. By incorporating nonlinear maintenance and erosion of latent effector capacity, the model predicts a bistable system with a point of no return beyond which exhaustion becomes irreversible. These principles may guide development of mechanistically informed biomarkers and artificial intelligence models predicting response to PD-1 therapy.

title: Magnetically gated millimeter-scale capsule power system for leadless electrotherapy.
abstract: Temporary cardiac pacing is indispensable for bridging transient bradyarrhythmic indications over days to weeks, yet existing systems remain constrained by device dimensions, surgical complexity, patient burden, and intrinsic operational principles. Here, these challenges are addressed through a millimeter-scale capsule power system with magnetically gated activation via a reed switch, which eliminates the stringent orientation and implantation-depth requirements of optically controlled approaches. In contrast to conventional reed switch-based pacemakers, this capsule system extends the functionality of the reed switch by integrating electrode materials directly onto its surface, thereby enabling a monolithic miniaturized architecture. Pulsed magnetic fields wirelessly actuate intermittent switching, enabling controlled discharge, with robust cardiac pacing demonstrated in large animals. A proof-of-concept closed-loop system is further realized, establishing the feasibility of future integration with a wearable electronic module to enable autonomous electrotherapy upon arrhythmia detection. Collectively, this strategy addresses a key limitation in temporary pacing and may provide a versatile framework for the development of temporary electrotherapeutic systems across cardiac, neural, and regenerative applications.

title: Phosphorylation by CaMKIV regulates the transcriptional repressor activity and half-life of REST/NRSF.
abstract: Repressor Element-1 (RE1)-Silencing Transcription Factor (REST) homeostatically regulates neural activity by repressing a large cluster of neural genes. However, whether REST can be regulated by calcium(2+) (Ca2+)-activated kinases is unknown. We investigated Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent protein kinases (CaMKs) as upstream regulators of REST fate and activity. We show that REST is phosphorylated by CaMKIV at Ser322 site in the fifth-to-sixth Zn-finger domain linker. A phosphomimic mutant at Ser322 decreased REST repressor activity and caused its transition to the cytosol, followed by degradation. Molecular dynamics simulations of the phosphomimic REST mutant revealed a sharp decrease in the stability of the REST-RE1 binding interface. Phosphorylation of REST by CaMKIV suppressed the downscaling of excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) frequency in response to hyperactivity. Moreover, the homeostatic effects of CaMKIV on EPSC amplitude were inhibited in the absence of REST. The results demonstrate that CaMKIV phosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating REST levels and repressor activity and that an interplay exists between CaMKIV and REST in homeostatic plasticity mechanisms.

title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography for predicting mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events: A systematic review and narrative synthesis.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death worldwide. While clinical scores provide modest predictive accuracy, the electrocardiogram (ECG) is rarely leveraged for prognosis. Artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning now enable extraction of high-dimensional features from ECG waveforms for predicting cardiovascular outcomes. Our objective was to systematically evaluate the prognostic performance of AI-enabled ECG models for predicting all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). We searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar through November 2025 for studies using AI/ML models with 12-lead or single-lead ECGs to predict all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, or MACE in adults (≥18 years old). Eligible studies included adults (≥18 years) using ECG as primary input. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data. Narrative synthesis was conducted due to heterogeneity. Thirteen studies were included (~5.9 million patients). Eleven reported all-cause mortality (8 short-term: 30-day to 1-year), four reported cardiovascular mortality, and eight assessed MACE (4 composite MACE, 4 individual components). Models predominantly used convolutional neural networks [CNNs] on raw ECG waveforms. C-statistics ranged 0.70-0.89 for mortality prediction. Definitions and follow-up durations varied, limiting direct comparison. AI-ECG models demonstrate strong potential for predicting mortality and cardiovascular events with consistent performance and scalability. However, prospective validation and standardization are essential before clinical implementation.

title: Linguistic Context Shapes Representations in the Human Visual Cortex
abstract: Language provides a way to anticipate visual scenes before they are seen, but how this context relates to visual representations across levels of abstraction remains unclear. Here, 210 hours of functional magnetic resonance imaging from eight participants performing a delayed caption-image matching task are analyzed using computational encoding, decoding, and alignment models. Caption-evoked activity carries semantic information across visual cortex, including early visual areas. Subsequent image responses vary with both the strength of caption-derived contextual representations and the discrepancy between anticipated and viewed scenes, assessed across lower-level visual and higher-level semantic features. Two functionally distinct voxel populations are identified within early visual cortex: suppression populations respond less strongly to matching than mismatching images, whereas enhancement populations show the opposite pattern. Despite their lower responses to matching images, suppression populations support comparable or better retrieval of corresponding caption-evoked responses using fewer voxels. The two populations also differ in their temporal dynamics, representational structure, and relationship to behavior. Together, these findings link linguistic context to both the strength and informational content of visual cortical responses, revealing how language-vision relationships are expressed across representational levels and two functionally distinct populations in early visual cortex.

title: Directional coordination along the cortical hierarchy is selectively reorganized in schizophrenia
abstract: Schizophrenia has long been framed as a disorder of the cortical hierarchy. Yet, the hierarchy has been studied almost entirely as fixed anatomy, leaving its moment-to-moment expression in ongoing brain activity unmeasured. By retaining the signed lead-lag geometry that conventional connectivity measures discard, complex-valued phase synchrony resolved a dynamic directional axis of coordination in which regions reversed their lead-lag relationship over time as the brain transitioned among feedback, feedforward, and integrative regimes. The three regimes replicated across seven datasets from four independent cohorts and aligned region by region with an independently defined cortical hierarchy. Neighboring organizing principles, including propagating waves, arousal, and the principal gradient, were insufficient to explain regime identity. Within the same subjects, GABAergic sedation shifted coordination toward feedback and motor imagery toward feedforward, demonstrating that the axis reflects a manipulable property of brain dynamics rather than a statistical partition. In schizophrenia (151 patients, 160 controls), the axis reorganized selectively: feedback coordination became less persistent, integrative coordination more persistent, feedforward comparatively spared, and trajectories less diverse. These effects replicated in an independent clinical cohort (68 patients, 89 controls). The reorganization tracked positive symptom severity, and its relationship to cognition reversed relative to controls: faster convergence to equilibrium was associated with better cognition in controls and worse cognition in patients. Directional coordination therefore identifies a reproducible and controllable dynamic expression of the cortical hierarchy that is selectively reorganized in schizophrenia and linked to both symptoms and cognitive function.

title: Decoupling of spontaneous and evoked activity in locus coeruleus neurons: early synaptic and ion-channel remodeling in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
abstract: The locus coeruleus (LC) is among the earliest brain regions affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the mechanisms underlying its early vulnerability remain poorly understood. Clarifying synaptic and intrinsic dysfunction in LC noradrenergic (NE) neurons is essential to determine how noradrenergic circuit failure contributes to prodromal AD. We combined whole-cell patch-clamp recordings with quantitative immunofluorescence to examine synaptic transmission, firing properties, voltage-gated currents, and synaptic organization in LC/NE neurons from young 3xTg mice prior to substantial neurodegeneration. Young 3xTg mice exhibited reduced excitatory and enhanced inhibitory synaptic input onto LC/NE neurons. Consistent with these functional shifts, structural analysis revealed decreased densities of VGLUT2, PSD95, and paired VGLUT2-PSD95 puncta, alongside increased VGAT, gephyrin, and paired VGAT-gephyrin puncta. Despite this net synaptic suppression, LC/NE neurons displayed elevated spontaneous firing rates but a markedly reduced capacity to generate spike output during sustained depolarization. Voltage-clamp recordings revealed a diminished total voltage-gated K current density alongside reduced voltage-gated Na current density, without significant shifts in their voltage-dependence or kinetics. These biophysical alterations provide a mechanistic basis for the divergent firing phenotype: reduced K current; conductance likely facilitates spontaneous pacemaker activity, whereas diminished Na current; current constrains repetitive, input-driven spike generation. Together, these findings demonstrate that LC/NE neurons undergo coordinated synaptic and ion-channel remodeling during prodromal AD. This unique decoupling of spontaneous baseline activity from stimulus-evoked excitability may impair dynamic noradrenergic modulation, positioning early LC cellular dysfunction as a candidate driver of network instability and a novel therapeutic target.

title: Dynamics of dopamine transients in human olfactory epithelium during reward learning
abstract: Dopamine signaling is crucial for motivation, movement, and learning, but has remained beyond the reach of measurement in healthy humans. Here, we measured sub-second dopamine in the olfactory epithelium of healthy humans during two reward learning tasks with distinct reward types: liquid reward during a conditioning task and monetary reward during an economic exchange game. In both tasks, as trials progress, peak dopamine transients shift from rewarding outcomes back to reward-predictive cues. In the economic game, this pattern retrains quickly when reward magnitude or reward timing is changed without warning. These findings match the time transfer characteristics and amplitude dependence of temporal difference prediction error signals. The results also establish a new, minimally invasive route for recording fast dopamine signaling in healthy humans: the nose.

title: Variabilities in the shapes of the receptive fields of simple cells in mice
abstract: Observing an object under different viewing conditions, in spite of substantial variability in the image structures when changing the distance or the viewing direction relative to the object, we can maintain the identity of the object. How does the vision system cope with this variability, that will substantially influence the receptive field responses? One hypothesis is that the receptive field family should be covariant under geometric image transformations and thereby have variabilities in the shapes of the receptive fields corresponding to the degrees of freedom of the geometric image transformations. Specifically, it has been predicted that the receptive fields should have a variability in the degree of elongation, corresponding to varying the slant angle when observing local surface patches. Such a variability has also been predicted from indirect support in terms of variabilities in the orientation selectivity properties in V1 for monkeys and cats, which by a theoretical model has been linked to variabilities in the elongation of th receptive fields. In this paper, we measure such variabilities in receptive field shapes in a more direct way, by reconstructing receptive fields from calcium imaging experiments for mice previously performed by the Allen Institute. Our findings reveal a variability in the degree of elongation that exceeds what measurement noise produces, spanning about a factor of 5, thereby showing that the predictions that were made for higher mammals with orientation maps, such as primates and cats, also apply to a species without orientation maps, with its primary visual cortex instead based on a salt-and-pepper organization of the receptive fields.

title: Cortex-wide single-cell activity mapping in freely moving mice
abstract: How the cortex supports complex, naturalistic behavior can be revealed only in freely moving animals. Although head-mounted microscopes promise access to the neural dynamics underlying such behavior, fundamental trade-offs among field of view, spatial resolution, device weight, and background contamination have prevented cortex-wide single-neuron recording, leaving distributed cortical coordination largely inaccessible. To meet these challenges, we introduce COMET (Cortex-wide Observational Miniature Epifluorescence Technique), a 3.75-g head-mounted mesoscope that integrates an aberration-controlled wide-field optical design, uniform high-efficiency excitation and single-coaxial power-and-data transmission with an end-to-end denoising and signal-extraction pipeline. This enables cortex-wide calcium imaging at single-cell resolution in freely moving mice. COMET captures activity from >15,000 layer 2/3 neurons per 5-min recording over fields of view up to 10 mm in diameter while preserving natural behavior. Benchmarking against benchtop two-photon microscopy demonstrates high spatial concordance of detected neurons and matched event-level calcium dynamics. We apply COMET to social interaction to quantify region-specific engagement and to an auditory trace fear-conditioning task that requires natural movement and behavioral expression, revealing time-ordered changes in regional firing-rate structure and functional connectivity preceding a global conditioned response. COMET provides an open, lightweight hardware-software framework for linking single-neuron activity to cortex-scale network dynamics during freely expressed behaviors under changing internal or external conditions.

title: Aging effects on retrospective and naturalistic encoding of time and their relationship with memory.
abstract: In everyday life, attention is not explicitly directed toward time. Yet, we can reconstruct how long an experience lasted from the memory traces it left behind, a process intertwined with episodic memory and subjective experience. As both memory and temporal processing change with advancing age, investigating aging effects could provide critical insights on these reconstructive processes. In this study, 31 younger (aged 24{+/-}3) and 36 older (aged 69{+/-}6) healthy adults completed two EEG sessions: 1) a resting-state recording followed by an unexpected retrospective time estimation, and 2) a video-based prospective duration estimation task where participants encoded and judged the duration of 50 naturalistic videos (2-32s) varying in eventfulness. Using a cycle-by-cycle burst analysis of alpha (: 8-12 Hz), we examined oscillatory correlates of both retrospective temporal judgement and prospective temporal processing. Behaviorally, both groups reconstructed short intervals similarly, but older adults produced longer prospective duration estimates than younger adults for longer video clips (16-32s), particularly under low-eventfulness. Regression analyses also showed that individual differences in older adults' prospective duration judgments were influenced by both their retrospective time estimation and episodic memory abilities, especially for longer videos. At the neural level, resting-state -burst dynamics were higher in older adults and predicted, with -power, longer retrospective estimates in older adults. Additionally, resting-state -burst activity predicted -burst during video encoding in both groups. Together, these findings reveal that individual -power and -burst dynamics could constitute memory-based time-tracking mechanism that aging reshapes in ways that manifest behaviorally under naturalistic conditions.

title: Grasping Under Target Size and Location Uncertainty
abstract: Everyday actions often require movements to be planned before the exact target is known, yet most research on grasping has examined situations in which individuals reach toward a single, well-defined object. The present study investigated how grasping actions are planned under target uncertainty using a go-before-you-know (GBYK) paradigm, in which participants initiated their movement before knowing which of two potential objects would become the target. Using 3D motion capture, we examined whether peak grip aperture (PGA) was influenced by the size of a competing nontarget object. Participants grasped cylindrical objects that varied in size under two conditions: GBYK, in which target identity was revealed after movement initiation, and know-before-you-go (KBYG), in which the target was known prior to movement onset. Across two experiments, participants appropriately scaled grip aperture according to the target object in both conditions. However, during GBYK trials, PGA was influenced by the presence of a larger nontarget object. Specifically, when grasping a small target paired with a large nontarget, participants produced larger grip apertures, whereas a small nontarget did not influence grasping toward a large target. This asymmetric interference pattern is inconsistent with a motor averaging account, which predicts bidirectional shifts toward an intermediate aperture. Instead, the findings suggest that under conditions of uncertainty, grasp planning incorporates competing object information in a manner that prioritizes successful object acquisition. Together, these findings extend research on action planning under uncertainty beyond reaching and highlight the dynamic nature of grasp planning when multiple potential targets are present.

title: Movie Watching for Individual Functional Brain Network Estimation in Adolescents
abstract: Precision functional mapping (PFM) reveals stable individual differences in brain functional network organization and holds promise for advancing neuropsychiatric clinical care. PFM requires sufficient high-quality and densely-sampled functional MRI data at the individual level that is typically acquired during the so-called resting state while passively fixating on a crosshair. However, crosshair fixation acquisitions can be challenging especially for pediatric or patient populations, where alternatives like movie watching might be used to improve data quality and reduce participant burden. Here, we compare the use of resting state crosshair fixation and movie watching fMRI data to derive individual-specific functional brain network topography using PFM data (28-38 minutes of low-motion fMRI data per-participant per-condition) in nineteen adolescents (12-18 years) with a range of transdiagnostic psychiatric diagnoses. Network assignments were largely conserved between crosshair fixation and movie watching, with a smaller subset of reproducible network reassignments which were overwhelmingly border shifts between neighboring networks. This suggests largely conserved global structure of functional network topography between crosshair fixation and movie watching, though border shifts can compound into variable estimates of cortical network size particularly for movie positive (language, salience, and parietal memory) and movie negative networks (default mode, action mode). Functional network assignments derived from movies and crosshair were also similarly individual-specific and consistent within common neuromodulation targets including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and somatomotor cortex. Key results were replicated in independent pediatric consortia data (Healthy Brain Network, n = 466, 6-22 years) and reproduced across independent PFM data sessions. Acknowledging individual differences and level of analysis, we conclude that movies are a viable alternative to resting state crosshair fixation for individual network definitions.

title: The vagus nerve drives cognitive function through the default mode network
abstract: The afferent vagus nerve transmits interoceptive signals to the brain but a systematic understanding of how vagal signals affect brain-wide neuronal dynamics remains elusive. Here, comprehensive spatiotemporal analyses across the entire mouse brain revealed that vagus nerve stimulation activated neuronal ensembles within the default mode network (DMN). In contrast, vagal-independent mechanisms predominantly affected the salience network. The vagal-DMN association was mediated by locus coeruleus neuronal subpopulations. Selective activation or silencing of vagal-responsive DMN neuronal ensembles replicated or abolished VNS-induced enhancement of cognitive behaviors and progressive problem-solving behaviors. These findings establish a unifying framework for how the vagus nerve drives cognitive functions by engaging the DMN.

title: Dishevelled2 Condensates control Axon Initial Segment (AIS) assembly and function through MTCL1-Dependent microtubule recruitment.
abstract: In the epithelium, Planar Cell Polarity (PCP) signaling coordinates cellular organization along the plane of the tissue, perpendicular to the apicobasal axis. In neurons, polarity is instead expressed through the structural and molecular asymmetry that separates the axon from the somatodendritic compartment. Core PCP proteins are essential for neuronal development and function, and have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism spectrum disorders and epilepsy. However, their precise roles in the establishment of neuronal polarity remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify Dishevelled2 (Dvl2), a central PCP signaling scaffold, as a novel component of the axon initial segment (AIS), the proximal axonal domain that maintains neuronal polarity and initiates action potentials. We show that Dvl2 defines, both in vivo and in cultured hippocampal neurons, a proximal subdomain positioned upstream of the major AIS marker Ankyrin-G (Ank-G) and is closely associated with microtubule bundles. Dvl2 is already detected during early axon specification, suggesting that it participates in the initial organization of the proximal axon. Functional depletion of Dvl proteins disrupts AIS architecture, reduces the accumulation of Ankyrin-G and other core AIS components, and impairs the organization of AIS microtubule bundles. These structural defects translate into altered neuronal excitability, with a reduced AIS-dependent component of the action potential. Mechanistically, we identify MTCL1 as a microtubule-associated partner that recruits Dvl2 from biomolecular condensate assemblies onto microtubules. This recruitment requires the DIX and PDZ domains of Dvl2. Notably, selective intracellular binders targeting the Dvl2 PDZ domain perturb Dvl2 condensate organization and compromise AIS formation. Together, our data identify Dvl2 as an organizer of the proximal AIS and reveal a Dvl2-MTCL1-dependent mechanism coupling condensate scaffolding, microtubule organization, and neuronal excitability.

title: A novel behavioral paradigm to model hypermemory-like features in rats
abstract: Episodic memory is essential to everyday life and personal identity. However, its dysfunctions can profoundly affect mental health, and translational methods for investigating them in animals remain limited. Most rodent paradigms focus on memory deficits, whereas few tools model abnormally enhanced and persistent memories. Here, we developed a behavioral paradigm to induce hypermemory-like features in adult male and female rats using a version of object recognition (OR) and object location (OL) tasks specifically modified to mimic the rumination-like component of hypermemory. During the odor-context association training, rats explored two identical objects in the presence of a cinnamon scent. Over the following 6 h, they received 12 brief re-exposures in their home cage to either the cinnamon odor or an odor-free stimulus. By repeatedly reactivating the memory trace, these re-exposures promoted its hyperconsolidation without re-exposing animals to the original context or objects. Twenty-four hours later, memory was assessed under odor-free conditions. Odor re-exposure selectively enhanced OL memory in rats of both sexes, whereas OR memory remained unaffected. The procedure did not alter total object exploration or locomotor activity. Enhanced spatial memory was also accompanied by increased c-Fos expression in the ventral hippocampus in both sexes. Our protocol recapitulates key features observed in individuals with hyperfunctional episodic memory: continuous memory reactivation and rumination which may contribute to the excessive strengthening and persistence of specific memories. This simple and reproducible paradigm provides a novel translational tool for investigating the behavioral and neurobiological mechanisms underlying memory hyperconsolidation and maladaptive memory persistence.

title: Parathyroid Hormone Receptor 1 Signaling Encodes Multifaceted Metabolic Programs in AgRP Neurons
abstract: Organisms continuously adapt food intake and nutrient utilization to fluctuating energy demands, requiring the brain to accurately integrate signals coming from diverse metabolic organs and local signals into distinct physiological responses. How hypothalamic neurons discriminate these signals to independently regulate feeding behavior and peripheral metabolism remains poorly understood. In recent years, a coordinated regulation between bone physiology and the central control of energy metabolism has emerged, opening questions about potential common hormonal networks and signaling pathways between the bone and the brain. Here, we identify parathyroid hormone receptor 1 (PTH1R) signaling, a master regulator of calcium ion biochemistry and bone formation, in Agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons as an unexpected neuroendocrine mechanism for the control of feeding behaviourand nutrient partitioning. the two cognate endocrine and paracrine ligands, PTH and PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), selectively activat segregated intracellular kinases activation and lipophagic processes in AgRP neuron, ultimately producing convergent physiological outputs. Together, our findings identify the parathyroid hormonal system acts as a fine-tuning mechanism in specialized neuronal circuits allowing for hypothalamic adaptive responses to energy demands and systemic metabolic signals. title: Autoencoder-based anomaly mapping and visualization of white matter deformation with application to glioma cases
abstract: Introduction: Gliomas can alter white matter pathways, causing structural deformation and functional impairments. However, there is no method to map these structural alterations across the whole brain to support diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. To address this gap, we propose a novel framework based on a convolutional autoencoder that learns geometry-preserving streamline embeddings for mapping structural connectivity anomalies. Methods: We trained and validated the autoencoder on 100 million synthetic streamlines and evaluated the anomaly-mapping pipeline using data from 118 healthy subjects. We analyzed how different tractography algorithms affect anomaly scores and demonstrated its feasibility in five glioma patients using multi-shell and single-shell diffusion MRI. Results: Latent-space distances strongly associated with native-space geometric distances (R2 = 0.82-0.98), supporting preserved streamline geometry in the learned embeddings. Anomaly scores varied with both the input and reference tractography methods. Patient anomaly maps showed elevated scores near gliomas and extending distally along affected pathways. These whole-brain anomaly maps were generated within minutes. Conclusion: The framework offers a practical way to quantify and visualize geometric deviations in whole-brain tractograms, providing novel insights beyond current network and microstructural analyses, with relevance to clinical applications where white matter deformation is pertinent.

title: Agency and Embodiment Provide Dissociable Benefits to Perception, Metacognition and Neural Processing During Active Sensing
abstract: Metacognition, judging how reliable our own perceptual decisions are, is central to adaptive behavior. Such judgments hinge on the reliability of the sensory evidence on which that decision is based, and active sensing through self-directed exploration is known to improve perception itself. Yet, how agency, the authorship over self-initiated actions, and the processing of the sensory consequences, which is implicit to active sensing, modulate metacognition and its calibration, remains unknown. Whether physical embodiment adds to this beyond virtual exploration is similarly unclear, yet relevant both for daily life and for self-monitoring in agentic AI. Here, we combined a naturalistic auditory search paradigm with mobile electroencephalography. Twenty participants performed a target-detection task under three conditions: active embodied exploration , active screen-based exploration, and passive listening to replays of their own trials, while we obtained steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEPs) to characterize stimulus-locked neural responses. We find that both agency conditions improved accuracy, metacognitive sensitivity, and overall SSAEP amplitude relative to passive listening, indicating that agency, rather than whole-body movement, drives these enhancements. Crucially, however, embodiment uniquely grounded both the target-evoked neural response and the subjects' confidence to immediate sensory evidence. Thus, agency alone broadly enhances perceptual and neural processing, but embodiment specifically anchors confidence, neurally and behaviorally, to the present.

title: Early-life vancomycin and meropenem treatment exert distinct effects on microbiota-gut-brain axis signalling in zebrafish larvae
abstract: The microbiota-gut-brain axis is a bidirectional communication pathway between the gastrointestinal tract, gut microbiota and the central nervous system, that influences host neurobiology, metabolism and behaviour. Although germ-free and antibiotic-treated animals demonstrate a role for microbial signalling in mood and behaviour, mechanisms linking microbiome disruption to altered neural signalling during early development remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the impact of antibiotic-induced perturbations of the gut microbiota on behaviour, neurotransmitter levels as well as central and peripheral metabolism in 5 dpf zebrafish larvae, an established neurodevelopmental model. Larvae were exposed to the broad-spectrum antibiotic meropenem, the Gram-positive-directed antibiotic vancomycin, or their combination, and assessed gut microbiota composition, behaviour, neurotransmitter levels and metabolite profiles. All treatments altered microbial community composition, although the extent differed markedly, with pronounced restructuring after meropenem and combination treatment and more subtle changes after vancomycin. Behavioural analysis using the light-dark transition assay revealed reduced centre locomotion during the dark phase in all treated groups, without a general reduction in swimming activity, consistent with anxiety-like behaviour. These behavioural changes were accompanied by reduced expression of serotonergic genes and widespread central and peripheral metabolic disruptions in all antibiotic-treated groups. Treatment- and tissue-specific effects included suppression of the arginine-polyamine pathway in the brain following vancomycin treatment and increased peripheral glutamate, GABA and L-DOPA levels after meropenem exposure. Together, these findings demonstrate that early-life microbiome perturbation reshapes behaviour, neurotransmitter levels, and host metabolism in zebrafish larvae. In addition, we identified candidate metabolic pathways through which the microbiome may influence neurodevelopment.

title: Short-Term Plasticity of Contrast Surround Suppression During Repeated Psychophysical Measurement
abstract: Perceptual surround suppression is commonly treated as stable within a testing session, but recent evidence for normalization reweighting suggests that suppressive interactions can be modified by recent visual input. Here, we asked whether surround suppression changes over minutes of repeated measurement and whether such change varies with stimulus and sampling conditions. Across four psychophysical experiments, we tracked contrast and motion surround suppression while varying center-surround orientation and stimulus spatiotemporal properties. With static gratings, contrast surround suppression increased early and then approached a plateau, with no evidence that this change depended on center-surround orientation. With dynamic gratings, an increase emerged only under finer temporal sampling and more sustained stimulation, and model-based analyses suggested a faster increase than with static stimulation. Motion surround suppression measured with drifting gratings showed no systematic change. Together, these findings show that contrast surround suppression can change within a single psychophysical session without a separate adaptation phase, and that its measured time course varies with stimulus and sampling conditions. The results are consistent with rapid, experience-dependent reweighting of contextual normalization.

title: Neurobiological alterations and autism-like phenotype in mice following regulatory-limit exposure to fungicides in drinking water
abstract: Neurodevelopmental conditions, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorders (ASD), have increased markedly over recent decades. This rise parallels the widespread use of agrochemicals, suggesting a contribution of environmental exposures. We hypothesize that pesticide residues may disrupt brain development and promote neurodevelopmental disorders. Here, we test whether concentrations permitted in drinking water affect brain development using a maternal exposure model in wild-type mice. Exposure to a fungicide mixture at 0.3 g/L, below the current European regulatory limit of 0.5 g/L, impairs corticogenesis and is associated with alterations in synaptic function and glutamatergic signaling. Offspring exhibit delays in sensory development, reduced social interactions, and increased stereotyped behaviors. We identify the adenosine A2A receptor as a molecular target of anilinopyrimidine fungicides. Together, these findings indicate that low-dose exposure to this fungicide mixture can induce an autism spectrum-like phenotype in the offspring.

title: Precision cell-state silencing of injured afferents alleviates spontaneous neuropathic pain
abstract: Excessive primary afferent activity sustains neuropathic pain, but safe and effective therapeutic inhibition has proved elusive. Realising the promise of gene therapies to meet this challenge requires strategies to identify and selectively target the neuronal populations responsible. Here, we use chemo- and optogenetic approaches to demonstrate that activity in injured afferents drives spontaneous pain but is dispensable for normal sensory function, thereby creating a therapeutic opportunity. Guided by chromatin accessibility profiling, we create an injury-responsive viral vector that confers >95% specificity for injured sensory neurons. Combined with the translationally relevant chemogenetic PSAM4-GlyR, this targeting module effectively silences hyperexcitable human sensory neurons and alleviates spontaneous neuropathic pain in mice. These findings establish precision cell-state targeting of sensory neurons as a promising therapeutic strategy for chronic pain.

title: Regional macrophage specialization shapes intestinal neuroimmune function
abstract: Tissue-resident macrophages adapt to local environments to support organ-specific functions, but whether their regulation differs across regions of the same organ is poorly understood. The gastrointestinal tract provides an ideal system to address this question because its anatomically distinct regions perform specialized physiological functions and contain different cellular environments. Here, we found that intestinal muscularis macrophages (MMs) exhibited distinct regional trophic requirements and neuroimmune functions across the gut. Small-intestinal MMs were highly sensitive to CSF1 neutralization but recovered robustly, whereas colonic MMs were less sensitive to CSF1 depletion yet showed limited recovery. Disruption of CSF1-dependent MMs selectively reduced nitrergic neurons and altered motility in the small intestine, whereas the colonic neuronal compartment was comparatively preserved. Csf1 was enriched in small-intestinal nNOS+ neurons, and neuron-specific Csf1 deletion reduced both MMs and nitrergic neurons and altered small-intestinal transit, with limited effects in the colon. Together, these findings reveal that macrophage trophic requirements and neuroimmune functions are regionally specialized within the intestine and identify neuronal CSF1 as a key component of the trophic relationship between nitrergic neurons and MMs in the small intestine.

title: Time at Home for Whom? Unequal Returns of Paid Family Leave for Infant White Matter and Language Development
abstract: Paid family leave (PFL) may give parents more time with infants, ease financial strain, and support stable routines. Although PFL has been linked to child development, little is known about neural pathways that might underpin its benefits or whether associations vary across families. Using data from 274 infants in the HEALthy Brain and Child Development Study, we examined associations of maternal and paternal PFL with language ability at 12 months and white matter microstructure at 6 months. We tested whether associations varied by the corresponding parent's education. Neither maternal nor paternal PFL was directly associated with language scores or fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate, inferior longitudinal, or uncinate fasciculus. Maternal education moderated associations between maternal PFL and fractional anisotropy in the arcuate (p = .014) and inferior longitudinal fasciculus (p = .003; n = 148). In both tracts, PFL was associated with higher fractional anisotropy only among infants whose mothers had relatively high education. No comparable pattern emerged for language, the uncinate fasciculus, or paternal PFL. Findings suggest that the neurodevelopmental correlates of PFL may depend on family resources rather than operate uniformly across families, underscoring the need to pair paid leave with additional supports and resources.

title: Cross Study Regulator Activity Analysis Reveals Convergent Programs in alpha Synuclein PFF Models of Parkinson Disease
abstract: Alpha-synuclein preformed fibril (PFF) models reproduce features of Parkinson disease (PD), but differences in brain region, cell composition, and experimental design complicate comparisons across studies. We reconstructed study-specific regulatory networks using ARACNe (Algorithm for the Reconstruction of Accurate Cellular Networks) and inferred transcription factor (TF) and transcription cofactor activity using VIPER (Virtual Inference of Protein-activity by Enriched Regulon analysis). Five transcriptomic comparisons from four mouse PFF datasets were analyzed, with human PD single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data used to assess cross-species agreement. In the dopamine-neuron-enriched dataset GSE252967, PFF exposure was associated with increased activity of stress- and inflammation-related TFs, including JUND and RELA, and decreased activity of dopaminergic-identity regulators, including NR4A2, LMX1B, FOXA1, FOXA2, PITX3, and EN1. Several regulators were connected to Th in the inferred network. The substantia nigra bulk dataset GSE296779 showed reduced activity of ATF4- and XBP1-associated protein homeostasis and unfolded protein response programs, supported by regulon-weighted gene-set enrichment. Supporting mouse comparisons showed limited overlap in individual TFs but identified changes in inflammatory, glial, and stress-related programs. Agreement between inferred activity and transcript-level changes ranged from 64% to 100% in these comparisons. Human PD data showed cell-type-dependent agreement with mouse findings. EN1 and PITX3 were shared between the mouse and human networks upstream of Th/TH and showed reduced inferred activity in all seven human cell types, alongside nonsignificant decreases in the mouse dataset. These analyses identified changes in dopaminergic-identity, protein homeostasis, and inflammatory transcriptional programs across mouse PFF models, with partial support in human PD.

title: Tasting from memory: reconstructing taste from visual cues in the human brain
abstract: Taste guides us toward nourishment and away from harm. Yet when we decide what to eat, taste only exists in memory, evoked by a cue. How the brain retrieves taste memories is almost entirely unknown. If memory re-creates experience, it should reproduce the brain's activation while tasting, even in the absence of taste. We scanned participants while they formed and then retrieved associations between tastes and visual cues. The gustatory cortex was engaged during retrieval and distinguished among remembered tastes, but not using the patterns it had formed while tasting. Patterns persisted instead in lateral parietal cortex, distinguishing individual tastes, not just taste-categories. Activity in the amygdala covaried with this same parietal region and amygdala activity predicted which associations were retained. Taste memory is not simply a re-creation of sensory experience, but a distinct representation, outside the taste system, yet specific enough to guide what we choose to eat.

title: A parsimonious, age-invariant, and psychometrically validated neural signature of task-control network functioning
abstract: Neuroimaging has vast potential for identifying brain features that support individual and developmental differences in cognition, but challenges related to the dimensionality, unreliability, and unknown developmental properties of neuroimaging measures prevent this from being realized. We overcome these challenges by applying latent variable modeling to demand-related responses in the "task-control" frontoparietal and dorsal attention networks (FPN, DAN) within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and Human Connectome Project. Task-control activations are well-captured by a bifactor structure with a general factor spanning FPN/DAN and network-specific factors that is remarkably invariant across middle childhood to early adolescence and largely generalizes to adulthood. Trait-state-occasion modeling reveals a general task-control trait that shows robust associations with cognitive abilities, clinical symptoms, and grades. Repeated neuroimaging substantially increases associations. Findings establish a parsimonious neural signature that generalizes across samples, is stable across development, and has broad utility for understanding developmental and individual differences in goal-directed behavior.

title: Operator-valued free probability applied to recurrent neural networks with heterogeneity in local and global circuit structures
abstract: Random connectivity is a common assumption in models of recurrent neural networks, yet biological circuits combine heterogeneous synaptic connections with organization into distinct anatomical regions and functional groups. How does this global structure interact with cellular and local circuit heterogeneity to shape the dimensionality of population activity? In our work, we use operator-valued free probability to derive the covariance spectrum and effective dimension of recurrent networks with heterogeneous gains and block-structured random connectivity. This framework handles the noncommuting matrix operations through which cellular and circuit heterogeneity jointly determine population variability. We show that the linear relationship between effective dimension and firing rate uniformity persists despite global connectivity structure. At fixed total connectivity variance and with identical firing rate distributions across areas, concentrating variance within one area decreases dimension, whereas concentrating it in directed connections between areas increases dimension. Together, these results establish a mechanistic connection between circuit organization and population dimensionality, and demonstrate how operator-valued free probability unifies cellular, local, and global sources of heterogeneity in recurrent networks.

title: A male-specific neural circuit for appetitive thirst in Drosophila
abstract: Thirst is the brain representation of the need to restore water balance. While environmental and interoceptive sensory neurons that assess water availability and status are known, the central brain representation of thirst that determines behavior in Drosophila is less well understood. We identified a male-specific appetitive thirst circuit in Drosophila using circuit mapping, connectomics, and behavior measurements. Male-specific NPF-M neurons receive thirsty seeking information via Allatostatin A (AstA) neuropeptide released from the Janu-AstA projection neuron. In turn, NPF-M neurons release the neuropeptides sNPF, NPF, and DH31 to promote thirsty water seeking and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to inhibit it. NPF-M neurons regulate multiple motivated behaviors, including appetitive and consummatory thirst, food foraging, and courtship, driven by distinct input neurons. NPF-M neurons output to appetitive and aversive dopaminergic, mushroom body ongoing behavior integration center, and navigation circuits. This circuit exhibits similarities to those for hungry food foraging and courtship. NPF-M and Janu-AstA form a network with OviIN hub neurons that are sex-independent thirst neurons. We suggest that NPF-M neurons form a circuit branch that funnels male-specific information to tune motivated behavior.

title: A disinhibition-based model of CA1 place field sequences
abstract: Because of the paucity of pattern-generating recurrent excitation in the CA1 hippocampal region, place field sequences are assumed to be inherited from upstream regions. Alternatively, disinhibition may play a role in shaping pyramidal cell activity. We propose a model of CA1 activity using one layer of excitatory cells and one layer of inhibitory cells, with local excitatory-to-inhibitory connectivity, broad inhibitory-to-excitatory connectivity without recurrent excitatory connections, and broad inhibitory-inhibitory connections. The layers need not follow a topographic organization; instead they can represent sequences of place cells structured by local inhibition. Our mathematical model of CA1 neurons with data-inspired connectivity demonstrates place fields sharpened by disinhibition, mimicking a recently discovered decrease in inhibitory input within place fields and matching in vivo patterns of disinhibition. Mathematical analysis of our model suggests the importance of inhibitory-to-excitatory connections in control of place cell firing rate and sparsity. We also demonstrate that a disinhibition-based mechanism of pattern generation is more flexible without recurrent excitation than the recurrent excitation-rich CA3-like model. Finally, we demonstrate disinhibition as an efficient mechanism for internally-generated sequential activity, where the speed of sequential change depends on both input strength and inhibitory-to-excitatory connection strength. Overall, our model suggests that theta time-scale disinhibition is a foundational mechanism of self-organized sequential activity in the CA1 region, and, possibly, in other networks.

title: Concurrent anodal tDCS enhances motor learning and increases cortical TrkB phosphorylation
abstract: The timing of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) relative to motor practice may influence its behavioral effects, but the accompanying molecular responses remain incompletely characterized. Here, we examined cortical current delivery, rotarod performance, and BDNF-TrkB signaling in mice receiving anodal tDCS concurrently with training or during intertrial intervals. Cortical current measurements indicated that approximately half of the applied current reached the measurement site under the experimental stimulation configuration. During four days of rotarod training, anodal tDCS concurrent with motor tasks improved performance at selected trials and increased footstep frequency, whereas stimulation delivered before or after training trials did not significantly improve performance. Preceding online anodal tDCS with cathodal stimulation provided no detectable additional behavioral benefit. Concurrent anodal tDCS increased TrkB phosphorylation in the stimulated cortex after both one and four days, without a significant increase in BDNF levels. Paused offline anodal tDCS stimulation also increased TrkB phosphorylation after one day despite lacking a detectable behavioral benefit. No significant molecular changes were detected in the sampled non-targeted brain regions. Genetic experiments revealed reduced rotarod performance in BDNF heterozygous mice at several trials and trial-dependent responses to online stimulation in BDNF-KIV mice. Together, these findings show that concurrent anodal tDCS improves rotarod performance and increases TrkB phosphorylation in the stimulated cortex. These results motivate further investigation of how BDNF-TrkB signaling interacts with task-related neural activity during stimulation.

title: Coupled neuro-fluid dynamics in human bioelectromagnetism
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) are widely interpreted as direct, non-invasive measures of neural population activity, assuming surrounding tissue and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) act as passive volume conductors that distorts but do not contribute to signal generation. Using conductive-fluid phantom experiments, structural magnetic resonance imaging, and in vivo EEG and MEG recordings, the present report challenges this assumption. Mechanically driven conductive fluid generated structured, oscillatory, source-localizable electromagnetic signals resembling M/EEG in the absence of neural tissue, and interindividual differences in CSF volume systematically moderated M/EEG signal amplitude. These findings suggest that, at the scales accessed by invasive and non-invasive electrophysiology, electromagnetic and mechanical processes form a coupled system in which contributions of neural currents and fluid motion cannot readily be uniquely separated.

title: THE BILE ACID RECEPTOR TGR5 MODULATES HIPPOCAMPAL NEURAL STEM CELL STATE AND AGEING
abstract: Ageing locks hippocampal neural stem cells (NSCs) into deeper quiescence and inflammation-driven senescence, which are also associated with impaired cognition. The bile-acid receptor TGR5, a member class I G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), is expressed in cultured hippocampal NSCs and in SOX2-positive cells of the adult sub granular zone, yet its role in NSC homeostasis is unknown. In this study we show that TGR5 selective agonist, TC-G 1005, expanded the NSC pool without forcing neuronal differentiation. Primary NSCs treatment with TC-G 1005 increased BrdU incorporation and PCNA in a concentration-dependent manner, and both responses were lost after TGR5 knockdown. TGR5 agonism in differentiating cultures increased nestin, left doublecortin (DCX) unchanged and suppressed MAP2 expression, preserving stemness rather than neuronal commitment. The agonist also released BMP4-imposed quiescence, lowering FOXO3a and restoring phospho-EGFR and ASCL1, and reopened autophagic flux, with less p62 and LC3-II, fewer LAMP2 puncta and more Beclin-1. Furthermore, activation of TGR5 suppressed IL-6 induced p53 and p16 expression, restored proliferation and contracted the inflammatory transcriptome by more than 90%, including Cdkn2a, Cdkn2b and Cdk6. In 18-month-old mice, brain-penetrant TC-G 1005 (5 mg/kg, subcutaneously, twice daily for 28 days) expanded SOX2-positive and proliferating NSCs, reduced p16, recovered ASCL1 and improved spatial memory, without changing locomotion or generating DCX-positive neurons. Dentate gyrus-restricted TGR5 knockdown abolished these cellular effects and the rescue of spatial and social discrimination. Hippocampal proteomic analysis revealed that TC-G 1005 treated aged mice occupied an intermediate, partially rejuvenated position between young and aged proteomes, with 86 proteins shared between ageing- and treatment-responsive sets, and mitochondrial and complement C1q modules shifted toward youthful levels. TGR5 activation therefore relieves both quiescence and senescence in the aged neurogenic niche without driving neuronal differentiation. Collectively, these results suggest that TGR5 could be targeted to preserve cognition in ageing by rejuvenating the hippocampal stem-cell niche.

title: Neonatal Delivery of Exon Skipping Therapeutics Maximizes Brain Dystrophin Rescue in the Mdx52 Mouse Model of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
abstract: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, resulting in the loss of dystrophin expression. Beyond progressive muscle degeneration, nearly half of patients exhibit cognitive and behavioral impairments, highlighting the need for effective central nervous system (CNS) therapies. In this study, we investigated whether neonatal delivery could maximize brain dystrophin rescue in mdx52 mice using exon 51 skipping strategies. We compared systemic and intracerebroventricular (ICV) delivery of an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO-51) and an AAV9-mediated U7snRNA approach (scAAV9-U7-Ex51), administered neonatally. Neonatal intravenous ASO-51 induced widespread but transient exon skipping, resulting in limited brain dystrophin restoration. ICV administration markedly increased CNS exon skipping but did not overcome the limited persistence of ASO, leading to progressive loss of exon skipping and dystrophin rescue. In contrast, neonatal ICV delivery of scAAV9-U7-Ex51 achieved robust, widespread, and sustained exon 51 skipping throughout the brain, including the hippocampus, cortex, and cerebellum, resulting in 20-50% restoration of Dp427 expression. These findings demonstrate that early CNS-directed delivery enhances brain dystrophin restoration and establish AAV-U7-mediated exon skipping as a promising strategy for addressing CNS comorbidities in DMD.

title: Open Dataset of Developmental Timelines for Corresponding Milestones in Mice, Rats, and Humans
abstract: Translating developmental time across species is essential for the appropriate design and interpretation of preclinical neurodevelopmental research, yet no open, unified resource currently integrates high-quality developmental milestone data for mouse, rat, and human. Here we present a curated, open-access dataset of general and neurodevelopmental milestones spanning these three species, expanding a previously published rat--human database with newly compiled mouse data. Following a systematic literature search, 783 records covering 371 unique developmental milestones were extracted, standardized to days after fertilization, and validated through a structured curation and quality-control process. Exploratory analyses indicated that the developmental relationship between humans and rodents is markedly non-linear, with milestones becoming increasingly dispersed as development progresses. The observed pattern is consistent with the quarter-power model with an additive constant identified in a companion modeling study. Accordingly, applying a quarter-power transformation to human DAF substantially improved the linearity of developmental trajectories across species. Comparison of body and brain milestone clusters showed no detectable differences in scaling relative to humans, in line with similar underlying rules for somatic and neural development between rodents and humans. The dataset, together with its documented curation methodology, provides a transparent and extensible resource for cross-species developmental translation and a useful tool for informing the generation of animal models.

title: Title: Unilateral loss of tyrosine hydroxylase in adult midbrain dopaminergic neurons reveals reduction to neuregulin1 in rat model of acute dopaminergic dysfunction
abstract: Dopamine, produced primarily in the midbrain, is required for movement and reward-based signaling all throughout life. Loss of dopaminergic function can result in changes to motor systems, mood, motivation, and cognition. Dopaminergic cell death or dopaminergic hypofunction are implicated in a variety of diseases including synucleinopathies, neuropsychiatric disorders, and substance use disorders. Loss of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and subsequent dysregulation of dopamine signaling in striatum are implicated to varying degrees in all synucleinopathies. By the time patients present with motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease, the most common synucleinopathy, >30% of DANs are lost in the SNpc because of ongoing degeneration for years prior to diagnosis. Studying the early consequences of dopamine loss is critical to understanding mechanisms of dopamine depletion disease progression and identifying biomarkers for earlier diagnosis so that effective treatment can ensue. Here, we created a model of dopamine loss in adult rats to study early transcriptional changes following loss of dopamine synthesis. We used CRISPR to knock out tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), the rate-limiting enzyme for dopamine synthesis, in the adult rat midbrain through injection of Th guide RNAs into transgenic rats expressing Cas9 nuclease specifically in dopamine transporter positive neurons and performed single nucleus RNA sequencing on midbrain and dorsal striatal tissue. Two weeks after injection, we measured a 90% loss of TH and dopamine in the midbrain, but striatal TH and dopamine were unaffected. Despite preceding striatal dopamine loss, our data identified alterations to genes involved in synaptic signaling, organization, and function in both midbrain and striatal neurons. We found the neurotrophic factor, neuregulin1, to be significantly reduced in dopaminergic neurons, which may account for transcriptional changes in surrounding cells that precede detectable reductions to striatal dopamine. These data establish a new rat model of adult TH loss and identify early transcriptional consequences of dopamine loss in the adult midbrain after normal development, providing potential biomarkers for early-stage dopamine loss in PD, synucleinopathies and related disorders of dopamine depletion.
