title: Heterochronicity shapes brain network formation.
abstract: Brain network formation unfolds on a nonuniform developmental timetable, with different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles underpinning the organization of connectomes by creating synthetic networks according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome's topology, operationalized here as the cumulative distributions of network metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography refers to the spatial embedding of the network-the actual anatomical positions of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of individual differences in network formation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Astrocytic facilitation of somatic NMDARs underpins hippocampal E-S potentiation.
abstract: EPSP-spike (E-S) potentiation is a form of plasticity defined by a persistent increase in neuronal spike output for a given synaptic input, reflecting enhanced E-S coupling independent of synaptic strength. However, its cellular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that brief induction of E-S potentiation triggers a sustained calcium activity increase in astrocytes adjacent to the hippocampal CA1 pyramidal layer. Mechanistically, E-S potentiation critically requires GluN2B-containing N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) localized to the neuronal soma. Sustained astrocytic activity promotes E-S potentiation through vesicular release of D-serine, which enhances tonic activation of somatic NMDARs, suppresses A-type potassium currents, and produces a lasting increase in neuronal excitability. Functionally, this astrocyte-dependent E-S potentiation lowers the threshold for subsequent long-term potentiation, conferring a metaplastic influence on hippocampal circuits. These findings identify an astrocyte-neuron signaling mechanism that drives intrinsic plasticity and establish somatic NMDARs as a key site of astrocytic regulation of hippocampal output.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: A Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex drives enhanced depotentiation in a mouse model of improved cognitive flexibility.
abstract: Memory updating promotes cognitive flexibility by enabling suppression of outdated information to optimize behavioral strategies in response to a changing environment. While some circuits involved have been identified, the synaptic mechanisms underlying this process remain uncertain. Here, using a recently developed Kv4.2 knock-in mouse model (Kv4.2TA), we identify a metaplasticity in the hippocampus that accompanies an improvement in cognitive flexibility. Mutation of a C-terminal phosphorylation site (T607) in the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated K+ channel protein Kv4.2 drives boosted depotentiation of spike timing-dependent long-term synaptic potentiation mediated by mGluR5 receptors, putative constituents of Kv4.2 macromolecular complexes. We found that mGluR5 receptors are required for the improved cognitive flexibility observed in Kv4.2TA mice. These findings reveal a synaptic correlate associated with memory updating in cognitive flexibility and spotlight the Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex as a therapeutic target for disorders characterized by impairments in cognitive flexibility.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Competing presynaptic protein assemblies coordinate basal neurotransmission with homeostatic plasticity.
abstract: Neural circuits establish a stable basal level of synaptic transmission that is maintained throughout life. When synaptic activity is perturbed, homeostatic mechanisms restore this set point, but how neurons reconcile long-term stability and rapid compensatory plasticity remains unclear. Here, we identify two competing presynaptic multimolecular complexes that control steady-state transmission and homeostatic potentiation and define the molecular switch that enables transitions between these functional states. At Drosophila neuromuscular junction, the transmembrane protein PlexinB (PlexB) and the auxiliary subunit Neto-α regulate both basal synaptic function and homeostatic plasticity. PlexB association with presynaptic KaiR1D/Neto-α receptor complexes modulates channel properties and fine-tunes neurotransmitter release, whereas PlexB signaling with Semaphorin2b (Sema2b) and Neto-α drives homeostatic potentiation. KaiR1D and Sema2b/PlexB compete for a limited pool of presynaptic Neto-α. Motor neurons switch from steady-state transmission to homeostatic potentiation by exchanging KaiR1D/Neto-α/PlexB complexes for Neto-α/PlexB/Sema2b. Critically, Neto-α must dissociate from KaiR1D-containing complexes to initiate the homeostatic response. Variants of Neto-α or KaiR1D that fail to dissociate support normal basal neurotransmission but abolish homeostatic plasticity. These findings demonstrate that dynamic reorganization of competing presynaptic protein assemblies enables neurons to preserve stable baseline transmission while mounting robust compensatory responses to perturbations. Given the widespread roles of presynaptic receptors and Semaphorin/Plexin signaling in synaptic regulation, this mechanism may represent a conserved strategy for balancing stability and plasticity in neural circuits.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT.
abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin, which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3' untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.

title: Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees.
abstract: Chaotic dynamics, commonly seen in weather systems and fluid turbulence, are characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, which makes accurate prediction challenging. Recent approaches have focused on developing data-driven models that attempt to preserve invariant statistics over long horizons since many chaotic systems exhibit dissipative behaviors and ergodicity. Despite the recent progress in such models, they are still often prone to generating unbounded trajectories, leading to invalid statistics evaluation. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce a modular framework that provides formal guarantees of trajectory boundedness for neural network chaotic dynamics models. Our core contribution is a dissipative projection layer that leverages control-theoretic principles to ensure the learned system is dissipative. Specifically, our framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator and an energy-like function, where the latter is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint within the projection layer. Furthermore, the learned invariant level set provides an outer estimate for the system's strange attractor, which is known to be difficult to characterize due to its complex geometry. We demonstrate our model's ability to produce bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserve invariant statistics for chaotic dynamical systems, including Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Double periodicity of the AnkyrinG-associated complex in the axon initial segment.
abstract: The axon initial segment (AIS), situated within the first 20 to 60 µm of the axon, is essential for action potential generation and maintenance of axonal identity [M. N. Rasband, Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 11, 552-562 (2010)]. Its structure relies on the beta (β)-IV-spectrin/AnkyrinG (AnkG) scaffold arranged periodically underneath the plasma membrane, harboring diverse membrane proteins [K. Xu, G. Zhong, X. Zhuang, Science 339, 452-456 (2013); K. L. Hedstrom, Y. Ogawa, M. N. Rasband, J. Cell Biol. 183, 635-640 (2008)]. Although a ~190-nm cytoskeletal periodic organization is well established, the precise stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of AIS proteins within the ~190-nm spatial period remain rudimentary, mostly for lack of sufficient spatial resolution and labeling efficiency. Here, using expansion microscopy and cryoelectron tomography, which overcome these technical limitations, we present data on the organization of the AnkG-associated complex within the ~190-nm spatial period. We demonstrate that exactly two AnkG molecules are situated within each period and with their C termini separated by ~80 nm. By contrast, the AnkG-associated cell-adhesion protein neurofascin-186 appears in clusters of varying sizes that are consistent with the periodic organization of AnkG pairs, yet suggesting a more complex molecular arrangement between the two molecules. Altogether, our approach provides insights into AIS molecular organization and protein stoichiometry.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Shedding light on left hippocampal mGlu5 in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer's disease (AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is lost in two distinct mouse models of AD, the J20 and 5xFAD mice, revealing a hemisphere-specific disruption of hippocampal mGlu5 regulation. Using the light-controllable negative allosteric modulator Alloswitch-1, we show that selective inhibition of left, but not right, hippocampal mGlu5 restores working and short-term memory in AD mice. This finding indicates that altered mGlu5 expression does not simply reflect receptor loss, but rather a dysregulated signaling state that remains functionally relevant and pharmacologically targetable. Left-specific modulation also normalizes pathological downstream signaling, including aberrant Pyk2 and GSK-3β activation and tau hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative disease.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Imaging and recording of synaptic zinc in the brain by covalent chemistry-based semisynthetic biosensors.
abstract: Labile zinc ions (Zn2+) are stored in glutamatergic vesicles at specific excitatory synapses in the central nervous system and released into synaptic clefts in an activity-dependent manner. However, the precise roles of synaptic Zn2+ remain unclear due to a lack of tools capable of analyzing Zn2+ with synapse-level spatial resolution in vivo. Here, we developed neuroreceptor-based semisynthetic biosensors that function as integrating dosimeters, recording synaptic Zn2+ by covalent chemistry in the living mouse brain. Using a chemical knock-in strategy, we introduced activity-based Zn2+ probes with distinct affinities into endogenous α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole-propionic acid or γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors. These in-brain-constructed Zn2+ sensors enabled region-specific mapping of Zn2+ in synaptic clefts in the living mouse brain. Imaging-based analyses revealed differences in apparent Zn2+ levels at excitatory and inhibitory synapses across hippocampal regions during kainate-induced seizures, providing insights into the physiological and pathological functions of synaptic Zn2+.

title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation.
abstract: Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation water has been proposed to be a signature of such hot spots at both the tau fibril-end surface and soluble tau monomers. Although jR2R3-P301L tau exhibits a heterogeneous hydration landscape in its intrinsically disordered state, with enhanced water structuring near the P301L mutation site, it is unclear whether a localized hotspot exists at the fibril end surface and surface water facilitates the initial contacts in templated aggregation. Using rapid 1H-15N SOFAST-HMQC NMR to track seed-induced aggregation of jR2R3-P301L in real time, complemented by molecular dynamics simulation of fibril surface hydration, we identify a residue-specific pinning hotspot that is prone to dewetting followed by sequential folding and incorporation of the remaining segment in a two-step dock-and-lock process. Site-specific spin labeling further demonstrates that blocking this pinning hotspot disrupts templated aggregation, leading to shorter fibrils. The identification of a dominant pinning site will facilitate the rational design of binders to effectively disrupt fibril extension or serve as diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Target engagement and efficacy in disease-modifying trials of synuclein-related disorders.
abstract: Disease-modifying trials in Parkinson's disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to demonstrate target engagement, de-risk subsequent phases of drug development and provide mechanistic evidence of biological activity. Whether biomarker modulation predicts clinical benefit remains unclear. We conducted a PRISMA-compliant review of phase II and III disease-modifying trials (2020-2025) that included at least one biomarker intended to assess target engagement. Twenty-six trials met inclusion criteria (PD=19, MSA=4, DLB=3; n=2,195 participants). Target engagement was reported in 14 of 19 PD trials (12 phase II/2 phase III), 1 of 4 MSA trials, and 2 of 3 DLB trials (all phase II). Concordance between target engagement and clinical improvement was uncommon, as only 8/26 studies (7 phase II/1 phase III) demonstrated both target engagement and statistically significant clinical benefit, and just two of these (both phase II, one in PD and one in MSA) were rigorously controlled with low or moderate risk of bias. Nine trials showed target engagement without clinical benefit, whereas two reported clinical improvement without measurable target engagement. Baseline biomarker-guided patient selection was uncommon and rarely aligned with the compound's mechanism of action. Patient-reported outcomes were widely used but rarely improved. Across recent disease-modifying trials in PD, DLB, and MSA, target engagement was frequently demonstrated, yet clinical benefit rarely followed. These findings question the predictive value of currently used target-engagement biomarkers and highlight the need to biologically align trial populations with the mechanisms targeted by experimental molecular interventions.

title: Synaptic vesicle undocking induces low-frequency depression.
abstract: Synaptic depression is often interpreted as reflecting depletion of the readily releasable pool (RRP) following exocytosis. Such a mechanism predicts little or no depression at low stimulation frequency, as RRP replenishment should then offset the loss of vesicles by exocytosis. Nevertheless, in several types of mammalian central synapses, repetitive presynaptic stimulation at low frequency (<5 Hz) elicits synaptic depression (low-frequency depression or LFD). In the present work, we count the number of synaptic vesicles released at individual active zones to study the RRP and its replenishment during LFD. Contrary to depletion models of synaptic depression, we find that LFD does not depend on previous SV consumption. We find that LFD displays a long recovery time course (tens of seconds) when challenged by isolated stimulations but is immediately reversed by a high-frequency train. We suggest that LFD results from undocking, a shift between two classes of synaptic vesicles organized sequentially inside the RRP (replacement vs. docked vesicles) in favor of the upstream (replacement) state. To explain the dependence of LFD recovery on stimulation frequency, we propose that, while undocking is apparent hundreds of milliseconds after a stimulation, calcium-dependent docking takes only a couple of milliseconds. Consistent with the undocking model, we find that double presynaptic stimulations alleviate LFD as they favor vesicular docking and RRP replenishment. Finally, we expand our model to explain how stimulation frequency shapes short-term synaptic depression, changing from depression at low frequency to a facilitation-depression sequence at medium- or high-frequency trains.

title: Synaptic connectome of a neurosecretory network in the Drosophila brain.
abstract: Hormones mediate inter-organ signaling, which is crucial in orchestrating diverse behaviors and physiological processes, including sleep and activity, feeding, growth, metabolism, and reproduction. The pars intercerebralis and pars lateralis in insects represent major hubs that contain neurosecretory cells (NSCs) that produce various peptide hormones. To obtain insight into how hormonal signaling is regulated, we have characterized the synaptic connectome of NSCs in the adult Drosophila brain. Identification of neurons providing inputs to multiple NSC classes implicates diuretic hormone 44-expressing NSCs as a major coordinator of physiology and behavior. Surprisingly, despite most NSCs having dendrites in the subesophageal zone (primary taste processing center), inputs from peripheral gustatory neurons to NSCs are largely indirect. We also deciphered pathways via which diverse olfactory inputs are relayed to NSCs. Using an influence metric, based on a linear dynamical systems approach, we identify enteric neurons as the strongest influencers of NSC activity compared to other sensory modalities. Further, our analyses revealed substantial inputs from brain descending neurons to NSCs, suggesting that descending neurons regulate both endocrine and motor output to synchronize physiological changes with appropriate behaviors. In contrast to NSC inputs, synaptic output from NSCs is sparse and mostly mediated by corazonin NSCs. We show that both corazonin-expressing NSCs and their downstream synaptic partner DNg27 influence egg-laying. We additionally explore putative paracrine interconnectivity between NSC classes and peptide hormone pathways from NSCs to peripheral tissues by analyzing single-cell transcriptomic datasets. Our comprehensive characterization of the Drosophila neurosecretory network connectome provides a platform to understand complex hormonal networks and how they orchestrate animal behaviors and physiology.

title: Robust and replicable effects of ageing on resting-state brain electrophysiology measured with MEG.
abstract: Non-invasive recordings of brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies. This makes it challenging to establish a clear consensus on the frequency, location, and direction of any single reported effect within the larger body of research. We estimate a full-frequency whole-head profile of the ageing effect on eyes-closed resting-state MEG using the GLM-Spectrum. This data representation is easily sharable, facilitates meta-analyses, and provides a framework for estimating statistical power of age effects for future study planning. We use this to show that the effect of age replicates across open-access MEG datasets and is robust to modelling of common covariates. Distinct components within the full-frequency profile have different effect sizes, indicating that sample-size planning for ageing effects must consider the specific features of interest. The frequency profile of ageing is strongly robust to a range of common covariates and partially robust to modelling of grey matter volume. We establish that what seems a well-powered study may become underpowered when analyses target an age effect that is linearly separable from an age-relevant covariate such as grey matter volume. These results provide a pathway towards formal comparison and assessment of candidate markers for brain health in ageing.

title: Identification of letters distorted by physiologically-inspired spatial scrambling.
abstract: In the geniculostriate pathway of the human visual system, neuronal projections carry signals from a particular retinal locus in parallel from one anatomical area to the next. Imprecision in the fidelity of these projections would place constraints on the ability of the system to perform tasks requiring positional information. We investigated the impact that "spatial scrambling" between stages would have on visual performance. We consider two stages in a simple canonical model of the early visual cortex where scrambling might occur: either the input to the first orientation-tuned mechanisms (analogous to V1 simple cells), or the output from those mechanisms. These are referred as "subcortical" (SCS) and "cortical scrambling" (CS). We developed a wavelet decomposition and resynthesis algorithm to mimic these effects, and measured human performance in letter identification affected by the two types of scrambling. Our results showed SCS and CS have distinguishable effects on both perceived noisiness of letters and letter identification threshold. Comparing human performance against a suite of pre-trained and custom convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that were trained on the scrambled stimuli, relative efficiency (calculated from the ratio of human:CNN thresholds) is higher for CS than SCS. However, in modelling human inefficiency by reducing the proportion of wavelets available to the CNNs, humans are less efficient in CS than SCS. These differences in efficiencies show humans are better at processing orientation redundant stimuli (CS) than orientation noisy stimuli (SCS). We hypothesize this reflects differences in integration properties at the input and output stages of simple cells in the cortex.

title: Latent encoding of movement in primary visual cortex.
abstract: Neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) are classically thought to encode spatial features of visual stimuli through simple population codes: each neuron exhibits a preferred orientation and preferred spatial frequency, both of which remaining invariant to other aspects of the visual stimulus. Here, we show that this simple rule does not apply to the representation of major features of stimulus motion, including stimulus direction and temporal frequency (TF). We collected an extensive dataset of cat V1 responses to stimuli covarying in orientation, direction, spatial frequency, and TF to assess the extent of motion selectivity. We show that preferred TF is mostly uniform across the cortical surface. Yet, in over half of V1, the preferred direction is reversed with changing stimulus TF, revealing four distinct map motifs embedded in V1's functional architecture. Similarly, despite the lack of spatial modulation for the preferred TF map and the lack of invariance for the preferred direction map, we found using convolutional neural networks that direction, TF and stimulus speed can be accurately decoded from V1 responses at all cortical locations. These findings suggest a latent encoding of information where subtle, spatially distributed modulations of V1 activity may convey fine information about stimulus motion, pointing to a novel primary sensory encoding mechanism despite complex co-variation of responses to multiple attributes across V1 neurons.

title: Enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals and musicians is due to reduced internal noise.
abstract: Although it is commonly assumed that early blind individuals have enhanced pitch perception, the literature to date has been contradictory. We measured performance on two tasks known to recruit early versus late stages of auditory frequency tuning in early blind and sighted human adults of both sexes with matched years of musical training. The two groups showed equivalent performance on a tone detection in notched-noise task that assesses cochlear frequency selectivity. In contrast, early blind individuals showed enhanced performance in a pitch discrimination task thought to be mediated by cortical mechanisms. Computational modeling revealed that this enhancement was best explained by reduced internal noise rather than narrower frequency tuning, with both blindness and years of musical training predicting a reduction in internal noise. These findings identify internal noise as a key factor in experience-driven auditory plasticity as a result of both musical experience and early blindness.Significance Statement For centuries, early blindness has been associated with superior auditory abilities. Here we find that the enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals is best explained by reduced internal noise at higher levels of auditory processing, rather than sharper frequency tuning. Years of musical training similarly resulted in lower internal noise, suggesting a shared mechanism through which experience improves auditory perception. These findings identify internal noise reduction as a key component of experience-dependent auditory plasticity.

title: Calibrating AlphaFold confidence scores for interface quality
abstract: AlphaFold confidence scores are widely used to rank protein complex predictions and to select subsets of models for downstream applications. Although these scores provide strong discriminatory power for distinguishing prediction quality, their numerical values were never intended to represent the probability that a prediction satisfies a given structural quality criterion. In this work, we calibrate commonly used confidence scores to estimate the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a chosen threshold of DockQ, an established measure of interface quality. On antibody-antigen and general multimer datasets, post-hoc isotonic calibration consistently improves agreement between predicted probabilities and observed DockQ success rates while preserving the underlying score ordering. The calibrated probabilities also provide more accurate estimates of the fraction of selected models expected to pass a given structural quality threshold. Although the mapping is fitted within a given prediction distribution and therefore transfers imperfectly across prediction domains, we show that reliable estimates are recovered from a small number of labeled target-domain samples. Because the calibration is entirely post hoc and requires no underlying AlphaFold model fine-tuning, it provides a straightforward and customizable way to convert existing model quality rankings into calibrated probabilities of passing a chosen structural quality threshold.

title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos
abstract: Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics. We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development. Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.

title: Beyond Successful Play: Diagnosing Opponent Modeling in Large Language Models
abstract: Language-model agents are expected to adapt to others whose behavior changes through interaction. Yet adaptation may rely on learned behavioral patterns rather than theory of mind (ToM): the ability to infer others' mental states, including beliefs and intentions. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic framework for repeated hide-and-seek against algorithmic opponents with explicitly defined recursive belief updates. Their ground-truth beliefs and action probabilities let us distinguish adaptive play, action prediction, and belief tracking through live interaction, fixed-history evaluation, and controlled information interventions. With structured elicitation and behavioral supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we find improved play in several tested settings, but diagnostics reveal limitations in opponent prediction and belief tracking. We test whether supervising opponent action probabilities can address this predictive deficit in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Predictions improve when the model is told the opponent's type and parameter settings, but become less accurate when it must infer the opponent from history without this information. Training on examples that also omit these details reduces the gap, although improvements vary across opponents. Is this limitation specific to smaller open-weight models, or does it also appear in a frontier model? GPT-5.4 also benefits from correct opponent beliefs: supplying them improves its predictions and choices, whereas deeper explicit belief reports and self-generated memory do not consistently improve forecasting from interaction history. This contrast suggests that using useful belief information is easier than inferring it autonomously, even for a frontier model. Together, our findings distinguish improved play and action prediction from reliable belief tracking, providing a framework for evaluating mentalizing and testing targeted improvements.

title: Learning Perceptual Geometry of Natural Odor Mixtures from LLM-Derived Descriptors
abstract: The relationship between odor chemistry and perception remains incompletely understood. Many existing studies focus on the perception of single molecules, whereas natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding extra layer of complexity to percept formation. Here, we explore the relationship between molecular composition and perceived similarity in natural odor objects. We study this using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures containing more than 8,000 molecular components, and use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for deriving mixture-level perceptual descriptions. We find that language-derived representations provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. The prediction was consistently strongest when perceptual targets were derived from chemosensory prompts than from other sensory prompts. Further, during the mixture-level training, we learned low-rank molecular embeddings that enabled better prediction of held-out mixture similarities than component-overlap metrics, even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used during training, the learned molecular geometry showed significant alignment with the independent human odor-descriptor space. Finally, we explored the use of external molecular features in our mixture-similarity prediction task. These features showed modest zero-shot alignment with mixture-level perceptual similarity. They improved prediction under limited supervision but offered little additional predictive benefit with the full training set. Together, these results show that language-derived descriptions can provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, contributing to a quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.

title: Probing the role of sequential sampling and integration in decisions about protracted, noiseless stimuli
abstract: Perceptual decision behaviour is known to be well-captured by models based on sequential sampling and temporal integration, but doubts have been raised about the generality and identifiability of these operations. Here we used neurally-constrained modelling to probe their role and temporal extent in the uncertain case of perceptual judgments about long-duration stimuli with no physical noise but weak evidence. We found that accuracy steadily improved across four covertly-manipulated evidence durations, indicating protracted sampling, but these delayed behavioural reports alone were insufficient to establish the operation of integration or of a decision-terminating bound. We then elaborated the models to prescribe how they would generate decision variable signals as well as choices, and fit them additionally to the average dynamics of a centroparietal electroencephalographic signal (CPP) that traces decision formation. This established the setting of a bound and ruled out some non-integration mechanisms. However, one extrema detection model, which evokes a stereotyped signal "flagging" the first bound-exceeding sample, rivalled the integration model in reproducing the evidence-dependent buildup dynamics of the CPP, alongside behavioural data. Moreover, the two models captured different features of neural motor preparation signals but neither captured all of them. We discuss the implications for the generality of integration and the technical challenges of neurally-informed modelling given limited behavioural data.

title: Neural prediction decorrelation reveals that adversarial robustness substantially improves DNN prediction accuracy across the entire human auditory cortex
abstract: Sensory neuroscientists seek to model the neural computations that encode complex stimuli. Distinct encoding models often make similar predictions for natural stimuli such as speech, posing a challenge for model comparison. We developed a method to synthesize stimuli that decorrelate model predictions across a neural population, termed neural prediction decorrelation (NPD). Using fMRI responses to NPD sounds, we compared standard and adversarially robust deep neural network models of human auditory cortex. Prediction accuracy for NPD sounds was substantially better for the adversarially robust model in every region tested, an effect completely masked with natural sounds. Population responses to natural and synthesized NPD sounds shared an interpretable low-dimensional organization that was reproduced by the robust encoding model. NPD provides a general approach for comparing encoding models and reveals that adversarial robustness expands the predictive power of DNNs beyond natural stimuli, which is likely critical for targeting population activity through stimulus synthesis.

title: NeuroGraphBench: Interacting with Drosophila Connectomes at Scale for Exploring the Functional Logic of Neural Circuits
abstract: Drosophila connectomic datasets provide increasingly comprehensive maps of neuronal morphology and synaptic connectivity, offering an unprecedented opportunity to explore the structural organization of its neural circuits. This calls for designing automated tools to interact with connectomic datasets at scale for efficiently exploring structural features embedded in the vast amounts of data. Yet the central challenge remains the understanding of the functional logic of neural circuits. In order to formulate a connectome-grounded hypothesis for what a circuit computes, it is critical to (i) characterize the objects in the natural environment in which brain circuits operate, and (ii) formulate how brain circuits represent and process the defined objects. To develop and demonstrate a methodology for these requirements, we focus on the Drosophila looming-evoked escape pathway. We modeled the trajectory of looming objects that are on a collision course (direct-hits) or pass by the fly (near-misses): their projected images on the retina can be characterized by the subtended solid angle and center elevation. By analyzing the sub-neuronal structure and retinotopic organization of the looming pathway embedded in connectomic datasets, we devised a pathway abstraction, and mapped each of its structural elements to a processing block to construct an executable circuit model. We demonstrate that this connectome-grounded functional model separates direct-hits from near-misses well before the trajectories can be distinguished based on the subtended solid angle alone. To accelerate the connectomic analysis step, we developed a Python toolset with an agentic, code-free workspace interface called NeuroGraphBench (NGB). NGB provides four composable morphology-analysis primitives and an AI Agent that composes them to interactively respond to natural-language queries aided by visualization on an interactive 3D canvas. Thus, NGB automates tedious and repetitive tasks to enable faster and scalable connectomic exploration, keeping human reasoning, instead of writing code, at the center of an open-ended research inquiry.

title: Linear NeuroPaint: An Efficient Baseline for Cross-Session Neural Alignment and Inpainting
abstract: Large-scale Neuropixels recordings sample many brain areas, but no single experimental session records every area of interest. NeuroPaint, a transformer-based autoencoder, integrates such recordings by aligning area-specific latent dynamics across sessions and "inpainting" activity in unrecorded areas. Could a linear model, which would be computationally efficient and potentially more interpretable, suffice to achieve this? To address this question, we introduce Linear NeuroPaint, a linear variant of NeuroPaint, and evaluate it on two multi-area Neuropixels datasets. Linear NeuroPaint achieves strong predictive performance on recorded areas, however, it is less accurate than nonlinear models at cross-area inpainting, despite extensive hyperparameter optimization. Moreover, its parameters are not readily interpretable: incomplete cross-session alignment leads parameter-defined neuron clusters to exhibit heterogeneous response profiles. Together, these results show that linear transformations are insufficient for cross-session alignment and cross-area prediction. Nevertheless, Linear NeuroPaint provides a computationally efficient baseline for benchmarking multi-session neural models.

title: Subtype-Selective Neuronal Vulnerability and Compensatory Neuroglial Remodeling in Human Cortical Dementia
abstract: Whether the nodal vulnerability in dementia is solely represented by changes in cellular abundance or attrition of cellular transcriptomic landscape attribute to that transition in aging brain is yet to uncover with minutiae. To understand this complication, we have analyzed two snRNA-seq data specific to (I) dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC): A comprehensive study of cellular profiling among cognitively normal and pathological ageing and dementia (AD) brain, (II) occipital cortex (OC) in the context of Nasu-Hakola disease along with a tissue level bulk RNA-seq data corresponds to temporal cortex. We pinpoint cellular subpopulations their proportional changes within the nodal points and their transcriptomic profiling. In DLPFC we observed alteration of mitochondrial and synaptic maintenance program in the pathological manifestation of disease. In OC we noticed depleted upper layer CUX2 neuron, PVALB and SST neurons on the contrary an enrichment of RORB and LAMP5 neurons with compromised metabolic states in the disease context. Glial populations are marked by representation of fibrous astrocyte, neuronal-supporting subpopulations associated with extracellular matrix remodeling programs. Proportional increment of intermediate myelinating oligodendrocyte and a decrease in mature myelinating subpopulation highlighted a compromised myelin repair attempt. In temporal cortex at tissue level we observed transcriptomic landscape adopted a neuroglial phenotypes in dementia brain. Cell-Chat analysis demonstrated a shift in cellular coordination towards glial population from neuron in NHD brain. A single cell-based drug reprofiling approach identified efatutazone and balaglitazone as broad-spectrum candidates for major cell types in occipital cortex, whereas major actionable biological targets belong to CDK subtypes and proteasome subunits. Overall, our findings imply cellular persistence do not necessarily substantiate molecular preservation, also the coexistence of cellular vulnerability alongside selective remodeling features, present a cellular framework on how to cope up with degenerative changes.

title: Continuous amyloid staging complements global amyloid burden in early Alzheimer's disease
authors: For the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
abstract: Introduction: Early Alzheimer's disease (AD) staging remains challenging because clinical categories and global amyloid PET measures provide only coarse characterization of disease progression. We developed a continuous amyloid staging score from regional amyloid PET to complement global amyloid burden. Methods: Using longitudinal florbetapir PET from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we trained an end-to-end deep learning model to directly estimate a continuous amyloid staging score. We evaluated longitudinal consistency, its relationship with global amyloid burden, regional contributors to early-stage variation, and whether the staging score stratified subsequent memory decline among participants matched for baseline global amyloid burden. Cognitive analyses were replicated in A4+LEARN. Results: The staging score better preserved longitudinal visit order than existing amyloid staging approaches. During early disease stages, it captured regional amyloid variation despite relatively stable global amyloid burden. Among participants with similar baseline global amyloid burden, higher staging scores were associated with faster subsequent memory decline in both ADNI and A4+LEARN. Discussion: A continuous amyloid staging score complements global amyloid burden for early AD staging and cognitive risk stratification. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; amyloid PET; disease staging; cognitive decline

title: Simultaneous recordings link intracranial and scalp correlates of somatosensory awareness in humans
abstract: The electrophysiological events underlying the conscious perception of touch in humans remain elusive. Scalp-EEG studies have identified a negative deflection peaking 120-200 ms after stimulus onset, known as the N140. This component, recently reinterpreted as the somatosensory awareness negativity (N140/SAN), has been proposed as a putative marker of tactile awareness, but its underlying neuronal dynamics are still unknown. Intracranial studies have shown that responses to median nerve stimulation include, after an initial phasic activation mainly localized to primary somatosensory cortices, a predominantly insulo-opercular tonic broadband high-frequency activity (BHA; 50-150 Hz) that has been linked to tactile awareness. Yet these scalp and intracranial signatures have never been directly linked. Using simultaneous high-density scalp EEG and intracranial EEG recordings, we show that the N140/SAN is the scalp manifestation of the insulo-opercular local field potential that follows the BHA response to stimulation. By bridging invasive and non-invasive recordings our results identify the neural origins of the N140/SAN and connect scalp and intracranial correlates of somatosensory awareness.

title: Identification of surface colors across environmental illuminations
abstract: When objects are embedded in a complex lighting environment, the illumination they receive depends on their geometric relationship to the environment. We measured performance in an odd-one-out color constancy task, with objects rendered in complex lighting environments. Observers identified the odd object among four objects, with two rendered under each of two lighting environments, sampled from a wide range of object orientations and camera positions. Constancy was high. The presence of a surrounding context increased accuracy. Gloss provided no measurable benefit. We also tested a condition in which the global color impression provided misleading information about the lighting environment, but this impaired performance only slightly. These findings suggest that human color constancy remains robust even under complex lighting environments, contrary to predictions of many simple models of illuminant discounting.

title: An Engineering Explanation of Human Vertical Reaching: Optimal Trajectory Planning of Asymmetric Velocity Profiles in the Vertical Plane via a Softplus-Based Generalized Dynamic Jerk Cost Function.
abstract: The results in this article demonstrate that the central nervous system CNS plans trajectories in the vertical plane by minimizing a Generalized Dynamic Jerk GJerk cost function, which we have proposed as an advancement of the traditional Minimum Jerk cost function. While the traditional Jerk cost function generates smooth trajectories by minimizing the third derivative of joint angle over time, it neglects real dynamic constraints most notably the effect of gravity. According to our engineering interpretation, the arm functions as a constrained manipulator where gravity acts as a non-linear, state-dependent bias; thus, the asymmetry in velocity profiles is not an anomaly but an optimal adaptation to the gravitational field. Consequently, it predicts mathematically symmetrical upward and downward movements, even in contexts where gravitational forces play a decisive role. The proposed GJerk cost function extends the classical framework by incorporating position-dependent dynamic coefficients into the cost function, thereby embedding gravitational effects directly within the planning process. As a result, the generated movements are not only smooth in a mathematical sense but also physically and mechanically consistent with the actual torque and energy demands imposed by the musculoskeletal system. The GJerk cost function reduces angular change in high-gravitational-torque regions because it makes the joint configuration with the highest gravitational torque more expensive within the cost function, prompting the planner to choose a slower and more conservative movement. This does not physically dissipate energy, but it acts as a behavioral damping mechanism, similar to how humans naturally slow down when approaching a high load or potentially dangerous configuration. In this way, the GJerk cost function reduces abrupt changes in joint kinetic energy and prevents sudden jumps in acceleration, ultimately producing a smoother and more stable trajectory that aligns with both biomechanical reality and observed human behavior. Within this framework, upward movements become inherently more costly than downward ones, penalizing configurations that require large torques to counteract gravity. This induces a biomechanically meaningful asymmetry, ensuring the resulting trajectories reflect the body's true mechanical constraints rather than mere geometric smoothness. Our empirical results demonstrate that the GJerk cost function provides a more realistic and physiologically grounded account of motor planning in the vertical plane, linking smoothness optimization with genuine dynamic requirements and offering a closer approximation to biological motor behavior

title: Global statistical constraint and local partner-sensitive inference support dynamic, open-ended verbal coordination
abstract: Effective verbal communication requires individuals to align their communicative intentions through the precise use of utterances, yet how this is achieved in dynamic, open-ended communication remains unclear. Combining predictive deep language models (DLMs) with cognitive computational modeling, we tested a computational division of labor between context-sensitive global constraint on the utterance space and partner-sensitive local adjustment of selection priorities. We formalized local adjustment using an active inference inspired updating rule within a statistical-pragmatic hybrid model. Thirty dyads performed a dynamic, open-ended collaborative word-generation task during functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning. Interlocutors converged in their lexical choices, and lexical alignment was best explained by a hybrid model integrating contextual selection priors with interaction-specific local adjustment among the models tested. This hybrid process formed a dynamic hypothesis landscape comprising a global semantic search region and local selection priorities. Critically, interaction did not simply reduce uncertainty: within individuals, the hypothesis space of global semantic search progressively narrowed while local uncertainty among plausible alternatives increased; between partners, both global hypothesis space and local selection became increasingly aligned, with alignment of local selection priorities most strongly predicting subsequent lexical alignment. The contribution of local adjustment was stronger during precise verbal communication than in the control tasks. Neural analyses further identified correlates of the local adjustment process: temporoparietal and anterior temporal regions supported partner-related inference and semantic prediction error, respectively, and their activity during thinking predicted subsequent inferior frontal activity associated with self-updating during speaking. The participant's own hypothesis landscape was also represented in the left inferior parietal-supramarginal cortex. The main findings generalized across language models and an independent Czech dataset. Together, these findings reveal that alignment in open-ended communication emerges from complementary statistical and pragmatic computations, providing a framework for understanding human and human-AI communication.

title: The Onset of Breathing at Birth Switches Off Regenerative Capacity
abstract: Many mammalian tissues, including the central nervous system (CNS), lose regenerative capacity in adulthood, but when and how this transition is initiated remains unclear. By monitoring mTOR activity, an evolutionarily conserved readout of cellular growth and intrinsic regenerative potential, we found that mTOR signaling declines within minutes after birth in murine CNS neurons and in other organs such as the heart and skeletal muscles. Focusing on retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), we show that this abrupt decline is driven primarily by CO2 exhalation following the onset of breathing after birth. Using real-time in vivo imaging of RGCs during the earliest postnatal period, we further discover that breathing-induced CO2 exhalation rapidly causes intracellular alkalinization, activates an AMPK-family kinase, SNF-related kinase (SNRK), which in turn suppresses mTOR signaling. Importantly, this process remains reversible in adulthood: CO2 inhalation or Snrk deletion restores mTOR activity in RGCs and enables robust regeneration of their axons after injury. Similar CO2 inhalation-induced mTOR reactivation occurs across multiple cell types and organs, suggesting a general mechanism by which breathing-associated CO2/pH signaling shapes the regenerative capacity across life and pointing to a potential CO2-based strategy for promoting tissue regeneration.

title: Brief Trains of Closed-loop TMS Induce Controllable Power in FM-theta Oscillations
abstract: Objective. Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta; 4-8 Hz) oscillations are thought to support cognition. Brief trains of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) can probe these oscillations with high temporal precision but have rarely changed theta power. One possible reason is that prior studies ignored the instantaneous phase of the oscillation, which strongly shapes the cortical response to TMS. We tested whether brief TMS trains triggered at specific FM-theta phases in real time directionally modulate post-train FM-theta power. Approach. Six healthy adults received TMS over dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (Fz) with concurrent electroencephalography during a whole-report working memory task. A beamformer and real-time phase-estimation pipeline triggered four-pulse 6 Hz trains (110% of resting motor threshold) at FM-theta peaks (0 degrees) or troughs (180 degrees), randomized trial by trial. Post-train spectral power was decomposed into total, induced (non-phase-locked) and evoked (phase-locked) components. Main results. Trough-triggered trains transiently increased post-train FM-theta power relative to peak-triggered trains; task performance did not differ. Cluster-based permutation tests showed trough-peak differences in total (4.6-7.1 Hz) and induced (5.0-7.8 Hz) power ~50-440 ms after the train, suggesting amplification of the oscillation . No evoked effect was detected. The total-power effect was robust at the subject level (Cohen's dz = 1.32, p = 0.023). Within-train theta power did not differ between conditions, suggesting a cortical origin. Significance. To our knowledge, this is the first study to lock brief rhythmic TMS trains to the real-time phase of an ongoing oscillation, and to show phase-dependent modulation of FM-theta power after individual trains on timescales relevant to behavior. Open-loop brief-train protocols may have missed such effects by mixing faciliatory and suppressive phases. Phase-locked brief trains offer a precise tool for testing the causal role of oscillations in cognition.

title: Milk-derived extracellular vesicles are functional mediators of postnatal neuroimmune rescue
abstract: Early parental experiences can be translated into biological signals that are transmitted to offspring. These signals influence developmental trajectories to both increase offspring vulnerability following adverse experiences or promote resilience when environments are supported and enriched. Among the potential routes of parental-offspring communication, milk-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) transferred through nursing are particularly interesting because they carry bioactive molecular cargos capable of influencing recipient cells. Previously, we found that milk-derived EV cargo is remodeled by both adverse and positive experiences and that environmental enrichment (EE) can rescue adversity-associated effects, including EV-miRNA cargo changes. Environmental programming of EVs during lactation may therefore have functional consequences on offspring development and adaptability. Here, we tested whether milk-derived EVs from our rat EE model are sufficient to rescue offspring outcomes following maternal immune activation (MIA). Milk-derived EVs isolated from donor EE dams were administered directly to MIA-exposed pups, mitigating MIA-associated reductions in social behavior. EE-EV administration also promoted social behavior in non-MIA exposed male offspring. To investigate microglia as a cellular target, EE-EVs were administered to LPS-activated BV2 microglial cells. EE-EV exposure attenuated LPS-associated transcriptional alterations across inflammatory pathways, including cytokine, chemokine, and NF-B signaling, while modulating genes associated with cellular homeostasis and metabolic responses. Together, these results 1) support milk-derived EVs as a biologically active interface through which environmental experience may be communicated to offspring, and 2) identify microglial transcriptional responses as a potential cellular pathway underlying these effects.

title: Whole-brain receptor markers and hub excitabilities determine acute and long-term outcomes in stroke
abstract: Following a stroke, changes in receptor systems have been observed that may influence the excitability of affected brain regions and drive recovery trajectories. Translating results from animal studies to patients remains a major challenge, and while imaging modalities have provided a wealth of findings, a mechanistic link between local receptor systems and observed imaging data is still missing. To bridge this gap, we built patient-specific digital twins with their own neuromodulatory profiles: we integrated 19 receptor and transporter density maps into a mechanistic whole-brain model, and estimated their influence on cortical excitability for each stroke patient and how these systems subsequently explain recovery trajectories. We found that distinct receptor profiles modulated excitability in perilesional versus non-perilesional tissue. Favourable acute motor outcomes were most strongly explained by increased inhibition mediated by non-perilesional GABA-A receptors, together with enhanced excitability driven by cannabinoid, histaminergic, and noradrenergic systems. For acute language outcomes, we identified receptor signatures that, together with motor findings, formed two cross-domain clusters linking excitability to either better or poorer performance. Remarkably, structurally highly connected hubs played a key role: their acute excitability explained cognitive and language deficits and predicted language recovery at one year. Together, our results establish a mechanistic link between receptor-specific modulation of cortical excitability and behavioural recovery, highlighting potential targets for pharmacological and non-invasive therapeutic interventions.

title: Genome-engineered C. elegans strains with sex-transformed neurons and gut
abstract: The sexual identity of specific tissues can be altered through cell-autonomous manipulation of the sex determination pathway in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Previously described sexually mosaic strains carried multicopy transgenic arrays that are potentially subject to transgene silencing or misexpression artefacts. We used here the CRISPR/Cas9 system to engineer strains in which coding sequences for either a masculinizing agent (FEM-3) or a feminizing agent (intracellular domain of TRA-2) are inserted with a trans-splicing system at the 3 end of endogenous genetic loci that are known to be expressed in either a neuron-specific (rab-3) or gut-specific (elt-2) manner. We validate the tissue-specific sex-transformations induced by these genomic manipulations through expression analysis of known sex-specific genes and through assaying behavioral readouts. These strains may serve the worm community as standard reference tools to study the consequences of tissue-specific sex transformations.

title: Oligodendrocyte ER-phagy Restricts Excessive Myelination by Degrading Sphingolipid Synthases
abstract: Myelination is critical for nervous system function. Numerous signaling pathways have been identified that promote myelin sheath growth, disruption of which can lead to hypomyelination, characterized by a reduction in myelin sheath thickness. However, the negative regulators of myelin sheath expansion remain poorly defined. Here, we identify a cellular brake on central nervous system myelination that restricts myelin sheath thickness during brain development. This brake is mediated by a selective form of autophagy, known as endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-phagy, which degrades the ER and its resident sphingolipid synthases. ER-phagy is highly active in oligodendrocytes during myelin membrane expansion, and its impairment leads to ER accumulation, elevated sphingolipid production, and excessive myelin thickening. Genetic reduction of de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis in the ER rescues the hypermyelination phenotype caused by ER-phagy disruption. In summary, our findings establish ER-phagy as a key regulator of sphingolipid metabolism and reveal a mechanistic link between ER homeostasis and myelin production by oligodendrocytes, providing insight into mechanisms underlying pathological hypermyelination.

title: From sensation to action: distributed mesoscale dynamics in the primate brain
abstract: Perceptual decisions engage distributed brain networks, yet how decision-related signals are organized across and within brain areas remains unclear. Mesoscale functional domains are established in visual cortex, but whether spatially distinct domains organize perceptual decisions across the brain is unknown. Here we used 7-T functional MRI at 1-mm isotropic resolution in two awake macaques performing a contrast-discrimination task to map brain-wide activity during sensation, decision formation and saccadic report. Voxel timecourses separated into three groups with distinct temporal profiles, associated with sensory, decision-related and action-related activity. Their spatial distributions formed a broad progression from visual cortex to parietal, prefrontal and motor regions, while revealing distinct response domains within these regions. Choice-related signals were distributed across sensory, associative, and motor systems before movement, including in visual cortex responses to physically identical stimuli that differed according to the animal's eventual choice. Moreover, within the intraparietal sulcus and other regions, mesoscale domains preferentially responsive to near-threshold conditions carried choice information under uncertainty, whereas domains responsive to high-contrast conditions carried choice information when evidence was strong. These findings reveal that perceptual decisions are organized across the brain through spatially differentiated mesoscale networks whose activity varies with task phase and sensory certainty. This spatial organization provides a framework for investigating how distributed neural signals support flexible choice.

title: Intracranial characterization of gamma in humans in response to auditory gratings
abstract: Activity in the gamma frequency range (>30Hz) serves as a neural hallmark of stimulus encoding across multiple sensory modalities. Based on its distinct properties, this activity could be classified as broadband or narrowband oscillations. Visual stimuli, such as a grating, induce narrowband oscillations, which have shown promise as diagnostic markers for neurological disorders. However, such tasks are discomforting for the subjects. These can be made subject-friendly by swapping the stimulus for an auditory one; however, most auditory stimuli elicit a broadband activity. In search of an ideal candidate to induce auditory narrowband oscillations, we previously recorded responses to auditory gratings in electroencephalography (EEG) recordings (Gulati & Ray, 2024) using a passive listening paradigm. We observed a focal sustained broadband increase in high gamma activity (70-150Hz), which was not selective towards any stimulus attributes. Nevertheless, since EEG represents activity of a large population, it remained unclear whether observed activity represented a broadband increase or comprised multiple narrowband rhythms, and whether it was indeed untuned. To elucidate this, we recorded invasively from the regions on and around the superior temporal gyrus, closer to Heschl's gyrus of seven patients undergoing epilepsy resection surgery. Patients were either under anesthesia or fully awake while we presented auditory gratings through loudspeakers. We found a transient increase in broadband gamma activity (30-100Hz) followed by a sustained suppression of beta rhythm (14-28Hz). This broadband gamma was selective for slower spectro-temporal modulations. Our result compares the responses obtained across different recording scales and corroborates that auditory gratings produce broadband but not narrowband gamma activity.

title: Raf-MEK-ERK signaling mediates FLT3-induced mechanical allodynia and reduced morphine analgesic efficacy in male rodents
abstract: The cytokine FL and its receptor, Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), contribute to chronic pain and to the maladaptive effects of morphine but the intracellular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the contribution of the Raf-MEK-ERK pathway to FLT3dependent nociceptive signaling and to the modulation of morphine analgesia. Using HEK293T cells expressing human or mouse FLT3, primary dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, and rodent models, we examined ERK activation, TRPV1 sensitization, and behavioral responses following FLT3 activation by its ligand, FL. FL induced concentration-dependent ERK phosphorylation through FLT3, while pharmacological inhibition of FLT3, Raf, or MEK reduced this response. In primary DRG neurons, MEK inhibition attenuated FLinduced potentiation of capsaicin-evoked calcium responses, supporting a role for MEK-ERK signaling in TRPV1 sensitization. In vivo, intrathecal FL increased ERK phosphorylation in DRGs and induced mechanical hypersensitivity, both of which were reduced by Raf or MEK inhibition. In FLT3/MOR-expressing cells, morphine potentiated FL-induced ERK activation, an effect reduced by naloxone and abolished by FLT3 inhibition. In rats, MEK inhibition prevented the FL-induced reduction of morphine analgesia and subsequent mechanical hypersensitivity. Together, these findings identify Raf-MEK-ERK signaling as an important downstream pathway linking neuronal FLT3 activation to nociceptor sensitization and impaired morphine analgesic efficacy.

title: Absence of the Earths magnetic field activates stress-related brain circuits in a mammal
abstract: The Earths magnetic field is a constantly available cue for animals with a magnetic sense. While magnetic navigation is best studied in migratory birds, a magnetic sense is also found in some mammals. Among these, it is most thoroughly studied in African mole-rats of the genus Fukomys, subterranean mammals that navigate in kilometre-long dark tunnel systems. Our understanding of the neural pathways involved in magnetoreception remains incomplete. To address this, we here performed an unbiased whole-brain screen for magnetically induced neuronal activity in the mole-rat brain. We set up MoBI-DisC (Mole-rat Brain Imaging with iDISCO and ClearMap), an experimental pipeline that combines global c-Fos immunolabelling, tissue clearing, light-sheet microscopy, and mapping to a novel 3D brain atlas. To identify brain areas involved in magnetosensation, we exposed mole-rats to a changing magnetic field and compared their brain activity to that of control animals exposed to a near-zero magnetic field. Unexpectedly, we found that the near-zero magnetic field exposure activated many brain areas, predominantly those involved in stress and anxiety responses. These included the amygdala, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, the substantia innominata, and the periaqueductal grey. This suggests that magnetic field deprivation acts as a physiological stressor in mole-rats. To test this, we conducted a place-preference test and found that mole-rats avoid entering a zone with a near-zero magnetic field, consistent with the hypothesis that this condition is not neutral for these animals. In summary, we present a novel pipeline for unbiased mapping of neural activity in subterranean mole-rats and uncover evidence of stress and avoidance responses to the absence of an Earth-strength magnetic field.

title: NREM sleep microarchitecture is associated with internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning in early adolescence
abstract: Study Objectives: Sleep disturbances are common in youth with anxiety disorders, yet most prior work relies on subjective measures and does not capture underlying neural processes. We examined whether alterations in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep oscillations are present in children with anxiety disorders and whether these features relate to internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning. Methods: Children aged 9-13 years with diagnosed anxiety disorders (ANX; n = 17) and typically developing non-psychiatric comparison participants (NC; n = 26) completed overnight polysomnography. Slow oscillations (SO) and slow and fast sleep spindles were characterized using validated automated detection algorithms. Participants also completed a pre-sleep emotional processing task, and parents provided standardized measures of youth mental health. Group differences and dimensional associations between NREM oscillations, internalizing symptoms, and behavioral indices of emotional processing were examined. Results: Sleep architecture did not differ between groups. Slow spindle duration was shorter in the ANX group. Across the full sample, shorter slow spindle duration was associated with greater internalizing symptoms, whereas higher SO density was positively associated with internalizing symptoms. Children in the ANX group exhibited greater facial emotional arousal and more frequent look-away behavior during the emotional processing task. Across participants, greater emotional arousal and look-away behavior were associated with shorter spindle duration during subsequent sleep. Conclusions: Specific features of NREM microarchitecture were associated with individual differences in internalizing symptoms and emotional functioning during early adolescence. These findings highlight the potential relevance of NREM oscillations for understanding developmental links between sleep and youth psychopathology.

title: Ultrastructurally planar growth cones during neocortical axon navigation
abstract: Neurons extend axons toward spatially defined but often distant targets to establish brain circuits. Callosal projection neurons exemplify this organization, linking corresponding cortical territories between the two hemispheres. Growing axons rely on growth cones to regulate direction and speed through densely packed tissues. Although growth cone morphology and dynamics have been extensively characterized in cultured neurons and invertebrate models, how growth cones navigate the three-dimensional environment of the developing mammalian brain remains poorly explored. Here, we combined a genetically encoded electron microscopy (EM)-labeling strategy and zero-shot deep-learning-based tracing with high-resolution volume EM to reconstruct growth cones of identified callosal projection neurons in the developing mouse brain. Mediolaterally extending growth cones exhibited a planar, fan-shaped morphology, preferentially expanded along the dorsoventral axis. Filopodia extended from the edges of this plane and aligned predominantly with the same axis but showed no directional bias toward the growing direction. Longitudinal in vivo imaging revealed that increased growth cone complexity associated with filopodial extension coincided with lower instantaneous velocity but preceded accelerated extension. Together, these findings reveal a dorsoventrally oriented planar growth cone architecture in which filopodial extension precedes accelerated axon growth, suggesting a structural constraint that may restrict axon navigation to the callosal plane.

title: Serotonin2A receptors in the medial prefrontal cortex do not drive DOI-induced head-twitch responses in rodents
abstract: Background The head-twitch response (HTR) is a serotonin2A receptor (5-HT2AR) dependent behavioral correlate of serotonergic psychedelic action in rodent models. Although cortical 5-HT2ARs have been implicated in HTRs, the contribution of specific cortical circuits to this behavior remains poorly defined, with a few reports implicating the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) in the generation of HTRs. Results The serotonergic psychedelic, 2,5-dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI), induced head-twitch responses (HTRs) in male and female rats and mice, with sex differences noted only in mice. DOI also increased ear-scratch responses (ESRs), and reduced digging and grooming behaviors only in mice. While the DOI-evoked HTRs and ESRs were absent in 5-HT2AR knock-out (5-HT2AR KO) mice, reduced digging and grooming occurred in both wild-type and 5-HT2AR KO mice. We assessed the role of 5-HT2ARs in the mPFC in regulating DOI-induced HTRs using pharmacological and genetic approaches. Targeted DOI microinfusion into the mPFC did not induce HTRs in rats, in contrast to the robust increase in HTRs noted following systemic DOI administration. Local delivery of the selective 5-HT2AR antagonist, MDL100907, into the mPFC also had no effect on the systemic DOI-evoked increase in HTRs in rats. Experiments capitalizing on genetic strategies to perturb 5-HT2AR expression in the mPFC, indicated that viral restoration of 5-HT2AR expression in mPFC CaMKII-positive excitatory neurons was not sufficient to reinstate DOI-evoked HTRs or ESRs in 5-HT2AR KO mice. Further, conditional 5-HT2AR deletion in CaMKII-positive excitatory neurons in the mPFC did not alter systemic DOI-induced HTRs and ESRs in mice. Conclusions These findings indicate that the serotonergic psychedelic DOI induces species- and sex-specific behavioral effects in rodent models, with a robust 5-HT2AR dependence noted for DOI-evoked HTRs and ESRs. Further, we show that 5-HT2ARs in the mPFC do not appear to contribute to the enhanced HTRs and ESRs elicited by DOI.
