title: A low-adhesion mechanism enables axon growth in the developing brain
abstract: During development, axons grow through complex tissue environments to wire the brain. Axon growth speeds measured in cell culture are incompatible with the distances axons must cover in vivo. Yet how axons achieve the growth speeds required to establish long-range connectivity within a narrow embryonic developmental window, and by what mechanism, remains unknown. Here, using long-term live imaging in brain sections, mouse genetics, molecular and pharmacological perturbations, together with AxoVivo, a newly developed intravital imaging platform that resolves subcellular structures, including growth cones and cytoskeletal dynamics, in living mouse embryos, we show that axons of cortical projection neurons (CPNs) employ a low-adhesion mechanism to grow. Even as growth cones change shape and turn, axons grow an order of magnitude faster than in vitro. The actin motor myosin II controls the growth cone actin cytoskeleton and its morphology but not axon growth itself, which is instead promoted by microtubule stabilisation. Finally, super-resolution shadow imaging (SUSHI) revealed that growth cones do not pull on the surrounding extracellular matrix. Taken together, this low-adhesion mechanism driven by protruding microtubules ensures the rapid growth necessary for long-distance wiring of the developing nervous system.

title: Spoken language comprehension relies on context-dependent neural weighting of syntax and prosody
abstract: Comprehending spoken language requires extracting syntactic structure and meaning from a continuous acoustic signal. Psycholinguistic evidence points to a key role for prosody in this process. However, because interactions between prosody and syntax are typically demonstrated using carefully controlled sentence constructions, it remains unclear whether such interactions constitute a general, default property of spoken language processing. Addressing this question requires naturalistic, broad-coverage data. Here, we combined experimental psycholinguistics with naturalistic neuroscience to investigate the joint neural encoding of syntax and prosody in MEG recordings of 26 participants (19 female) listening to narrative speech. Linguistic annotations revealed that strong prosodic boundaries tend to coincide with syntactic phrase closures, and that the strength of prosodic boundaries scales with the number of phrases closed. Using time-resolved regression with temporal response functions, we modeled how these features relate to delta-band neural activity during continuous speech processing. Our results reveal a bidirectional interaction between syntax and prosody. Prosodic marking modulates the neural processing of syntax, with phrase closures being encoded more strongly when accompanied by strong prosodic boundaries. Conversely, syntactic structure shapes prosodic encoding, such that boundary strength is neurally encoded primarily at points of syntactic phrase closure. These findings demonstrate that syntax and prosody are encoded not independently, but in a context-dependent and mutually constraining manner, highlighting their joint role in guiding structure building during naturalistic spoken language comprehension.

title: Mapping reward processing circuits: the orbitofrontal-nucleus accumbens white matter pathways and their associations to psychopathological traits
abstract: Dysfunctions in reward circuits, including projections from the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) to the nucleus accumbens (NAcc), have been implicated in psychopathology. The OFC is functionally divided into the medial OFC (mOFC), which processes rewards, and the lateral OFC (lOFC), which responds to non-reward or punishment stimuli. We investigated the structural connectivity of the lOFC-NAcc and mOFC-NAcc pathways and their associations with psychopathological traits using tractography-defined ROI analysis. Diffusion-weighted imaging data from 165 participants (aged 22 - 35, 53% male) in the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were analysed using spherical deconvolution tractography. MegaTrack, a novel tool, enabled tract segmentation via a single manual dissection mapped back to native space. Virtual dissection identified four bilateral pathways connecting the lOFC and mOFC to the NAcc, from which fractional anisotropy (FA) was extracted, and an lOFC/mOFC ratio was computed. Psychopathological traits were measured using HCP Achenbach Adult Self-Report scores. The lOFC-NAcc pathway showed positive associations with psychopathology and the mOFC-NAcc pathway negative associations. The lOFC/mOFC ratio emerged as a stronger predictor than individual pathways, with significant associations for depression, somatic problems, anti-social personality traits, and inattention. Effects were lateralized to the left hemisphere. These findings show that the lOFC-NAcc and mOFC-NAcc pathways can be structurally separated with tractography and display opposing correlations with psychopathological traits in a healthy population. Their ratio may index reward-processing dysfunction, and future research should test whether it is sensitive to dysfunction in clinical populations.

title: Mitochondrial NAD+ import gates neuronal resilience to active SARM1
abstract: SARM1 is an inducible NADase that executes pathological axon degeneration, but how NAD+ destruction causes neuronal failure remains unclear. Because SARM1 is predicted to act outside the mitochondrial matrix, cytosolic NAD+ loss has been viewed as the critical lethal lesion. We show that SARM1 activation rapidly depletes cytosolic and mitochondrial NAD+ and collapses ATP in both compartments, revealing early, coupled metabolic failure. Enhancing mitochondrial NAD+ import through SLC25A51, the mitochondrial NAD+ transporter, preserves mitochondrial NAD+, maintains mitochondrial function, and delays axon degeneration and neuronal death despite ongoing SARM1 activity. Unexpectedly, SLC25A51 restores cytosolic NAD+-dependent metabolism, reversing a glycolytic block and increasing NAD+ synthesis during stress. Glycolytic inhibition attenuates protection, identifying cytosolic metabolic recovery as an important component of neuronal resilience. AAV-SLC25A51 improves function in a chronic SARM1-dependent neuropathy model. Thus, mitochondrial NAD+ import gates SARM1-driven degeneration by limiting coupled mitochondrial-cytosolic metabolic failure, presenting a downstream intervention point for axon preservation.

title: A Hypothalamic Pathway for Energy Conservation
abstract: Many animals utilize a survival strategy of hypothermia, inactivity, and a dramatic decrease in their energy metabolism when faced with a shortfall in energy supplies. Mice, for example, show daily torpor that may last several hours to bridge the lack of energy availability in a cold environment. While our recent studies identified a population of neurons in the median preoptic nucleus (MnPO) necessary for fasting-induced torpor regulation, the specific brain circuits that trigger energy conservation in response to food restriction are unknown. We show here that the energy state of the animal is conveyed to preoptic neurons by inputs from the arcuate nucleus (ARC), a region known to be indispensable for driving metabolic and behavioral adaptations to the fasted state. We first found that the activity of ARC neurons expressing Agouti-Related Peptide (ARCAgRP) is required for the generation of fasting-induced torpor. Then, we showed that torpor-active ARCAgRP neurons innervate the preoptic area of the hypothalamus (POA), including the MnPO. Using optogenetic methods, we also found that activating the ARCAgRP-MnPO pathway induces key features of torpor: decreased body temperature, bradycardia, reduction of energy expenditure, and suppression of brown adipose tissue thermogenesis. Remarkably, we also show that inhibition of the ARCAgRP-MnPO brain circuit entirely prevents fasting-induced torpor. Furthermore, we identified that both NPY and GABA are neuromodulators used by ARCAgRP neurons to enable hypothermic responses during starvation. Our studies provide a detailed view of a hypothalamic pathway enabling energy conservation, a survival mechanism in conditions of low energy availability.

title: Newborns modulate and synchronise their Non-Nutritive Sucking behaviour to the temporal structure of sound
abstract: Sensorimotor synchronization, the ability to align motor behaviour with the temporal structure of external stimuli, is thought to emerge gradually during development, but its origins remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether newborns can adapt their sucking behaviour and synchronise it to the temporal structure of auditory stimuli within the first days of life. Forty-one healthy full-term newborns (24-72 hours old) were exposed to two three-minute auditory streams differing in temporal structure: a highly structured stream with a stable temporal pattern and a highly variant stream with greater temporal variability, while their non-nutritive sucking (NNS) was continuously recorded. We assessed changes in NNS frequency and pressure and quantified NNS-sound coupling using magnitude-squared coherence at frequencies distinctive to each auditory stream. Structured stimulation promoted a more organised NNS, with more suck bursts than the variant stream, and increased sucking vigour, with a transiently higher suck peak rate during the first minute relative to the variant stream and greater suck pressure relative to silence. Coherence analyses revealed that coherence was selectively higher at the frequencies distinctive to each auditory stream, both for the structured and the highly variant stimulus. These findings show that, within hours of birth, NNS behaviour can selectively align with stimulus-specific temporal regularities, even when these are weakly predictable and lack a dominant periodicity. This early capacity to extract temporal structure and coordinate motor behaviour may provide a foundation for the subsequent development of sensorimotor synchronisation.

title: Meis2 is required for GABAergic amacrine cell survival in the developing retina.
abstract: Amacrine cells (ACs) are the most diverse neuron in the retina, with more than sixty different subtypes, each contributing to the detection of specific visual features. Despite their importance in visual feature detection, the genetic basis for this diversity is still not well understood. Recent single-cell transcriptomic datasets have identified several potential genes that may regulate cellular diversity, but the underlying mechanisms have not been investigated. For example, the transcription factor Meis2 is selectively expressed in the GABAergic subclass of ACs. In this study, we focused on how Meis2 regulates the development of GABAergic ACs. We hypothesized that Meis2 is required for specification and survival of GABAergic ACs. To test this, we used the Meis2 conditional knockout mouse (Meis2-CKO) where Meis2 was deleted from either the entire retina or specifically from AC precursor cells. The deletion of Meis2 led to a ~60% reduction in total GABAergic ACs in the retina. This loss of GABAergic ACs occurred only after postnatal day 5 (P5), suggesting Meis2 is not required for early specification but may be required for survival. To further investigate cell death and survival, we quantified cleaved caspase-3 positive cells in the retina at several developmental timepoints. In Meis2-CKO mice, we found an increase in cleaved caspase-3 immunolabeling at P5 and P6 timepoints coinciding with the reduction of GABAergic ACs. Further analysis of GABAergic AC subtypes demonstrated a subtype-specific cell death in Meis2-CKO retinas. For example, the total number of dopaminergic (TH) ACs were significantly reduced, whereas starburst (ChAT) ACs remained unchanged. These findings suggest that Meis2 is important for the survival of a subset of GABAergic AC subtypes in the mammalian retina. In addition, Meis2 may control the expression of specific survival factors that prevent apoptosis during developmental cell death in the retina.

title: Outgrowth of Mouse Sensory Neurons is not Mediated by Regeneration Associated Genes in Early Postnatal Stages
abstract: Peripheral neurons exhibit robust regeneration after nerve injury in adulthood; a process linked to the activation of regeneration-associated genes (RAGs). However, the mechanisms underlying nerve regeneration during early postnatal development remain poorly understood. In a previous work, we observed that motoneurons axotomized at early postnatal stages regenerate without overexpressing RAGs, contrasting with the expected RAG activation observed in postnatal day 30 (P30) mice. To determine whether this phenomenon extends to sensory neurones, we investigated two paradigmatic dorsal root ganglia populations: proprioceptive (PV) and nociceptive (TrpV1) neurones, which exhibit distinct regenerative capacities in adult mice. Following sciatic nerve crush injury at P4, P10, and P30, both neuronal subtypes demonstrated robust axonal regeneration across all postnatal stages, with nociceptors exhibiting significantly superior regeneration compared to proprioceptors. Remarkably, no substantial neuronal death was observed at any developmental timepoint. However, RNA sequencing revealed that P4 and P10 sensory neurones failed to upregulate RAGs following injury, whereas P30 neurones exhibited the expected pro-regenerative transcriptional programme. Pathway enrichment analysis confirmed that classical regeneration-associated signalling pathways were activated exclusively in young adults, whilst developmental and inflammatory pathways predominated in early postnatal stages. Using the conditioning lesion paradigm in primary dorsal root ganglia cultures, we demonstrated that only P30 neurones exhibited enhanced neurite outgrowth following conditioning lesion, whilst P4 and P10 neurones showed no conditioning effect or reduced outgrowth, respectively. These findings indicate that early postnatal sensory neurones possess intrinsic growth capacity independent of RAG activation, suggesting fundamentally distinct regenerative mechanisms across developmental stages.

title: Autonomic neurons are intrinsically hyperexcitable in a Friedreich ataxia iPSC model
abstract: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is an inherited multisystem disorder caused by a GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene and consequent frataxin deficiency, causing progressive neurodegeneration and heart disease. Clinical studies have documented autonomic dysfunction in FRDA, including elevated resting heart rate, raised plasma catecholamines and a high burden of urinary, bowel and sexual symptoms. Consistent with this, autopsy studies show degeneration of the cardiac conduction system and its associated ganglia in FRDA. Whether these features are intrinsic to FRDA autonomic neurons has been untestable without a human cellular model. Here, a human model of FRDA autonomic neurons was established by differentiating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from individuals with FRDA and from their CRISPR/Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. FRDA autonomic neurons expressed canonical autonomic lineage markers and retained reduced FXN mRNA and frataxin protein levels. Electrophysiological analysis revealed pronounced hyperexcitability, with an approximately five-fold increase in spike number, shortened interspike intervals, and longer bursts. FRDA autonomic neurons also exhibited increased cell death, elevated mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and a shift from networked to tubular mitochondrial morphology. Bulk RNA sequencing of all three isogenic pairs revealed loss of extracellular matrix programs and activation of stress response pathways. The top differentially expressed gene was MEG3, a maternally imprinted long noncoding RNA, which was consistently upregulated across all three isogenic pairs. MEG3 sits within the imprinted 14q32 DLK1-DIO3 locus, whose maternally expressed noncoding transcripts were co-ordinately de-repressed in FRDA autonomic neurons. Competitive gene-set testing of 43 imprinted genes across 20 domains showed this to be specific to 14q32: no other imprinted domain was co-ordinately altered. Together, these findings establish hyperexcitability of autonomic neurons as a cell autonomous consequence of frataxin deficiency, accompanied by mitochondrial dysfunction. This provides a cellular basis for the increased sympathetic tone observed in clinical studies.

title: Tonotopic mapping in children shows an overrepresentation of high frequencies in autism
abstract: Altered sensitivity to sounds despite normal peripheral hearing is common in neurodevelopmental disorders but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we investigate tonotopic organization in 86 children (6-11 years) with autism spectrum and related neurodevelopmental disorders as well as typically developing (TD) peers, using a child-friendly, passive listening, functional magnetic resonance imaging design. In TD children, tonotopic maps in primary auditory cortex resembled the typical high-low-high frequency gradients previously reported in adults, while children with autism showed an overrepresentation of high frequencies consistent with what has been observed in animal models of autism. Higher frequency tuning further correlated with greater caregiver-reported sound but not touch sensitivities. Importantly, tonotopy is a core organizational feature of auditory cortex that develops early in life and remains relatively stable after the critical period of heightened plasticity ends. Thus, these results suggest that atypical auditory processing in autism may result from early disruption to tonotopic map formation. Longitudinal neuroimaging studies are needed to understand the genetic and environmental causes of altered auditory cortex topology and its long-term consequences for higher-level auditory, language, and social communication development.

title: Recruitment of the local GABAergic population engages complex network interactions in the ventral subiculum
abstract: The ventral subiculum (vSub), a major output node of the hippocampal formation, has been implicated in diverse neurological disorders. Disruption of excitatory-inhibitory balance is a common feature of neurological disorders, with altered GABAergic signaling representing a critical component. More recently, the vSub has gained increasing attention as a component of neural circuits underlying emotional and motivational regulation, through its extensive connections with regions implicated in mental health disorders such as addiction and anxiety. Our previous work in models of alcohol use disorder and comorbid anxiety identified an important role for GABAergic inhibition in regulating vSub excitability, prompting us to investigate the functional consequences of recruiting the broader local GABAergic population. Although previous studies have examined individual interneuron subtypes, the network consequences of activating the global population of local GABAergic neurons remain poorly understood. To address this question, we expressed channelrhodopsin using an mDlx-dependent strategy to target GABAergic neurons in the ventral hippocampus and performed in vivo electrophysiological recordings from vSub neurons in anesthetized rats. Repeated activation of this GABAergic population at 20 Hz, a stimulation frequency commonly used in behavioral optogenetic studies, produced robust suppression of pyramidal neuron firing during stimulation. This direct inhibition was accompanied by network-dependent increases in post-stimulus activity that varied as a function of baseline activity, sex, and trial number. Complementary ex vivo electrophysiological experiments further supported network-dependent effects and revealed short-term synaptic plasticity that evolved across repeated stimulation trials, reflecting contributions from both pre- and postsynaptic mechanisms. Together, these findings demonstrate that recruitment of the broader GABAergic population produces effects extending beyond direct inhibition and can engage dynamic network responses that depend on stimulation history and circuit state. These findings highlight the importance of stimulation frequency, timing, and network context when interpreting the functional consequences of GABAergic circuit manipulation.

title: A neural circuit algorithm for action grammar
abstract: How does the brain generate sequences of discrete elements, such as actions or words, that follow an abstract rule (a grammar)? Motivated by an experiment in which monkeys learned to draw multi-object images according to grammatical rules, we trained a recurrent neural network to generate sequences Am Bn: producing shape A m times, then B n times, or vice versa. Our findings are threefold. First, the network plans the sequence by moving to an initial state encoding m and n along orthogonal directions for upcoming execution. Second, the network repeats each shape by progressing along a shape-specific manifold. Third, transitions from Am to Bn follow parallel trajectories between manifolds across values of n, thus preserving n. Each of these is an experimentally testable prediction. The network generalizes to longer novel sequences by starting further along the same orthogonal directions. These results reveal a neural circuit implementation of a symbolic algorithm for generating rule-based action sequences.

title: Developmental prefrontal myelination shapes inhibitory interneuron function and adult social behavior
abstract: Early-life adversity and abnormal myelination are implicated in psychiatric disorders, but how developmental myelination influences adult social cognition remains unclear. Here, we tested whether disrupting developmental myelination in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) impairs adult social behavior. Using complementary genetic strategies in male mice, we suppressed Myelin Regulatory Factor (Myrf)-dependent myelination locally in the juvenile mPFC or broadly in oligodendrocyte-lineage cells. Both approaches selectively impaired adult social novelty preference while sparing sociability, locomotion, and affective behaviors. Focal prefrontal dysmyelination also reduced social dominance. Spatial transcriptomics revealed coupling between myelin-related genes and parvalbumin (PV) interneuron markers in the healthy mPFC, which was disrupted by developmental hypomyelination. Consistent with this transcriptional alteration, PV interneurons showed reduced high-frequency firing despite preserved intrinsic excitability. In the human prefrontal cortex, MBP-PV expression was correlated in controls but not in individuals with schizophrenia. These findings indicate that developmental prefrontal myelination contributes to PV interneuron maturation and suggest that disrupted oligodendrocyte-interneuron coordination may contribute to impaired social recognition.

title: Differential utilization of PACAP and glutamate in parabrachial neurons shapes pain and stress
abstract: The external parabrachial nucleus (elPBN) contributes to diverse behaviors, including pain and stress. Neurons in this region use glutamatergic and neuropeptidergic signaling, with pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) expressed in a subset of glutamatergic neurons. Deletion of PACAP in elPBN neurons attenuates behavioral responses to stress, but the contribution of PACAP to pain sensitization and of glutamatergic neurotransmission to pain- and stress-related responses remain poorly understood. Here, we show that constitutive loss of PACAP markedly attenuated nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity across heat, pressure, cold and tactile modalities without altering baseline nociception, while also reducing inflammation-induced spontaneous pain-related behavior. Notably, selective deletion of PACAP within elPBN neurons phenocopied the suppression of injury-induced hypersensitivity, but left inflammation- induced pain-related behavior unaffected. Ex vivo optogenetic-assisted circuit mapping showed that activation of PACAP-expressing elPBN terminals elicited glutamatergic transmission onto central amygdala (CeA) PKC{delta}-expressing neurons. Selective deletion of VGluT2 in elPBN neurons reduced nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity but, unlike PACAP deletion, also reduced inflammation-induced pain-related behavior, while leaving stress-induced hypophagia intact. Together, these findings reveal differential requirements for PACAP and glutamatergic neurotransmission within the elPBN across pain- and stress-related behaviors.

title: Impacts of different SETD1A mutations and genetic backgrounds on human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived hippocampal neurons
abstract: Abstract Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) provide a translational platform to interrogate the impact of genetic risk factors for various disorders on human biology. It has been a common practice to engineer premature stop codons to model predicted loss-of-function mutations using isogenic hiPSCs, yet effects of mutation position for the same gene and genetic background have been rarely tested systematically and at multiple levels for comparison to those of patient-specific mutations. Ultra-rare, heterozygous, and predicted loss-of-function mutations in the SETD1A gene, which encodes a H3K4 methyltransferase, are highly penetrant genetic risk factors for schizophrenia. Here, we generated a large panel of isogenic heterozygous SETD1A mutant hiPSC lines, including premature stop-codon mutations in one early exon and one late exon in five genetic backgrounds and two patient-specific mutations, to gain insight into molecular, cellular, and functional changes in a disease-relevant and highly pure population of human hippocampal dentate granule cell-like neurons. Our multi-level analyses showed that different SETD1A mutations lead to divergent molecular and cellular phenotypes related to synapses, but convergent neuronal network deficits, while the genetic background influences gene expression with no substantial effects at cellular and network levels. Mechanistic analysis confirmed the early exon patient mutation as loss-of-function, but revealed that the predicted loss-of-function patient mutation in the late exon is likely gain-of-function. Consequently, while all mutations decreased global H3K4me3 levels, deficits were only partially rescued by inhibiting H3K4 demethylase LSD1 for early exon mutations, but not for late exon mutations. Together, these results suggest that highly penetrant mutations can lead to similar cellular and functional phenotypes across different genetic backgrounds, whereas different premature stop-codon mutations could have contrasting impacts due to distinct mechanisms. Our findings have practical implications for applying genome-editing in hiPSCs to model disorders, highlight the value of modeling patient-specific mutations and testing multiple mutations, and suggest the need for tailored mutation-dependent therapeutic strategies.

title: FMR1 Perturbations Disrupt Sensory Corticostriatal Circuits and Mitochondrial Energetics in Fragile X Syndrome
abstract: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) features sensory, social, and cognitive dysfunction, but how fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) deficiency disrupts sensory corticostriatal circuitry and whether distinct FMR1 perturbations converge on shared cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. We integrated diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in individuals with FXS and Fmr1-knockout (KO) mice with projection-defined calcium recording, bidirectional optogenetic manipulation, primary somatosensory cortex (S1)-targeted expression of three patient-associated FMR1 missense variants, regional transcriptomics, and optical manipulation of mitochondrial energetic state. Individuals with FXS exhibited disrupted sensory corticostriatal structural connectivity, with mouse analyses further localizing abnormalities to S1-striatal pathways. Fmr1 deficiency impaired recruitment of the S1-dorsomedial striatum (DMS) pathway during social interaction, and projection-specific manipulation demonstrated that S1-DMS dysfunction contributes to social and cognitive deficits. Three patient-associated FMR1 variants, I234T, E329G, and R586Q, converged on social behavioral deficits, which were improved by S1-DMS activation. Transcriptomic analyses revealed convergent oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-related mitochondrial remodeling in S1 and DMS across Fmr1 deficiency and variant models. Systemic treatment with the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ attenuated novel-location-recognition, social-interaction, and social-novelty deficits in Fmr1-KO mice. Moreover, mt-EcGAPR-based Mitochondrial OptoEnergetic Activation (Mito-OptoEA) enhanced mitochondrial energetic state in S1 and improved novel-location recognition and sociability in both Fmr1-KO and I234T models. Together, these findings define a sensory corticostriatal circuit-metabolic framework for FXS in which S1-DMS circuit dysfunction and convergent mitochondrial energetic abnormalities contribute to FMR1-related social and cognitive phenotypes.

title: Modulation of the speed of Intrinsic Alpha Frequency (IAF) with tACS modulates variability of illusory speech perception
abstract: Navigating the world requires our brains to constantly process a massive influx of information from the environment. One of the most remarkable yet complex feats the human brain performs daily is speech perception. It is a multifaceted, hierarchical process that relies heavily on the integration of auditory and visual cues, particularly in noisy environments. Neural integration of these streams is hypothesized to depend on temporal mechanisms governed by individual alpha frequency (IAF, 8-12 Hz), which serves as a key neural correlate of the temporal binding window (TBW). While IAF has been linked to multisensory integration, its role in shaping multisensory illusions remains largely unexplored. Here, we tested this directly using transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to modulate occipital activity during multisensory conflict. In a two-day protocol involving 27 healthy participants, resting-state EEG was recorded to determine IAF. On Day 2, participants then performed a multisensory speech task involving congruent (pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and incongruent McGurk stimuli (auditory /pa/, visual /ka/), both at baseline and during tACS applied at IAF and offset frequencies (IAF +/- 2 Hz) over occipital electrodes. While accuracy for congruent syllables remained high across conditions, results revealed that tACS significantly reduced the perception of illusory /ta/ percepts during McGurk trials. Finally, using a phenomenological model based on Kuramoto oscillators, we provided a mechanistic explanation for the percentage of illusory responses observed across participants under the influence of tACS at IAF and offsets. This study highlights the potential for targeted neuromodulatory interventions to influence multisensory processing in clinical or professional settings.

title: Mapping the Trade-Offs That Shape Mammalian Brain Network Architecture
abstract: A brain's wiring must satisfy conflicting pressures, from the outside world (be capable) and from the inside (stay within finite resources). These pressures often have opposing requirements. Prior work studies these trade-offs mostly between 2-3 pressures at a time, and thus cannot say how many pressures shape brain wiring or for which trade-off brains decide. To see all possible trade-offs at once and to uncover the set of most important pressures, we generate 25,000 synthetic brain networks and describe each by 29 network properties. We then place 635 human (ages 6-22) and 224 mammalian (12 taxonomic orders) brain networks in this property space. The space is triangular, and follows three pressures: computational capability, robustness to damage, and metabolic efficiency. No network is optimal at all three, and biological brains cluster in one small niche of this triangle. There, they accept higher metabolic cost to gain both robustness and capability. Development and evolution move brains in the same direction; additionally, human maturation first raises capability, and later optimizes for efficiency. This study underscores the triangular trade-off between metabolic efficiency, computational capacity and robustness, and the narrow region brains occupy in this trade-off triangle, visible only from a multi-property, cross-species perspective.

title: Gradients of local circuit architecture shape stability and information integration across the cortical hierarchy
abstract: The mammalian neocortex is a complex structure with many interacting regions and cell types. Multiple efforts have recently generated large datasets from multiple cortical regions to determine generalizing principles of cortical organization and activity. One such generalizing principle is the concept of a cortical hierarchy - low-dimensional macroscopic gradients of biological properties across cortical areas and a hierarchy of timescales for information processing. Such gradients in properties along a cortical hierarchy may explain how different cortical regions serve different computational roles (i.e. sensory processing versus working memory). We set out to investigate such principles using biologically realistic simulations. Starting from our previously published model of the mouse primary visual cortex (VISp) with updated connectivity reflecting recent large-scale connectomics and synaptic physiology datasets, we generated multiple versions of the cortical circuit model with increased connectivity as measured along the cortical hierarchy. We then measure the resulting neural activity in response to a simulated single-cell photostimulation paradigm and thalamocortical inputs. We found that overall circuit stability increased across the cortical hierarchy, due to both increases in connection density and increases in the relative proportion of SST cells. The results of this study link cortical cell types to population-level activity, generating insight into the function of local circuits across cortex.

title: A representation of the visual environment in the human basolateral amygdala supports learning and choice
abstract: Animals continuously transform sensory inputs into representations that guide behavior. Although the amygdala is a brain structure critical for learning and choice, how natural sensory experience is represented within this circuit remains unknown. Here, we identify a representation of the visual environment in the human basolateral amygdala (BLA) that contains information relevant for learning and choice. Using image-computable encoding models trained on responses to naturalistic videos, we recover a continuous, low-dimensional representation of visual experience in the BLA. The representation generalizes across individuals and independent datasets and prospectively predicts BLA responses to novel visual stimuli generated through closed-loop image synthesis. Signals derived from the representation also informed reinforcement-learning models of human choice. Together, these findings show that the human BLA organizes complex visual experience into a structured representation that can support learning and flexible behavioral responses.

title: Serum Electrolyte Concentrations Are Associated With Motor Nerve Conduction Velocity in Children
abstract: Axonal action potential propagation critically depends on tightly regulated intra and extracellular electrolyte concentrations and acid base homeostasis. Experimental studies have demonstrated that changes in extracellular sodium, potassium, and calcium concentrations alter axonal excitability and conduction properties. However, it remains unknown whether small variations in electrolyte concentrations within the physiological range are associated with measurable changes in nerve conduction velocity in humans. In this study, data from neurologically healthy children who underwent both nerve conduction studies and blood gas analysis were analyzed to investigate the relationship between electrolyte concentrations and median motor nerve conduction velocity. Nerve conduction velocity was significantly negatively correlated with ionized calcium concentration and positively correlated with sodium concentration, whereas no significant correlation was observed for potassium. In an a priori defined multiple linear regression model, ionized calcium, sodium, and bicarbonate remained significantly associated with nerve conduction velocity after correction for multiple testing. These findings indicate that even small variations in electrolyte concentrations within the physiological range are associated with measurable differences in peripheral nerve conduction velocity and suggest an additional contribution of acid base status to nerve conduction.

title: DAP12-deficient microglia adopt a TREM2-independent antigen-presenting state with a glial-to-neuronal cascade in Nasu-Hakola disease
abstract: Nasu-Hakola disease (NHD), a dementia with about 200 cases worldwide, is caused by loss-of-function mutation of TYROBP, encoding DAP12, or its receptor TREM2. TREM2-DAP12 is the switch that converts microglia from a surveillant to a reactive state; what DAP12-deficient microglia become and to what extent they reshape their microenvironment is unknown. We profiled prefrontal cortex and hippocampus from an NHD donor and control by single-nucleus RNA sequencing and mapped the glial changes in situ by spatial transcriptomics. NHD microglia adopted a CIITA-driven, MHC class II-high antigen-presenting state with complement, iron and glycolytic programs and Fc receptors but not the TREM2-dependent lipid program. Astrocytes became pan-reactive and lost metallothionein expression, oligodendrocytes lost mature cells and cholesterol synthesis, and excitatory neurons lost presynaptic and activity programs, consistently between regions and across a published cohort. DAP12 deficiency left microglia in an antigen-presenting state short of the TREM2-dependent arm, accompanied by a glial-to-neuronal cascade.

title: A gut-brain microbial sensing pathway mediates host defense and bacterial clearance
abstract: The digestive tract is a major site of nutrient absorption. It also harbors the densest microbial communities in our body. It is well known that the brain perceives ingested nutrient information through the intestinal epithelium enteroendocrine cell (EEC)-vagal pathway. Little is known about how the brain senses gut bacteria that reside in the intestinal lumen. In this study, we combined novel in vivo EEC calcium imaging, EEC optochemical stimulation, and vagal sensory neuron calcium imaging in the zebrafish model, and revealed that segregated pathways mediated by different EEC and vagal sensory neuron subtypes differentially perceive beneficial nutrient information and harmful irritant pathogenic bacterial information. Our study revealed that a group of EECs that express the nociceptive receptor Transient receptor potential ankyrin A1 (Trpa1) can be activated by the pathogenic bacterium Edwardsiella tarda (E. tarda) or E. tarda-produced irritant metabolites. These Trpa1+EECs do not sense nutrients. Trpa1+EECs, but not other EECs, uniquely and highly express both Serotonin and the neuronal peptide Pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (Pacap). Using pharmaceutical and genetic approaches, our data showed that Pacap synergizes with Serotonin and is required for Trpa1+EEC-induced vagal activation. Stimulating the Trpa1+EEC-vagal sensory pathway potently inhibits a group of vagal motor neurons that innervate visceral organs in the caudal dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (cDMV). However, the same group of cDMV neurons is activated by nutrients. Microbially induced cDMV inhibition enhances liver gluconeogenesis and promotes intestinal neutrophil recruitment. Inhibiting glucose metabolism, disrupting Trpa1+EEC-vagal sensory pathway, or optogenetically activating cDMV neurons in E. tarda colonized zebrafish induces intestinal E. tarda to switch from an aggregated phenotype to a diffused phenotype and hinders E. tarda clearance. Furthermore, our data show that disrupting the Trpa1+EEC-vagal sensory pathway impairs intestinal neutrophil recruitment and hinders survival, suggesting a protective role of the Trpa1+EEC-vagal microbial sensing pathway in pathogen defense. Together, our data revealed that a distinct non-nutrient-sensing Trpa1+EEC-vagal circuit senses gut microbial irritants, coordinating neuronal, metabolic, and immune responses to enhance host defense and pathogen clearance.

title: Human single-neuron correlates of somatosensation
abstract: Understanding the neural correlates of consciousness poses a central challenge in neuroscience, with longstanding debate over which cortical areas underlie subjective sensory perception. In the tactile domain, posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) are candidate cortical substrates for neural correlates of consciousness due to their crucial roles in somatosensory processing. Yet whether and how these regions contribute to conscious tactile perception remains unclear. Here, to address this issue, we leveraged chronic intracortical recordings to simultaneously monitor large ensembles of single neurons in grasp related cortical areas from three participants with tetraplegia while natural vibrotactile stimuli were delivered to a sensate region of the upper limb. We demonstrate that an orchestration of neural activity emerged across the grasp-related parietal-frontal network at near-threshold perception. Within this distributed network, we then focused on PPC and S1. While S1 responses closely tracked the amplitude of the physical stimulus, PPC activity covaried more strongly with awareness and confidence. This single-neuron evidence reveals PPC and S1 have complementary neural codes with PPC transforming physical stimulation into conscious perception whereas S1 is more sensitive to stimulus amplitude.

title: Inflections in adolescent cortical maturation signal psychopathology risk
abstract: Cerebral cortical maturation supports emotional, social, and cognitive development during adolescence1. Neurodevelopmental theories of psychiatric illnesses, which peak in onset around age 182, implicate subtle alterations in adolescent cortical development3. However, mechanistic links between cortical maturation and emergent psychopathology have remained elusive. This gap likely reflects a need for more nuanced understanding of cortical development4, larger, longitudinal samples powered to detect small effects,5 and more uniform image quality control.6 Using 29,482 structural MRI scans from 11,720 adolescents in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we demonstrate reproducible differences in the contour and tempo of maturation across the cortical surface. Regional trajectories are robust to image quality variance and align with increasing functional specialization over time. Thicker cortex in early-maturing sensory regions predicts psychiatric symptoms as early as four years prior to their emergence, a pattern that subsequently spreads to association cortex. Overlap with spatially and temporally organized gene co-expression networks implicates prenatal programming of this sequence of maturation and its links to psychopathology. These findings present a novel, versatile neurodevelopmental framework for cortical maturation during adolescence that sequentially implicates sensory and association cortex in risk for emergent psychiatric symptoms.

title: Plasticity-induced actin polymerization positions endocytic compartments at the bases of stimulated spines
abstract: The endocytic pathway plays key roles in facilitating and regulating synaptic plasticity, but how its components are organized at spines undergoing plasticity is not fully understood. Here we use live-cell imaging and single-particle tracking to examine the localization of endosomes and lysosomes in response to plasticity-inducing stimuli. We find that endosomes and lysosomes are positioned and retained near the bases of stimulated spines after the induction of structural plasticity in a manner dependent on actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft. Spines with endocytic compartments near their bases exhibit greater glutamate receptor turnover and more sustained enlargement after stimulation than spines lacking them. These results suggest that actin polymerization in the dendritic shaft acts as a hub to organize critical cellular machinery at the bases of spines undergoing synaptic plasticity.

title: Ordinal position in auditory sequences is encoded in population dynamics in macaque frontal cortex
abstract: The ability to extract structure from sensory sequences requires tracking not only stimulus identity but also ordinal position within a sequence. How and where ordinal information is represented in the primate brain remains unclear. Here, we recorded activity in populations of single neurons simultaneously from auditory cortex and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex in macaques passively listening to structured auditory sequences. Population-level analyses revealed that frontal cortex activity evolved progressively across the sequence, occupying distinct regions of neural state space for successive ordinal positions. In contrast, auditory cortex population activity reset with each element, producing stereotyped, stimulus-locked trajectories. Consistent with this dissociation, frontal cortex populations robustly decoded ordinal position independently of stimulus identity, whereas auditory cortex showed weak positional decoding despite strong identity representations. Frontal neurons further exhibited longer intrinsic timescales and reduced synchronization to element presentation, supporting integration of information across multiple elements. Together, these findings identify frontal activity as a key substrate for ordinal position encoding during auditory sequence processing, while auditory cortex primarily supports element-specific sensory representations.

title: Disrupting the Right Inferior Frontal Gyrus Increases Social Brain Activity During Emotion Recognition
abstract: Neuroimaging studies have identified a specialised social brain network that supports emotion recognition and social cognition. This network performs a range of functions that include facial expression recognition and inferring the mental states of others. Studies of neuropsychological patients report that damage to the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), the top-down control area in this network, impairs facial expression recognition. To investigate how transient disruption of the right IFG affects the wider social brain we combined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Participants (n=20) were scanned across two sessions while performing a delayed match-to-sample emotion recognition task in which happy or fearful expressions were preceded by a congruent or incongruent word cue. Prior to each scan, thetaburst TMS was delivered over the right IFG or over the vertex control site (session order was balanced across participants). A group whole-brain analysis revealed that TMS to the IFG increased neural activity in multiple regions of the social brain network. These included the bilateral temporal pole, precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). This pattern of results shows that the disruption of top-down control mechanisms localised in the IFG alters the neural processing in remote nodes of the social brain network. Our findings are discussed within the wider context of how we recognise and understand the emotions of other people.

title: Domain-specific and domain-general signatures of dyscalculia in computational models of behavior and parietal cortex
abstract: Developmental dyscalculia is a learning disorder characterized by marked difficulties in numerical cognition, yet its cognitive and neural underpinnings remain debated. Competing accounts attribute dyscalculia either to domain-specific imprecise representations of number or to domain-general deficits in the maintenance and integration of numerical information. Here, we test both accounts in 33 adolescents and young adults with dyscalculia and 33 age- and gender-matched controls (15-23 years) who performed a sequential numerosity comparison task during fMRI. Joint computational modeling of choices and response times allowed us to dissociate perceptual and memory noise from decision variables governing the speed-accuracy tradeoff, while complementary neuroimaging analyses characterized neural number representations and their network embedding. Specifically, we quantified the precision of parietal numerosity tuning with numerical population receptive field (nPRF) modeling and derived individualized functional network maps of the same region using community detection algorithms applied to connectivity patterns. Dyscalculic participants showed greater perceptual and memory noise but also a more cautious response criterion, trading speed for accuracy to compensate for representational imprecision. Neurally, the numerosity model explained less variance in parietal cortex, suggesting less precise numerical representations, and individualized network maps assigned less of this cortex to the dorsal attention network and more to a visual network. Rather than supporting a dichotomy between the two accounts, our findings suggest that dyscalculia reflects both less precise numerical representations in parietal cortex and an altered allocation of this cortex to distributed functional systems.

title: Attention warps visual-semantic representations across the human cerebellum
abstract: Humans effortlessly shift their attention between objects and events in the environment. These attentional shifts modulate the representation of information in many regions of the cerebral cortex, including those that represent visual-semantic information. Based on recent evidence that the cerebellum also represents semantic information, we hypothesized that attention would also shift semantic representations in the cerebellum. To test this hypothesis, we used fMRI to measure brain activity while participants watched naturalistic movie clips and were instructed to attend to either people or vehicles. We used a voxelwise encoding model framework to recover visual-semantic representations in the cerebral cortex and cerebellum under the two conditions, and quantified the direction and magnitude of visual-semantic tuning shifts between conditions. Attention to different semantic categories had a large effect on visual-semantic tuning in the cerebellum. Representations in some regions shifted toward the attended category, and representations in other regions shifted away from the attended category. Within cerebellar regions that best represent visual-semantic information, the tuning shifts were most pronounced in Crus I and II and in lobule VI. Further, the magnitude of attentional tuning shifts was greater in the cerebellum than in the cerebral cortex, particularly for tuning shifts towards the attended category. These differences suggest that attentional modulation in the cerebellum is different than in the cerebral cortex and may not solely be driven by cerebral inputs.

title: An astrocytic AMPAR-dependent parity signal preserves synaptic strength
abstract: Astrocytic processes closely associate with excitatory synapses and express AMPARs, positioning them to sense the same glutamate signals as neurons. Whether a mismatch between neuronal and astrocytic glutamate sensing affects synaptic physiology is unknown. Using AstroHTP, an extension of Drug Acutely Restricted by Tethering (DART) for cell-type-specific pharmacology, we found that acute astrocytic AMPAR inhibition spared neuronal AMPARs and basal transmission yet converted ongoing glutamatergic activity into a remarkably potent form of long-term depression (LTD) in mouse striatal projection neurons (SPNs). Unlike canonical presynaptic LTD, this form of LTD manifests postsynaptically, requires non-ionotropic NMDA receptor signaling, and arises when glutamate transmission occurs without a matching astrocytic signal. Astrocytic glutamate sensing through AMPARs, therefore, acts as a parity signal that verifies transmission and stabilizes active synapses.

title: rpSTS Stimulation Disrupts Shared Neural Responses to Social Content during Naturalistic Viewing
abstract: Shared understanding of common experiences can foster feelings of social closeness and friendship, and help us understand those experiences. Recent work has suggested that patterns of neural activity shared across individuals, especially throughout the default mode network, may underlie shared representations. Here we used repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and functional magnetic resonance imaging during movie watching to show that shared neural patterns to common experiences rely on the encoding of social information from the environment by the right posterior superior temporal sulcus (rpSTS). An encoding model of movie features showed that rTMS selectively degraded social feature encoding in rpSTS, leaving low-level visual encoding in early visual cortex intact. Using natural language processing (NLP)-based analysis, we found that rpSTS stimulation was associated with reduced memory and intersubject pattern similarity across DMN and limbic networks during scenes central to the movie narrative. Projecting scene embeddings onto NLP-based concept axes revealed reductions in memory and neural pattern similarity for scenes conveying helplessness and empathy following rTMS. These findings provide causal evidence that the rpSTS is a key region that encodes shared social information into common neural representations, and suggest that disrupting its input leads DMN representations to become idiosyncratic.

title: A large, comprehensive labeled MRI dataset of the human lateral ventricle choroid plexus
abstract: The choroid plexus (ChP) is a highly vascularized structure located in the brain ventricles that plays important roles in multiple central nervous system functions. ChP enlargement has been implicated in many neuropsychiatric conditions such as multiple sclerosis, depression, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer's disease. However, limitation in the accuracy of the current segmentation tools highlight the need for more reliable methods to quantify ChP volume in healthy and clinical human populations. The shape and size of the ChP vary drastically from person to person, and currently there are no large ChP datasets which allow comprehensive training of segmentation models. Here we introduce DataPlex, a collection of 700 structural MRI brain images where the lateral ventricle ChP has been manually labeled and checked by expert human raters. DataPlex is balanced and representative across a wide range of scanning parameters, demographics, and clinical profiles, and subject-level information will be available for each labeled image. DataPlex will be open source to support the creation of reliable segmentation tools for the human lateral ventricle ChP.

title: ATP1A3 E815K Disrupts Sodium Homeostasis and Excitability in Human Alternating Hemiplegia of Childhood Neurons
abstract: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood (AHC) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder primarily caused by heterozygous de novo mutations in the ATP1A3 gene, which encodes the neuron-specific catalytic 3 subunit of the P-type Na/K-ATPase. Among these, the E815K variant is the second most frequent ATP1A3 mutation in AHC and is associated with the most severe clinical phenotypes, characterized by frequent epileptic and dystonic episodes and profound developmental impairment, making it a key target for mechanistic study. Although E815K was shown to disrupt pump function in heterologous systems and animal models, its impact on human neurons remain poorly understood. To investigate its disease-relevant pathophysiology, we generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from an AHC patient carrying the E815K mutation and differentiated them into mature neurons. Patient-derived neurons displayed normal differentiation and synaptogenesis, with preserved evoked synaptic transmission. However, 3-specific Na/K pump currents were nearly abolished, whereas 1 activity remained intact. This selective dysfunction was associated with a depolarized resting membrane potential, reduced input resistance, and diminished intrinsic excitability. Patient neurons generated fewer action potentials in response to depolarizing current steps, displayed altered firing patterns, and showed significantly decreased voltage-gated sodium current densities, while potassium conductance remained unaffected. Taken together, these results indicate that the ATP1A3 E815K mutation disrupts intracellular sodium homeostasis and consequently modifies the excitability of human neurons. Overall, these findings provide mechanistic insight into the molecular pathophysiology underlying this AHC variant and thereby establish a patient-derived neuronal model which serves as a platform for future drug screening approaches and therapeutic investigation.

title: EARLY-LIFE STRESS INDUCES SEXUALLY DIMORPHIC BRAIN AGING VIA MESOLIMBIC ALTERATIONS AND FRONTO-STRIATAL DYSFUNCTION
abstract: Prenatal stress influences brain development; however, its long-term, region-specific effects on brain aging in males and females remain insufficiently characterized. This study examined the impact of unpredictable mild prenatal stress on behavior, cognition, and maternal care in C57BL/6J mice at middle (12 months) and old (18 months) ages. Stressed dams showed fragmented, unpredictable maternal behaviors, creating a stressful postnatal environment without impairing caregiving capacity. Both male and female offspring were born with lower birth weights and showed rapid postnatal growth, a trajectory associated with central insulin resistance and hippocampal signaling deficits. Sex-specific behavioral differences emerged with age. Middle-aged stressed males exhibited anhedonia, which progressed to hyperactivity, stereotypy, and persistent spatial memory deficits in old age. These outcomes corresponded with accelerated fronto-striatal decline, likely mediated by insulin resistance and increased rigidity of medial prefrontal cortex structures due to diminished local estrogenic activity. In contrast, middle-aged stressed females displayed hypoactivity and reduced anxiety, later developing anhedonia in old age while maintaining hippocampus-dependent memory. In females, this pattern supports a model in which a neuroestrogen - and growth factor-dependent feedback loop transiently preserves hippocampal plasticity but compromises dopaminergic function in reward circuits. This balance may deteriorate with reproductive senescence. Both sexes retained cognitive flexibility, indicating domain-specific rather than global cognitive impairment. These findings demonstrate that excessive prenatal glucocorticoid exposure and unpredictable postnatal care produce a combined hormonal and metabolic insult, resulting in sexually divergent trajectories of brain aging. The results underscore the necessity of incorporating sex as a biological variable in fetal programming research across the lifespan.

title: The anterior insular cortex mediates higher-order threat learning and memory
abstract: Learning about potential threats is indispensable for survival, and its deficits underlie numerous neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain imaging suggests the anterior insular cortex (AIC) as a key neural correlate of threat learning, yet its mechanistic role remains unclear. Leveraging multimodal systems neuroscience approaches, we demonstrate that AIC excitatory neurons, specifically layer 5 pyramidal neurons projecting to the basolateral amygdala, are essential for higher-order threat learning/memory. They are specifically required when a predictor is temporally separated from an aversive event or when the predictive information is embedded within a diffuse context. In contrast, the AIC is dispensable for elementary, temporally contiguous threat learning. Surprisingly, while the AIC promotes memory formation, it also constrains the level of fear expression during retrieval in a context-dependent manner. This bidirectional control is mediated by the recruitment of distinct AIC neuronal ensembles. Together, we identify a novel circuit mechanism for bidirectional regulation of higher-order threat learning/memory.

title: Intracellular accumulation of AAV6 genomes governs microglia reactivity and the inflammatory response in retinal gene therapy
abstract: Adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors possess immense potential for gene therapy applications. However, microglia can mount an immune response against AAV vectors. Yet, microglia are therapeutic targets since they play a driving role in the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. Thus, it is critical to understand the cellular processes driving the microglia-mediated immune response against AAV vectors. To this end, we modelled AAV6 induced inflammation upon retinal gene therapy in minipigs. Upon AAV6 administration, the IBA1+ cells demonstrated a morphological transition to the amoeboid form, indicating microglial reactivity. We also observed the invasion of peripheral immune cells in the retina. To elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms, we transduced human iPSC derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs) in vitro with AAV6 and AAV8 respectively. Only AAV6 transduced iMGLs exhibited morphological features and a transcriptomic signature of microglial reactivity. The magnitude of intracellular AAV6 viral genomes was significantly higher as compared to the AAV8 condition. The elevated levels of intracellular AAV6 genomes induced a DNA damage response in AAV6-transduced iMGLs, which is a key feature of neuroinflammation-linked microglial reactivity. Thus, our work highlights the impact of intracellular viral genome accumulation on microglial reactivity and its implications for retinal gene therapy associated inflammation.

title: A perturbation atlas of mouse neural organoids resolves macroglial reactivity and nominates drivers of degeneration
abstract: Understanding neuro-glial roles in homeostasis and disease requires scalable central nervous system (CNS) models, particularly as macroglia like astrocytes and Muller glia remain challenging to study in slow-developing human systems. Here, we generate and map the cellular diversity of mouse neural organoids spanning multiple brain regions and the retina. Benchmarking transcriptomic maturation against in vivo references captures postnatal neuro-macroglial states within a month. We show that macroglia are highly responsive to inflammatory cues and adopt specific transcriptomic states also found in vivo. Through a single-cell perturbation screen targeting 13 Muller-glia-specific pathways, we map how certain inflammatory cytokines drive degeneration-like stress programs in photoreceptors and distinct reactive states in Muller glia, including an Oncostatin M-driven chaperone-associated state. Mechanistically, we identify gp130-STAT3 signaling as a targetable driver of macroglial reactivity and photoreceptor distress. Together, these single-cell atlases provide a foundation for dissecting cellular crosstalk and neuro-glial pathology in the mature CNS.

title: Neural Dissociation of Cognitive Maps and Graphs in the Human Brain
abstract: Cognitive maps and graphs offer two distinct ways of organizing knowledge: maps arrange items within a spatial layout, whereas graphs thread them together through experiential transitions. However, spatial proximity and experiential contiguity are typically correlated, and content represented in one format can often be transformed into the other, making their neural representations difficult to disentangle. Here, we orthogonally manipulated Euclidean distance, indexing spatial proximity, and shortest-path distance, indexing experiential contiguity, within the same learned environment. Using fMRI and whole-brain searchlight representational similarity analysis, we identified dissociable representations of these two formats in the human brain. Euclidean distance was represented in the intraparietal sulcus, whereas shortest-path distance was represented in the hippocampal/parahippocampal region and in cortical areas that overlapped substantially with scene-selective regions. ROI analyses further supported the specificity of these representations across regions. Together, these findings provide neural evidence for a dissociation between cognitive maps and cognitive graphs.

title: ATP1A3 dysfunction alters excitability and developmental trajectory of human neurons in alternating hemiplegia of childhood
abstract: Pathogenic variants in ATP1A3, encoding the neuronal Na/K-ATPase, are associated with a spectrum of neuro-developmental disorders including alternating hemiplegia of childhood (AHC). ATP1A3 is expressed throughout the cortex during early development, and later becomes enriched in GABAergic neurons. Here, we interrogated the underlying mechanisms and neurophysiological consequences of a recurrent AHC-associated variant (ATP1A3-G947R) in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) derived glutamatergic and GABAergic neu-rons. We found that glutamatergic and GABAergic AHC neurons exhibited smaller ouabain-sensitive pump cur-rents compared to isogenic mutation-corrected control neurons. This impairment of pump function correlated with a depolarized potassium reversal potential, lower intracellular potassium concentration, and depolarized resting membrane potential for both cell types compared to isogenic control neurons. Additionally, using a Na+ sensitive dye, we observed that AHC neurons had a higher basal intracellular Na+ concentration that recovered more slowly following Na+ loading compared to isogenic control neurons. As an additional consequence of impaired pump function and abnormal Na+ dynamics, glutamatergic and GABAergic AHC neurons were more prone to depolarization block. Finally, the time course by which GABA neurotransmission switches from excita-tory to inhibitory was delayed in glutamatergic AHC neurons compared to isogenic controls. Our findings pro-vide evidence that impairment of ATP1A3 function has direct effects on ionic homeostasis, leading to cascading effects on intrinsic neuronal firing and maturation of GABAergic neurotransmission that advance understanding of the pathophysiology of AHC.

title: Hemispheric Complementarity is Associated with Distinct Functional and Structural Brain Profiles
abstract: Hemispheric specialization is thought to follow a principle of complementarity, with homotopic functions such as language and attention lateralizing to opposite hemispheres, yet its consistency across individuals and relevance for cognition remain unclear. Using multimodal neuroimaging and twin-family data from 987 Human Connectome Project participants, we identified three sustained attentional lateralization phenotypes (right, left, bilateral) that were independent of handedness, differed by sex, and tracked broad shifts in brain organization, with bilateral individuals showing stronger intrahemispheric and homotopic connectivity. Examining attention and language revealed three multidomain profiles (crowded, mixed, split) reflecting whether functions colocalize within or are distributed across hemispheres. Mixed organization was linked to higher planum polare myelination, whereas crowded organization showed higher fiber density connectivity across dorsal attention-default network. Both phenotypes were heritable, yet neither predicted cognitive performance. These findings reveal a brain organization in which specialization emerges from flexible, heritable patterns linking function, structural connectivity, and myeloarchitecture.

title: A human CHRNA6 3' UTR variant alters the molecular environment and microRNA engagement of the adolescent VTA without changing Chrna6 transcript abundance
abstract: A single nucleotide polymorphism (rs2304297) in the 3' untranslated region (UTR) of CHRNA6, encoding the alpha6 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit, is associated with adolescent smoking behavior. Humanized rats carrying the 'C' or 'G' allele show sex- and genotype-dependent responses to adolescent nicotine, yet the variant does not alter the protein sequence and the mechanism has remained unknown. We examined the molecular consequences of rs2304297 in vivo in the adolescent ventral tegmental area (VTA). Chrna6 transcript abundance did not differ by genotype, nor did transcript stability or polyadenylation site selection. The variant was instead associated with a transcriptional signature spanning myelin maintenance (Enpp6), lipid metabolism (Retsat), and genomic repair (Polq), and with elevated basal lipid peroxidation in alpha6GG animals. Computational folding predicted greater conformational flexibility of the 'G' allele, and spatial colocalization of Chrna6 with miRNA-365-5p was reduced in alpha6GG animals of both sexes. Coordinated expression of the two transcripts, however, followed a sex-by-genotype pattern, absent in alpha6CC females and alpha6GG males. These same groups showed elevated tyrosine hydroxylase expression and dopaminergic neuron number, and expansion of the Chrna6 co-expression network following nicotine. We propose that rs2304297 acts through two distinct layers: genotype determines spatial engagement of miRNA-365-5p with the transcript, while sex determines whether that engagement produces functional regulation. These findings identify a post-transcriptional mechanism for a non-coding nicotine addiction risk variant and demonstrate that its molecular effect can be uniform while its consequences are not.

title: Cortical projection neurons exhibit early maturation defects and selective degeneration in a mouse model of spinal muscular atrophy
abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is usually considered a lower motor neuron disease; however, growing evidence from both experimental models and clinical studies indicates that SMN deficiency affects the whole CNS, beyond the spinal and brainstem motor system. Here, we investigated the temporal progression and selective vulnerability of cortical projection neurons in the SMN{Delta}7 mouse model at early (P5) and late (P11) symptomatic stages. Combining subtype-specific immunohistochemistry, DiI tracing associated with morphometric reconstruction, and dendritic spine analysis, we identified stage- and subtype-dependent cortical alterations. At P11, corticospinal and infragranular callosal projection neurons were selectively reduced in number and showed marked dendritic remodeling and altered excitatory synaptic organization, whereas corticothalamic neurons and supragranular SATB2-positive populations were comparatively preserved. Notably, cortical abnormalities were already detectable at P5, before overt neuronal loss: indeed, corticospinal neurons exhibited reduced soma size and dendritic complexity, while dendritic spine density remained preserved, but spine morphology was shifted toward immature phenotypes. These early maturation defects persisted during disease progression and preceded the reduction in spine density observed at P11. Together, our findings identify cortical projection neurons as selectively vulnerable to constitutive SMN deficiency and suggest that impaired neuronal and synaptic maturation represents an early feature of cortical pathology preceding subtype-specific neurodegeneration. These results expand the pathophysiological spectrum of SMA beyond lower motor neurons and highlight early brain alterations as a potential component of disease progression.

title: A touch that lingers: synchronized patting strengthens neural tracking of auditory rhythm in newborns
abstract: Rhythmic auditory stimulation in early life rarely occurs in isolation. Caregivers naturally combine singing and speech with rhythmic touch, rocking, and visual cues. Newborns are sensitive to auditory rhythm from birth, yet little is known about how temporally aligned information across sensory modalities shapes the neural encoding of auditory rhythmic structure. Here, we tested whether rhythmic touch can alter how the newborn brain tracks an ongoing auditory signal beyond the period of tactile stimulation. We recorded high-density electroencephalography from full-term newborns (N = 40), 1-3 days after birth, while they were exposed to recorded French lullabies presented either alone or accompanied by gentle patting synchronized with the metrically strong beat. Patting was delivered intermittently, allowing us to compare neural responses to lullabies across conditions, notably during periods without concurrent tactile stimulation. We quantified neural tracking of the lullabies using brain-stimulus coherence and temporal response function modeling. Newborns' neural activity synchronized with the rhythmic structure of the lullabies at frequencies corresponding to both the beat and the metrically accented strong beat. Critically, neural tracking was stronger when the lullabies had been accompanied by synchronized touch than when they were presented alone, and this enhancement persisted during subsequent periods in which no touch was delivered. Although rhythmic touch enhanced tracking in newborns with both weaker and stronger auditory-only tracking, there was a larger gain in those who initially showed weaker auditory tracking. Together, our findings reveal that the newborn brain exploits rhythmic touch to strengthen its encoding of auditory rhythm, and that this benefit outlasts the touch itself. This provides neural evidence that patting an infant in time with a song, a caregiving practice shared across cultures, does more than simply provide a tactile stimulation. It shapes how the newborn brain encodes the song's rhythm.

title: Primate Gaze Behavior Reflects Change of Mind in a Naturalistic Navigation Task
abstract: Revising a decision while acting on it is a fundamental aspect of natural behavior, yet the underlying computations are difficult to track in real time. To explore how such belief updates unfold, we tested whether eye movements reveal a subject's change of mind during a naturalistic navigation task with a binary target choice. Humans and monkeys were required to navigate to one of two goal locations presented either simultaneously or sequentially in a virtual environment where explicit position cues were absent. Our findings reveal that gaze continuously tracks the latent variable, including changes of mind. We found that the target tracking accuracy before the second target is even presented during sequential target trials predicts whether the subject's navigational goal persists (first target choice) or changes (second target choice). These results underscore the importance of gaze in action planning and changes of mind, supporting the hypothesis that eye movements embody not only the current latent variable but also its uncertainty.

abstract: Cryogenic Electron Tomography (cryo-ET) is an emerging experimental technique used to visualize cell structures and macromolecules in their native cellular environment. Accurate segmentation of cell structures in cryo-ET tomograms, such as cell membranes, supports the study of cellular organization and function. However, several inherent limitations in cryo-ET, including the very low signal-to-noise ratio, missing wedge artifacts from limited tilt angles, and other noise artifacts, collectively hinder the reliable identification and delineation of these structures. In this study, we present ETSAM, a two-stage Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2)-based fine-tuned AI method that effectively segments cell membranes in tomograms. It is trained on a diverse dataset comprising 83 experimental tomograms from the CryoET Data Portal (CDP) database and 28 simulated tomograms generated using PolNet. On an independent test set of 17 experimental tomograms for which ground-truth annotations are available, ETSAM outperforms other deep learning based methods by robustly identifying cell membranes with high sensitivity while also maintaining better precision.

abstract: Dynamic remodeling of immune cell-surface glycans reflects cellular state and immune activity. Despite advances in single-cell glyco-profiling, current methods primarily capture pre-existing glycan epitopes, providing limited information on dynamic sialoglycans. Here, we present GlycoStamp-seq, a method to profile nascent sialoglycan dynamics by coupling Ac₄ManNAz-based metabolic glycoengineering with single-cell RNA/TCR sequencing (scRNA/TCR-seq) and scDyna-seq. We apply GlycoStamp-seq by injecting Ac₄ManNAz into oxaliplatin-treated mice with subcutaneous bladder tumors, days before extracting tumor-derived single-cell suspensions for sequencing. Following oxaliplatin treatment, a subset of CD8⁺ T cells in the tumor immune microenvironment exhibits elevated nascent sialoglycan activity, enhanced effector programs, and increased clonal expansion. Furthermore, elevated nascent sialoglycan levels mark antigen-reactive CD8⁺ T cells with increased anti-tumor efficacy in vitro and in vivo. GlycoStamp-seq may thus serve as a versatile platform for profiling nascent sialoglycan dynamics in complex tissues, thereby expanding the single-cell multi-omics toolkit and providing insights into sialoglycan dynamics during therapeutic response.

abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

title: Simple model of neurogliovascular unit activity with noradrenaline leading force
abstract: In this work we present a model of a neuroglivascular unit associated with a neuronal ensemble. We combine calcium dynamics in the astrocyte, the cascade of synthesis of arachidonic acid and its derivatives, as well as the activity of the network of inhibitory and excitatory neurons with changes in local blood flow. We add equations to the model for extracellular neurotransmitters such as GABA, glutamate, and norepinephrine. We show that the resulting model can exhibit different types of behavior, and also shows a significant connection between the functioning of the neural network and its supporting components.
